cases.title: Elective high-risk surgery under competent blood refusal
cases.concise: A competent adult needs elective surgery with a meaningful risk of major bleeding and refuses allogeneic blood transfusion, while accepting evidence-based blood-conservation methods. The hospital must decide whether to proceed and what safety threshold or safeguards should apply.
cases.detailed: A competent adult is considering elective surgery that offers substantial expected benefit but carries a meaningful risk of major blood loss. The patient consistently refuses allogeneic blood transfusion for religious reasons after discussing the risk of severe anemia, disability, and death, but accepts specified blood-conservation techniques and nonblood alternatives. A multidisciplinary team can reduce, but not eliminate, the bleeding risk. Some surgeons are willing to operate under a documented bloodless-management plan; others believe the residual risk may exceed what they can responsibly accept for an elective procedure. Transfer to another experienced center is possible but would delay care. The hospital must decide whether to proceed and what risk threshold or safeguards should govern that decision.

policies.text: Proceed when informed refusal is documented and a patient-specific bloodless plan keeps residual operative risk within the team's defensible professional range
policies.text_detailed: Proceed when the refusal is documented after counselling and a patient-specific bloodless plan keeps residual operative risk within the range the team can defend. The plan names the conservation measures to be used, the point at which the operation would be abandoned, and who decides intraoperatively; if it cannot meet that range, the operation does not proceed under this policy.

policies.text: Proceed only with enhanced safeguards: experienced bloodless team/center, explicit product-by-product preferences, blood-conservation protocol, contingency planning, and documented shared understanding of residual mortality risk
policies.text_detailed: Proceed only with enhanced safeguards in place: an experienced bloodless team or centre, product-by-product preferences recorded in writing, an agreed blood-conservation protocol, contingency planning for major bleeding, and a documented shared understanding of residual mortality risk. A safeguard that cannot be met is a reason to defer rather than to proceed with a weaker version of it.

policies.text: Modify, postpone, or decline the elective procedure when the unavailability of transfusion makes residual risk exceed the clinician/institution's defensible threshold, while actively facilitating alternatives or referral
policies.text_detailed: Modify, postpone or decline the elective procedure when the unavailability of transfusion puts residual risk above the threshold the clinician or institution can defend, stating that threshold and the estimate it was applied to. Declining carries a duty to offer modification, alternative timing or referral to a centre that can meet the plan, arranged rather than suggested.

policies.text: Treat the competent patient's informed refusal as controlling and do not make willingness to receive blood an independent condition of access when the operation otherwise remains professionally acceptable
policies.text_detailed: Treat the competent patient's informed refusal as controlling, and do not make willingness to receive blood an independent condition of access where the operation is otherwise professionally acceptable. Access may still turn on ordinary clinical criteria, but any decision to decline must name a reason that would apply equally to a patient who accepted transfusion.

policies.text: Give the competent patient unusually broad authority to accept personal procedural risk; clinicians should proceed unless the operation falls outside accepted technical standards or imposes material risks on others
policies.text_detailed: Give the competent patient unusually broad authority to accept personal procedural risk: proceed unless the operation falls outside accepted technical standards or imposes material risk on others. Where the patient's own risk is high but the technique is standard, the patient's acceptance settles it, recorded after counselling that states the mortality estimate.

policies.text: Permit an individual clinician to decline participation on professional-integrity grounds even when another competent team would regard the bloodless plan as acceptable, provided nonabandonment/referral duties are met
policies.text_detailed: Permit an individual clinician to decline participation on professional-integrity grounds even where another competent team would accept the bloodless plan, provided the patient is told at once, care continues until transfer, and an alternative clinician or centre is arranged rather than left to the patient to find.

policies.text: Keep the operation available at the patient's own hospital rather than transferring or postponing, so that refusing transfusion does not cost a patient timely access to care others receive locally.
policies.text_detailed: Keep the operation available at the patient's own hospital rather than transferring or postponing, so that refusing transfusion does not cost timely access others receive locally. Where the local capability is genuinely absent, the hospital arranges the transfer, manages the delay clinically, and records what was unavailable and why.

cases.title: Capacity, risk, and supported decision-making
cases.concise: An adult with an acute mental-health episode must decide within about six hours whether to undergo urgent surgery for a serious infection. With simplified explanations, the patient can describe the operation, alternatives and major risks and repeatedly says they want to avoid surgery, but during periods of greater symptoms has difficulty applying the risk of life-threatening deterioration to their own situation. The preference remains consistent, a trusted supporter is available, and further communication support and reassessment can occur without using up the treatment window. For this benchmark, assume the hospital may legally use supported decision-making, a surrogate if capacity is absent, or a temporary protective intervention. The team must decide what process to require before moving away from the patient's own decision.
cases.detailed: An adult experiencing an acute mental-health episode has a serious infection for which the clinical team recommends urgent surgery. The decision can be delayed for about six hours to improve communication and reassess, but a longer delay would materially increase the risk of life-threatening deterioration. Using short explanations and teach-back, the patient accurately describes what the operation involves, the main alternative and the possibility of major complications. The patient consistently says they want to avoid surgery. During periods when symptoms intensify, however, the patient has difficulty applying the possibility of severe deterioration to their own situation and treats a favorable outcome from antibiotics as effectively guaranteed. A trusted supporter chosen by the patient is available and the team can repeat the discussion when symptoms are quieter. For this benchmark, assume the hospital may legally use supported decision-making, a surrogate if capacity is absent, or a temporary protective intervention. The team must decide what support and reassessment must occur before moving away from the patient's own decision.

policies.text: Individualize support to the patient's expressed preferences and reassess during the best available period before transferring authority
policies.text_detailed: Individualise support to the patient's expressed preferences and reassess during the best available period before transferring authority: adjust timing, setting, communication and symptom control first, and record what was tried. Authority transfers only after that support has been attempted and documented.

policies.text: Maximize supported exercise of the person's own will and preferences throughout the available decision window; where the person's will cannot be directly ascertained, use the best interpretation of will and preferences rather than transferring authority through substitute decision-making
policies.text_detailed: Maximise the supported exercise of the person's own will and preferences throughout the decision window, using their preferred communication, chosen supporters and best time of day. Where their will cannot be directly ascertained, act on the best interpretation of it drawn from what they have said and done, rather than transferring authority to a substitute decision-maker.

policies.text: Provide reasonable support, make a decision-specific capacity assessment, and transition to an appropriate surrogate when the relevant capacity remains absent
policies.text_detailed: Provide reasonable support, make a capacity assessment specific to this decision rather than global, and move to an appropriate surrogate only where the relevant capacity remains absent after that support. The assessment records what was assessed, what support was given, and what the person could and could not do.

policies.text: When the treatment window is closing and supported reassessment still shows inability to appreciate a grave consequence, permit a narrowly bounded protective/surrogate decision while continuing to involve the patient
policies.text_detailed: Where the treatment window is closing and supported reassessment still shows an inability to appreciate a grave consequence, permit a protective or surrogate decision bounded to that decision, for that period, while continuing to involve the patient. The bound is stated in advance and revisited when the window changes.

policies.text: If the patient cannot presently decide, use substituted judgment anchored in the person's prior values and stable commitments rather than current welfare maximization
policies.text_detailed: If the patient cannot presently decide, use substituted judgment anchored in their prior values and stable commitments, drawn from recorded statements, documented conversations and their own long-standing choices rather than from a single recent remark or from what those around them prefer.

policies.text: When prior values do not resolve the choice, use a best-interests standard focused on expected benefits, burdens, and preservation of future agency
policies.text_detailed: Where prior values do not resolve the choice, use a best-interests standard focused on expected benefits, burdens and the preservation of future agency, and record which of those considerations decided it so that the reasoning can be revisited when the person's situation changes.

policies.text: If clinically safe, defer the irreversible choice and optimize communication/environment/acute symptoms before deciding that authority must transfer
policies.text_detailed: If it is clinically safe to do so, defer the irreversible choice and optimise communication, environment and acute symptoms before concluding that authority must transfer, setting a review point rather than an open-ended delay.

cases.title: Emergency treatment when wishes are unknown
cases.concise: An unconscious adult arrives with internal bleeding that requires an emergency operation. No advance directive, surrogate or prior refusal is immediately available, and nothing currently suggests that the patient would refuse treatment. A rapid record-and-phone search could plausibly locate a surrogate or prior instruction, but it would consume much of the remaining treatment window. For this benchmark, assume the operation must begin within about ten minutes for a meaningful chance of survival and that delaying through most of that window materially worsens the prognosis. The emergency team must decide whether to begin immediately under presumed consent or spend part of the window searching for reliable evidence of the patient's wishes.
cases.detailed: An unconscious adult arrives with severe internal bleeding after collapsing in public. The emergency team believes an operation is required for a meaningful chance of survival. The patient cannot participate, no family or surrogate is present, the immediately available record contains no advance directive, and the team has no specific evidence that the patient would refuse surgery. Staff could search an external record exchange and call an emergency contact listed on the patient's phone; either might reveal a surrogate or prior instruction, but doing both would consume much of the remaining window. For this benchmark, assume the operation must begin within about ten minutes for a meaningful chance of survival and that delaying through most of that window materially worsens the prognosis. Treatment could be stopped or redirected if reliable wishes are discovered later, but the lost opportunity from a long initial delay cannot be recovered. The team must decide whether to begin immediately under presumed consent or spend part of the window searching for reliable evidence of the patient's wishes.

policies.text: Begin the time-critical lifesaving intervention immediately under presumed consent while searching for prior wishes/surrogates in parallel and redirecting care if reliable contrary wishes emerge
policies.text_detailed: Begin the time-critical lifesaving intervention immediately under presumed consent, while records, registries and surrogates are checked in parallel by someone other than the treating team. If reliable contrary wishes emerge at any point, care is redirected then, not at the next convenient interval.

policies.text: Reserve a short predefined high-yield interval for record/surrogate checks before irreversible treatment, then proceed if no reliable contrary wishes are found
policies.text_detailed: Reserve a short predefined interval for the checks most likely to find prior wishes — the record, an accessible directive, a surrogate already present — before any irreversible treatment step, then proceed if nothing reliable is found. The interval is fixed in advance for the presentation rather than judged case by case under pressure.

policies.text: Begin reversible stabilization immediately but defer the most irreversible treatment step for the maximum clinically tolerable preference-search interval
policies.text_detailed: Begin reversible stabilisation immediately, and defer the most irreversible step for the longest interval the clinical situation tolerates while preferences are sought. The deferral applies only to the irreversible step; everything reversible proceeds.

policies.text: Treat absent contrary evidence as sufficient authorization for immediate emergency treatment; preference search should not consume a clinically meaningful fraction of the rescue window
policies.text_detailed: Treat the absence of contrary evidence as sufficient authorisation for immediate emergency treatment, and do not let the search for preferences consume a clinically meaningful part of the rescue window. Searching continues alongside treatment and changes it if something is found.

policies.text: Give recovery of the patient's prior autonomous wishes priority even at a material reduction in expected rescue benefit when the proposed intervention would be highly invasive/irreversible
policies.text_detailed: Give recovery of the patient's prior autonomous wishes priority even at a material reduction in expected rescue benefit where the proposed intervention is highly invasive or irreversible, stating the reduction accepted and the point at which it becomes too large.

policies.text: Use a proportional search rule: the stronger the reason to suspect a contrary prior wish and the lower the marginal cost of delay, the more search is required; otherwise treat while searching
policies.text_detailed: Scale the search to the case: the stronger the reason to suspect a contrary prior wish and the lower the cost of delay, the more searching is required before proceeding; otherwise treat while searching. What counts as a reason to suspect one — a document, a bracelet, a family member en route — is named in advance.

cases.title: Adolescent confidentiality
cases.concise: A 16-year-old seeks contraception and STI testing and asks the clinic not to disclose the visit or results to a parent. The adolescent understands the care and its risks and benefits. There is no evidence of abuse, exploitation, self-harm or other serious imminent danger, and the clinic can prevent routine portal and billing disclosures. The clinician believes supportive family involvement can sometimes help and can encourage it without making care conditional on disclosure. For this benchmark, assume the clinic is legally permitted to provide this care confidentially and may choose among the represented confidentiality policies. The clinic must decide what rule to apply.
cases.detailed: A 16-year-old attends an adolescent clinic for contraception and STI testing and explicitly asks that the visit, testing and results not be disclosed to a parent. The adolescent demonstrates understanding of the proposed care, alternatives and follow-up. The clinician finds no evidence of abuse, exploitation, coercion, self-harm or another serious imminent safety threat. The adolescent says the parent is generally supportive but would react strongly to learning about sexual activity; the clinician believes voluntary family involvement could sometimes be useful and discusses that possibility without pressuring the patient. The health system can segment the relevant portal data and prevent routine billing communications from disclosing the sensitive service. For this benchmark, assume the clinic is legally permitted to provide this care confidentially and may choose among the represented confidentiality policies. The clinic must decide what rule to apply.

policies.text: Protect confidential access to sensitive care for adolescents who can participate meaningfully, with disclosure limited to defined safety/mandatory-reporting exceptions
policies.text_detailed: Protect confidential access to sensitive care for adolescents who can participate meaningfully in the decision, with disclosure limited to defined safety and mandatory-reporting exceptions. Those exceptions are stated to the adolescent before care, and billing, portal and record routes are configured so that confidentiality is not lost through them.

policies.text: Preserve private clinical time but allow parents broader routine access to sensitive information except where law or a defined clinical reason protects confidentiality
policies.text_detailed: Preserve private clinical time with the adolescent, but allow parents broader routine access to sensitive information except where law or a defined clinical reason protects confidentiality. Which categories are protected is set in advance rather than decided visit by visit.

policies.text: Maintain confidentiality, explain its limits, and actively encourage—but do not compel—developmentally appropriate voluntary parent involvement
policies.text_detailed: Maintain confidentiality, explain its limits at the start of the visit, and actively encourage voluntary parental involvement in a developmentally appropriate way without making care conditional on it. Encouragement is recorded; refusal to involve a parent does not change what is offered.

policies.text: Give the adolescent presumptive control over disclosure for the sensitive service because confidentiality is necessary for access, trust, and developing autonomy
policies.text_detailed: Give the adolescent presumptive control over disclosure for the sensitive service, on the ground that confidentiality is a condition of access, trust and developing autonomy. The presumption yields only to the stated safety exceptions, and the adolescent is told when it has.

policies.text: Give parents a presumptive informational role while the patient is a minor, subject to a strong adolescent confidentiality exception where disclosure threatens welfare, access, or protected agency
policies.text_detailed: Give parents a presumptive informational role while the patient is a minor, subject to a strong adolescent-confidentiality exception where disclosure would threaten the adolescent's welfare, access to care, or protected agency. The exception is applied by the clinician and recorded, not left to the parent's agreement.

policies.text: Use a graduated policy in which confidentiality authority increases with the adolescent's demonstrated understanding and the sensitivity of the service, while parental access increases as safety stakes rise
policies.text_detailed: Use a graduated policy: confidentiality authority increases with the adolescent's demonstrated understanding and with the sensitivity of the service, while parental access increases as safety stakes rise. The gradations are written down in advance so that two clinicians reach the same result for the same adolescent.

cases.title: Family asks clinicians not to disclose a serious diagnosis
cases.concise: A capacitated adult has a newly confirmed serious cancer diagnosis. Before the clinician discusses the result, close family members ask that the diagnosis and prognosis not be told directly because they fear disclosure will destroy hope. The patient has previously welcomed family involvement in routine care but has never said that the family should receive serious information first or decide what the patient is told. Treatment choices requiring informed consent must be made soon. The clinician has not yet asked how the patient wants serious medical information handled. The oncology service must decide what disclosure process to use.
cases.detailed: A capacitated adult has a newly confirmed serious cancer diagnosis and will soon need to choose among treatment options with materially different burdens and expected benefits. Before the clinician discusses the result, close family members ask that the diagnosis and prognosis not be disclosed directly, explaining that they believe the information would cause despair and reduce the patient's willingness to pursue treatment. The patient routinely invites family members into visits and values their help, but has never said that they should receive serious information first, withhold it, or make disclosure decisions on the patient's behalf. The clinician has not yet asked whether the patient prefers full direct information, gradual disclosure, family-mediated communication or delegation of some information to relatives. The oncology service must decide what disclosure process to use before informed treatment decisions are required.

policies.text: Tell the patient the diagnosis and material prognosis directly, involving family to the extent the patient chooses
policies.text_detailed: Tell the patient the diagnosis and material prognosis directly, involving family to whatever extent the patient chooses, and record that choice. Family involvement is arranged at the patient's request rather than assumed from their presence.

policies.text: First elicit the patient's information and family-involvement preferences, then tailor disclosure to those choices
policies.text_detailed: First elicit what the patient wants to know and who they want present, then tailor disclosure to those answers, revisiting them as the illness changes rather than treating the first answer as standing indefinitely.

policies.text: When the patient affirmatively prefers it, route serious information through a chosen family member or relational mediator
policies.text_detailed: Where the patient affirmatively prefers it, route serious information through a family member or other mediator they name, recording the delegation and confirming it still holds before each major disclosure.

policies.text: Use paced/gradual disclosure when the patient wants information but prefers it staged, with a definite route to all information the patient wishes to receive
policies.text_detailed: Where the patient wants information but prefers it staged, disclose gradually on a schedule agreed with them, with a definite route to all the information they wish to receive rather than an open-ended deferral.

policies.text: Temporarily delay selected detail when immediate disclosure would create a narrowly evidenced, serious clinical harm, while preserving the capable patient's ultimate access and decision authority
policies.text_detailed: Temporarily delay selected detail where immediate disclosure would create a narrowly evidenced and serious clinical harm, naming that harm, setting a review date, and preserving the capable patient's ultimate access and decision authority.

policies.text: Honor a family's request for nondisclosure until the clinician has assessed the patient's information preferences, but do not treat the family's request itself as authority for continuing concealment
policies.text_detailed: Honour a family's request for non-disclosure only until the clinician has assessed what the patient wants to know; the request itself is not authority to continue concealment, and the family is told at the outset that this is how it will be handled.

policies.text: Permit family-requested concealment from a capable patient even without patient delegation when relatives reasonably believe disclosure will undermine hope or coping
policies.text_detailed: Permit family-requested concealment from a capable patient without that patient's delegation where relatives reasonably believe disclosure would undermine hope or coping, recording the belief, its basis, and the point at which concealment ends.

cases.title: Disclosure of a consequential medical error
cases.concise: A hospitalized patient received an excessive medication dose because of a known infusion-pump programming error and developed severe hypotension before the error was recognized and corrected. The patient is now stable, but clinicians do not yet know whether a new kidney abnormality will resolve or whether the error will have lasting effects. The programming error itself is established; the event investigation has not yet determined all contributing causes or preventability at the system level. The hospital must decide what to disclose immediately, including responsibility and apology, and what should be identified as uncertain and updated after investigation.
cases.detailed: A hospitalized patient received an excessive medication dose after a clinician entered the wrong infusion-pump setting. The patient developed severe hypotension for approximately 30 minutes before the discrepancy was recognized, the infusion was stopped and supportive treatment restored stable blood pressure. A new kidney abnormality is being monitored, but clinicians do not yet know whether it is transient, whether the hypotension caused it, or whether there will be lasting effects. The incorrect programming and resulting overdose are established facts. A formal investigation has begun to determine why normal checking processes did not prevent the error and whether additional system factors contributed. The hospital must decide what to disclose immediately, including the known error, possible consequences, responsibility and apology, and what should be explicitly labeled uncertain pending follow-up investigation.

policies.text: Disclose the known error promptly, explain known consequences and uncertainty, apologize, describe current care, and commit to scheduled updates as investigation continues
policies.text_detailed: Disclose the known error promptly: what happened, its known consequences, what remains uncertain, an apology, the care now being given, and a commitment to scheduled updates as the investigation continues. The updates happen on the stated dates whether or not there is new information.

policies.text: Disclose the occurrence and known facts promptly but defer claims about preventability, individual responsibility, and long-term consequence until those facts are established
policies.text_detailed: Disclose the occurrence and the established facts promptly, and defer claims about preventability, individual responsibility and long-term consequence until those are established, saying explicitly which of the three is being deferred and when it will be answered.

policies.text: Disclose the event and investigation promptly but withhold an apology/admission of responsibility until causation and institutional responsibility are confirmed
policies.text_detailed: Disclose the event and the fact of an investigation promptly, and withhold an apology or admission of responsibility until causation and institutional responsibility are confirmed, while stating plainly that the delay concerns responsibility rather than the facts of what happened.

policies.text: Provide the fullest current causal account, including clearly labeled preliminary hypotheses, so the patient can participate immediately in decisions about follow-up and accountability
policies.text_detailed: Give the fullest current causal account, including preliminary hypotheses clearly labelled as such, so that the patient can take part immediately in decisions about follow-up and accountability. Each hypothesis is revisited in writing when the investigation settles it.

policies.text: Delay substantive disclosure until the internal investigation can provide an accurate consolidated account, unless immediate information is needed for the patient's care
policies.text_detailed: Delay substantive disclosure until the internal investigation can give an accurate consolidated account, unless information is needed sooner for the patient's care, with a stated maximum period and an interim notification that an investigation is under way.

policies.text: Separate clinical disclosure from compensation/accountability: disclose promptly, then use an independent resolution process for preventability, apology, and compensation once facts mature
policies.text_detailed: Separate the clinical disclosure from accountability: disclose promptly and fully, then route preventability, apology and compensation through an independent process once the facts have matured, telling the patient at the outset which route handles what.

cases.title: Conscientious objection and referral for lawful abortion
cases.concise: A patient requests a lawful abortion from a clinician who has a longstanding conscientious objection to providing abortions and also believes that making a direct referral would make the clinician complicit. Another qualified provider is available. For this benchmark, assume a direct referral or warm transfer can secure care within about two days, while requiring the patient to locate a provider without facilitation is likely to add roughly a week and may narrow available procedural options, although it is not expected to create an immediate medical emergency. The health system must decide what advance disclosure, unbiased information, referral or other access duties to require of the objecting clinician.
cases.detailed: A patient seeking a lawful abortion is seen by a clinician who has a longstanding, previously disclosed conscientious objection to performing abortions. The clinician is willing to explain that abortion is a lawful option and to transfer records if the patient independently identifies another service, but believes making a direct referral or arranging the appointment would constitute moral complicity. Another qualified provider in the region is accepting patients. For this benchmark, assume a direct referral or warm transfer can secure care within about two days, while requiring the patient to find care without facilitation is likely to add roughly a week and may narrow available procedural options, although the delay is not expected to create an immediate medical emergency. The institution can reassign care and has authority to set referral rules. It must decide what advance disclosure, unbiased information, referral or other access duties to require of the objecting clinician.

policies.text: Allow conscientious refusal to provide the service, but require accurate information, advance notice, and timely direct referral to a willing provider
policies.text_detailed: Allow conscientious refusal to provide the service, subject to accurate information, notice given early enough to preserve timing, and a direct referral to a willing provider that the objecting clinician arranges rather than describes.

policies.text: Allow refusal of both provision and personal referral when referral is understood as moral complicity, but require the institution to supply an immediate neutral access pathway that does not shift navigation burden to the patient
policies.text_detailed: Allow refusal of both provision and personal referral where the clinician understands referral as complicity, on condition that the institution supplies an immediate neutral access route — a named service, contactable at once — so that no navigation burden falls on the patient.

policies.text: Permit nonfacilitation so long as the clinician gives accurate neutral information and the patient can obtain timely alternative care through a transparent institutional process
policies.text_detailed: Permit non-facilitation provided the clinician gives accurate neutral information and the patient can obtain timely alternative care through a transparent institutional process, with timeliness defined against the clinical window rather than against convenience.

policies.text: Require the objecting clinician to provide or directly facilitate care when refusal would cause material clinical harm or timely alternative access is unavailable
policies.text_detailed: Require the objecting clinician to provide or directly facilitate care where refusal would cause material clinical harm or where timely alternative access is unavailable, with the threshold defined in advance and assessed at the time of the request rather than afterwards.

policies.text: Treat provision of lawful standard reproductive care as a professional-role obligation that should not be defeasible by individual conscience in patient-facing practice
policies.text_detailed: Treat provision of lawful standard reproductive care as an obligation of the professional role that individual conscience does not defeat in patient-facing practice, while leaving conscience its ordinary scope in choosing a field of practice.

policies.text: Give conscience strong protection, including refusal to refer, provided the institution rather than the patient bears responsibility for maintaining equivalent timely access
policies.text_detailed: Give conscience strong protection, including refusal to refer, provided the institution rather than the patient carries responsibility for equivalent timely access, and provided that access is demonstrated in practice rather than asserted in policy.

policies.text: Tell the patient at first contact who will provide the service and by when, so that a clinician's objection is never left as the patient's problem to solve.
policies.text_detailed: Tell the patient at first contact who will provide the service and by when, so that a clinician's objection is never left as the patient's problem to solve. The name and the date are recorded, and the institution follows up if the appointment does not happen.

cases.title: Confidentiality versus serious preventable harm to an identifiable third party
cases.concise: During outpatient treatment, a patient tells a mental-health clinician about a concrete plan to seriously injure an identifiable former partner, has access to the means described, and refuses voluntary warning or safety planning. After assessment, the clinician judges serious physical harm to that person reasonably probable rather than merely possible. A limited disclosure to people able to reduce the risk could materially improve safety. For this benchmark, assume disclosure is legally permitted but not automatically required in these circumstances and that the clinician may choose among the represented policies. The service must decide whether confidentiality should be maintained, whether targeted disclosure should occur, and what threshold and limits should govern it.
cases.detailed: During outpatient treatment, a patient describes a specific plan to seriously injure an identifiable former partner, identifies when the confrontation is intended to occur, and has access to the means described. The clinician conducts a structured risk assessment and, based on the specificity, means and recent escalation, judges serious physical harm to the former partner reasonably probable rather than merely possible. The patient refuses to contact the person, involve a trusted supporter or participate in another voluntary safety plan. A limited disclosure to the intended person and/or an appropriate protective service could materially reduce risk, but broader disclosure could damage privacy and the therapeutic relationship. For this benchmark, assume disclosure is legally permitted but not automatically required and that the clinician may choose among the represented policies. The service must decide what confidentiality rule and disclosure threshold should apply.

policies.text: Disclose the minimum necessary information to people able to mitigate the serious threat once the defined probability/severity/identifiability threshold is met
policies.text_detailed: Disclose the minimum information necessary to those able to reduce the threat, once the defined probability, severity and identifiability threshold is met. The threshold is written down in advance, the disclosure is limited to what those recipients need to act, and what was said to whom is recorded.

policies.text: First pursue voluntary warning, safety planning, treatment intensification, or other collaborative mitigation; breach confidentiality only if those measures fail or time does not permit them
policies.text_detailed: Pursue voluntary warning, safety planning, treatment intensification or other collaborative steps first, and breach confidentiality only where those fail or the time available does not allow them. What was attempted, and why it was insufficient, is recorded before any disclosure.

policies.text: Maintain confidentiality unless the threat is imminent or highly certain, because overprediction and broad warning duties can damage trust and treatment
policies.text_detailed: Maintain confidentiality unless the threat is imminent or highly certain, on the ground that over-prediction and broad warning duties damage the trust and treatment that reduce risk in the first place. Uncertainty is resolved in favour of continued treatment rather than disclosure.

policies.text: Warn the identifiable potential victim directly when doing so is the most effective minimum-necessary protective action
policies.text_detailed: Warn the identifiable person directly where that is the most effective minimum-necessary protective step, telling them what they need to protect themselves and no more, and telling the patient that the warning has been given unless doing so would itself increase the danger.

policies.text: Notify an appropriate protective authority/clinical crisis pathway rather than the potential victim directly unless direct warning is necessary
policies.text_detailed: Notify a protective authority or clinical crisis pathway rather than the person at risk, unless direct warning is necessary because no pathway can act in time. The referral names the specific concern rather than the diagnosis, and the patient is told it has been made.

policies.text: Preserve confidentiality and intensify treatment/containment when risk remains materially uncertain, reserving disclosure for a higher evidentiary threshold
policies.text_detailed: Preserve confidentiality and intensify treatment or containment while the risk remains materially uncertain, reserving disclosure for a higher evidentiary threshold that is stated in advance and reviewed at defined intervals rather than left open.

policies.text: State at the start of care exactly what would be disclosed and to whom, and hold any disclosure to that stated limit, so people can seek help without learning the rules afterwards.
policies.text_detailed: State at the start of care exactly what would be disclosed and to whom, and hold any disclosure to that stated limit, so that people can seek help without learning the rules afterwards. The statement is given in writing and repeated when the treatment changes.

cases.title: Requested CPR judged medically non-beneficial / unreasonable
cases.concise: An adult with advanced progressive disease is in the ICU and lacks decision-making capacity. The surrogate asks that CPR be attempted if cardiac arrest occurs, citing the patient's earlier general request to “keep fighting.” For this benchmark, assume that if arrest occurs, CPR has less than a 1% chance of survival to hospital discharge with enough recovery to leave the ICU and cannot reverse the underlying terminal disease; it would predictably cause substantial physical injury. The clinical team believes CPR cannot achieve the agreed goal of recovery to leave intensive care. The surrogate understands these facts but continues to request CPR. The hospital must decide what process should govern whether CPR is offered.
cases.detailed: An adult with advanced progressive disease has developed multiorgan failure in the ICU and no longer has decision-making capacity. Before this illness the patient made a general statement to family members to “keep fighting,” but left no specific instruction about CPR in a terminal condition. The surrogate asks that full CPR be attempted if cardiac arrest occurs. For this benchmark, assume that CPR would have less than a 1% chance of survival to hospital discharge with enough recovery to leave the ICU, cannot reverse the underlying terminal disease, and would predictably cause substantial physical injury. The team and surrogate agree that the relevant treatment goal is recovery sufficient to leave intensive care; the disagreement is whether CPR should still be attempted despite the probability and burdens stated. The surrogate has received a clear recommendation against CPR and understands the prognosis but continues to request it. The hospital must decide what fair process should govern whether CPR is offered.

policies.text: Do not offer or provide CPR when it falls outside medically reasonable options; explain the judgment and use a fair conflict-resolution/second-opinion process
policies.text_detailed: Do not offer or provide CPR where it falls outside medically reasonable options, explain the judgment and its basis to the surrogate, and route disagreement through a fair conflict-resolution process with a second opinion. The judgment is recorded with the prognosis it rests on.

policies.text: Make a strong recommendation against CPR and use informed nondissent: explain that clinicians will write a DNR order unless the patient/surrogate objects, then escalate disagreement through fair process
policies.text_detailed: Make a strong recommendation against CPR and use informed non-dissent: explain that a DNR order will be written unless the patient or surrogate objects, allow a stated period to object, and escalate any objection through fair process rather than treating silence as agreement.

policies.text: Continue to offer CPR as an option when there remains any nonzero prospect of the outcome the patient values, allowing the informed patient/surrogate to decide after burdens and prognosis are explained
policies.text_detailed: Continue to offer CPR while any non-zero prospect of the outcome the patient values remains, and let the informed patient or surrogate decide once burdens and prognosis have been explained in terms of what recovery would look like rather than survival alone.

policies.text: Maintain full-code status temporarily while a second opinion, ethics consultation, and structured goals-of-care process test whether disagreement reflects prognosis misunderstanding or a genuine value conflict
policies.text_detailed: Maintain full-code status temporarily while a second opinion, ethics consultation and a structured goals-of-care conversation establish whether the disagreement is about prognosis or about values, with a stated period after which the question is decided rather than left open.

policies.text: Permit unilateral nonoffer when the probability of meaningful survival is extremely low and CPR cannot reverse the terminal process, because professional integrity and nonmaleficence set limits on requested intervention
policies.text_detailed: Permit unilateral non-offer where the probability of meaningful survival is extremely low and CPR cannot reverse the underlying process, on the ground that professional integrity and non-maleficence limit what may be demanded. The threshold is institutional and stated, not set by the individual clinician at the bedside.

policies.text: Give a capable patient's prior specific CPR request or a surrogate's substituted judgment presumptive priority unless CPR is physiologically incapable of achieving circulation at all
policies.text_detailed: Give a capable patient's prior specific request for CPR, or a surrogate's substituted judgment, presumptive priority unless CPR could not restore circulation at all. Physiological futility is the only defeater, and it is documented as such.

policies.text: Use a proportional rule: as expected benefit approaches zero and burdens rise, clinician authority to withhold increases; where benefit remains uncertain, shared decision authority remains stronger
policies.text_detailed: Scale clinician authority to the expected benefit: as benefit approaches zero and burdens rise, authority to withhold increases; where benefit remains genuinely uncertain, the decision stays shared. The point at which authority shifts is stated in advance rather than asserted afterwards.

policies.text: Keep the surrogate's request in force until a documented conversation about what CPR would and would not achieve for this patient has happened, and record the family's view in the chart when the team decides otherwise.
policies.text_detailed: Keep the surrogate's request in force until a documented conversation about what CPR would and would not achieve for this patient has taken place, and record the family's view in the chart where the team decides otherwise, so that the disagreement is visible in the record.

cases.title: Family member versus qualified interpreter for consequential consent
cases.concise: A competent adult with limited English proficiency must consent to a high-stakes procedure with material risks and alternatives. A qualified in-person interpreter is immediately available at no cost, but the patient prefers an adult family member who speaks both languages and has helped in prior medical visits. There is no evidence of coercion, abuse or conflict of interest. For this benchmark, assume the hospital must offer qualified interpretation and the patient may decline it, but the hospital may set additional safeguards for consequential consent. The service must decide whether family interpretation alone is acceptable, whether a professional interpreter must participate, or whether a dual approach should be used.
cases.detailed: A competent adult with limited English proficiency is considering a procedure with material risks, alternatives and possible long-term consequences. A qualified in-person medical interpreter who speaks the patient's preferred dialect is immediately available at no cost. The patient nevertheless asks that an adult family member interpret because the relative is trusted, understands the patient's values and has helped during previous visits. The relative is fluent conversationally but has no interpreter credential. The clinician finds no evidence of coercion, abuse, financial conflict or an effort to hide information. For this benchmark, assume the hospital must offer qualified interpretation and the patient may decline it, but the hospital may require additional safeguards for consequential consent. The service must decide whether family interpretation alone is acceptable, whether a professional interpreter must participate, or whether a dual approach should be used.

policies.text: Allow the patient's chosen adult family member to interpret after a qualified interpreter is offered, no conflict is found, and understanding is verified
policies.text_detailed: Allow the patient's chosen adult family member to interpret once a qualified interpreter has been offered and declined, no conflict of interest is apparent, and the clinician has verified understanding by asking the patient to state the plan back. All three steps are recorded.

policies.text: Use a qualified medical interpreter for material consent while allowing the chosen family member to remain for relational/decisional support
policies.text_detailed: Use a qualified medical interpreter for the material parts of consent, while the chosen family member remains present for support. The division is explained to the patient in advance so that the family member's presence is not mistaken for their exclusion.

policies.text: Require qualified interpretation to remain part of the high-stakes consent discussion; family may support but not replace it
policies.text_detailed: Require qualified interpretation throughout the high-stakes consent discussion; family may support but not replace it, including where the family member is fluent and willing, because the record must show that the words consented to were accurately conveyed.

policies.text: Permit family interpretation after a private, documented request with qualified interpreter present and clinician finding of appropriateness
policies.text_detailed: Permit family interpretation only after a private request made without the family member present, documented, with a qualified interpreter available and a clinician finding that the arrangement is appropriate for this decision.

policies.text: Require qualified interpretation because informed consent and equitable language access require reliable comprehension
policies.text_detailed: Require qualified interpretation, on the ground that informed consent and equitable language access both depend on reliable comprehension, and that the burden of arranging it falls on the service rather than on the patient's family.

policies.text: Respect the competent patient's choice of a trusted adult family interpreter after independent coercion/conflict screening and verification of understanding
policies.text_detailed: Respect the competent patient's choice of a trusted adult family interpreter, after independent screening for coercion and conflict conducted without that family member present, and after the clinician has verified understanding directly.

cases.title: Expanded access to an investigational intervention
cases.concise: A 46-year-old adult with metastatic cancer has progressed after all standard therapies. A phase 1/early phase 2 investigational drug targeting the patient’s tumor alteration has shown acceptable short-term safety and a preliminary response signal, but its efficacy remains uncertain and it is not approved. The patient cannot enter the ongoing trial because no recruiting site is accessible and the sponsor confirms that trial enrollment is not otherwise available. The oncologist believes there is a plausible chance of benefit and no comparable satisfactory alternative. The manufacturer can supply an individual course without reducing drug already allocated to enrolled trial participants, but doing so requires additional staff, monitoring, regulatory and manufacturing work. The patient understands the uncertainty and requests treatment. The institution and manufacturer must decide what policy should govern whether expanded access is pursued.
cases.detailed: A 46-year-old adult with metastatic solid-tumor cancer has received and progressed through all standard therapies appropriate to the disease. Molecular testing identifies an alteration targeted by an investigational drug now in an early efficacy trial. Completed phase 1 data provide a clinically usable safety picture and early trial data show a response signal in a small number of patients with similar tumors, but the evidence is too limited to establish effectiveness or predict this patient’s outcome. The patient is medically fit enough to receive the drug and has no comparable satisfactory approved therapy. The nearest recruiting trial site is not accessible to the patient and the sponsor confirms that no alternative enrollment pathway is available. The treating oncologist judges that potential benefit could justify the known and unknown risks, and the patient demonstrates understanding that treatment may not help and may cause serious unexpected toxicity. The manufacturer has enough product to supply this patient without taking drug already allocated to enrolled trial participants, but each non-trial use requires additional manufacturing release, monitoring, regulatory documentation and staff effort. The patient asks the oncologist and manufacturer to pursue individual-patient expanded access. The institution and manufacturer must decide what policy should govern such requests.

policies.text: Pursue individual expanded access when regulatory criteria are met, the patient understands uncertainty, potential benefit plausibly justifies risk, and access will not materially interfere with trials or development
policies.text_detailed: Pursue individual expanded access where regulatory criteria are met, the patient understands the uncertainty, the potential benefit plausibly justifies the risk, and access will not materially interfere with trials or development. Each of those four is assessed and recorded before the request is made.

policies.text: Require independent institutional/manufacturer review before access, including evidence threshold, safety monitoring, supply impact, and a plan for reporting outcomes
policies.text_detailed: Require independent institutional or manufacturer review before access, covering the evidence threshold, safety monitoring, the effect on supply, and a plan for reporting the outcome, with the review completed within a stated period so that the process does not become the refusal.

policies.text: Decline individual access when evidence is too immature or the request would materially compromise a fair development program, even if the patient has no satisfactory alternative
policies.text_detailed: Decline individual access where the evidence is too immature or the request would materially compromise a fair development programme, even where the patient has no satisfactory alternative, stating which of the two grounds applies and what would change it.

policies.text: Give strong priority to the identifiable patient's rescue interest once risk is tolerable, even when efficacy is highly uncertain and population-level evidence generation would be cleaner without access
policies.text_detailed: Give strong priority to the identifiable patient's rescue interest once risk is tolerable, even where efficacy is highly uncertain and evidence generation would be cleaner without access, provided the patient is told plainly that the intervention may not work.

policies.text: Protect fair access by using transparent, consistent eligibility and allocation criteria rather than ad hoc influence, publicity, wealth, or clinician advocacy
policies.text_detailed: Protect fair access through transparent and consistently applied eligibility and allocation criteria, rather than through publicity, wealth or clinician advocacy. The criteria are published, and departures from them are recorded and reviewed.

policies.text: Restrict use to trials except in exceptionally high-evidence or near-certain rescue circumstances, because premature individual access can undermine collective knowledge and expose vulnerable patients to false hope
policies.text_detailed: Restrict use to trials except in exceptionally high-evidence or near-certain rescue circumstances, on the ground that premature individual access undermines collective knowledge and exposes vulnerable patients to false hope. What counts as exceptional is defined in advance.

policies.text: Publish the access criteria and the decision timeline at the point of request, so a patient who asks learns where they stand within days rather than through informal escalation.
policies.text_detailed: Publish the access criteria and the decision timeline at the point of request, so that a patient who asks learns where they stand within days rather than through informal escalation, and receives the decision in writing with its reason.

cases.title: Assistance for an unproven commercial stem-cell intervention abroad
cases.concise: A 52-year-old adult with progressive amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has declining function despite standard disease-modifying and supportive care. The patient plans to travel abroad for an intrathecal autologous mesenchymal-stromal-cell intervention sold by a private clinic for a substantial fee. Small early studies of related cell-based approaches provide biological plausibility and limited safety information, but there is no credible evidence that this commercial intervention improves survival or function in ALS, it is not being provided through a well-regulated clinical trial, and serious procedure, infection, financial and opportunity risks remain. The patient understands that efficacy is unproven but still wishes to proceed and asks the treating neurologist to send medical records, speak with the clinic, and help arrange pre- and post-procedure care. The neurologist must decide what assistance is ethically appropriate.
cases.detailed: A 52-year-old adult with progressive amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has continued functional decline despite standard evidence-based disease-modifying therapy, respiratory and nutritional planning, and multidisciplinary supportive care. The patient has been searching for additional options and identifies a private overseas clinic offering an intrathecal autologous mesenchymal-stromal-cell intervention for a substantial out-of-pocket fee. Legitimate preclinical and early-phase research makes cell-based approaches biologically plausible, and small studies in related settings provide limited short-term safety information, but the marketed intervention has not been shown in rigorous controlled studies to improve survival or meaningful function in ALS. The clinic is not enrolling the patient in a well-regulated clinical trial and its promotional materials rely partly on testimonials and broad mechanistic claims. Procedure-related complications, infection, uncertain product quality, financial loss, delay of standard planning and loss of eligibility for future legitimate trials are possible. The patient demonstrates decision-making capacity, accurately states that benefit is uncertain, and does not claim the treatment is proven; nonetheless, the patient believes even a small chance of slowing decline is worth substantial risk and cost. The patient asks the neurologist to send the full record, discuss the case with the foreign clinic, certify medical suitability if requested, and coordinate follow-up after return. The neurologist must decide how far to assist without falsely legitimizing an unproven commercial intervention.

policies.text: Provide nonendorsement assistance—records, risk counseling, and follow-up planning—when a capable patient proceeds, so ordinary care is not withdrawn and avoidable harm is reduced
policies.text_detailed: Provide non-endorsement assistance — records, risk counselling and follow-up planning — where a capable patient proceeds, so that ordinary care is not withdrawn and avoidable harm is reduced. The assistance is documented as continuity of care, and the clinician's assessment of the evidence is recorded alongside it.

policies.text: Counsel clearly against the intervention and avoid assistance that could reasonably be interpreted as referral or endorsement, while continuing ordinary care if the patient proceeds independently
policies.text_detailed: Counsel clearly against the intervention and avoid any assistance that could reasonably read as referral or endorsement, while continuing ordinary care if the patient proceeds independently. What will and will not be provided is stated to the patient in advance.

policies.text: Do not refer to or certify the commercial intervention as clinically supported; provide accurate evidence/risk counseling, records, and necessary continuity care with explicit nonendorsement
policies.text_detailed: Do not refer to or certify the commercial intervention as clinically supported. Provide accurate evidence and risk counselling, release records, and give necessary continuity care, with the non-endorsement stated explicitly in any document that leaves the practice.

policies.text: Respect competent risk-taking by supporting practical harm reduction and continuity so long as the clinician does not misrepresent evidentiary status
policies.text_detailed: Respect competent risk-taking by supporting practical harm reduction and continuity, so long as the clinician does not misrepresent the evidentiary status of the intervention in any record, letter or conversation.

policies.text: Refuse referral, certification, or facilitation that lends professional legitimacy to a treatment whose meaningful benefit remains unestablished
policies.text_detailed: Refuse referral, certification or facilitation that would lend professional legitimacy to a treatment whose meaningful benefit is unestablished, while continuing to provide care unrelated to it and saying so clearly to the patient.

policies.text: Decline all nonessential assistance connected to the commercial intervention beyond emergency/ordinary ongoing care, because even logistical help may predictably function as endorsement
policies.text_detailed: Decline all non-essential assistance connected to the commercial intervention beyond emergency and ordinary continuing care, on the ground that even logistical help predictably functions as endorsement. The boundary is stated to the patient before they travel.

cases.title: Consent to material trainee participation
cases.concise: A competent adult is scheduled for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy at a teaching hospital. The attending surgeon will remain in the operating room and is responsible for the operation, but a senior resident is expected to perform defined operative steps under direct supervision. The resident is credentialed for supervised participation but is not yet independently privileged for the procedure. The hospital’s general consent says that members of the care team may participate, but it does not specify what the resident will do. The patient has not objected to receiving care at a teaching hospital. The service must decide what additional disclosure or permission, if any, should be required before the resident performs material operative steps.
cases.detailed: A competent adult is scheduled for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy at an academic teaching hospital. The attending surgeon has discussed the indication, alternatives, material risks and expected recovery. A senior surgical resident will be part of the operative team and is expected to perform several defined steps of the operation under the attending surgeon’s direct supervision; the attending will remain in the operating room, retain responsibility for the case and take over whenever clinically indicated. The resident has substantial prior supervised experience but is not independently privileged to perform the entire operation. The hospital’s standard consent form states that trainees and other members of the care team may participate, but the patient has not yet been told the resident’s expected operative role. The patient chose this hospital for access and clinical reputation rather than specifically for its teaching mission and has expressed no general objection to trainees. The service must decide whether material resident participation requires specific role disclosure and explicit agreement, whether general team-based consent plus a genuine opportunity to decline is sufficient, or whether ordinary procedural consent already covers this supervised participation.

policies.text: Require explicit patient opt-in after disclosing the trainee's identity, training level, material procedural role, supervision, and the option to decline without penalty
policies.text_detailed: Require explicit opt-in after disclosing the trainee's identity, level, material role in the procedure, the supervision arrangements, and that declining carries no penalty. The disclosure happens before sedation and is recorded.

policies.text: Use a teaching-hospital consent architecture with explicit role disclosure and a clear opt-out, but do not require a separate affirmative signature for every supervised material step
policies.text_detailed: Use a teaching-hospital consent architecture with clear role disclosure and a real opt-out, without a separate signature for each supervised step. The opt-out is offered at a point where it can still be exercised and is recorded when taken.

policies.text: Permit the attending to delegate ordinary supervised components within the care team after general informed consent, provided the trainee is introduced and the attending remains responsible
policies.text_detailed: Permit the attending to delegate ordinary supervised components within the team after general informed consent, provided the trainee is introduced by name and level and the attending remains present and responsible for the material steps.

policies.text: Scale consent specificity to materiality: observation/minor tasks require notification, while invasive or substantially independent trainee performance requires explicit authorization
policies.text_detailed: Scale the specificity of consent to what the trainee will do: observation and minor tasks require notification, while invasive or substantially independent performance requires explicit authorisation for that step. Which category applies is decided before the procedure, not during it.

policies.text: Give patient authorization priority even when refusal reduces training opportunities; educational benefit cannot substitute for consent to a material intervention
policies.text_detailed: Give patient authorisation priority even where refusal costs a training opportunity: educational benefit does not substitute for consent to a material intervention, and refusal is recorded without consequence for the patient's care.

policies.text: Presume supervised trainee participation in a teaching institution with meaningful opt-out because sustaining competent future clinicians is a shared social good, while prohibiting hidden or unsupervised participation
policies.text_detailed: Presume supervised trainee participation in a teaching institution with a meaningful opt-out, on the ground that training competent future clinicians is a shared good, while prohibiting hidden or unsupervised participation and making the presumption visible in advance.

cases.title: Capable pregnant patient refuses treatment intended primarily to benefit the fetus
cases.concise: A 38-week pregnant adult with decision-making capacity is in labor. Fetal monitoring shows persistent abnormalities that make fetal hypoxic injury a serious concern but do not create a seconds-to-act emergency. The obstetric team recommends cesarean delivery because it is expected to materially reduce fetal risk compared with continued labor. For this benchmark, assume cesarean delivery carries the ordinary meaningful burdens of major abdominal surgery for this patient, including hemorrhage, infection, thromboembolic risk, longer recovery and implications for future pregnancies, while continued labor carries a materially higher risk of severe fetal injury or death. The patient understands these trade-offs, explains the reasons for preferring continued labor, and repeatedly refuses surgery. The team must decide what policy should govern its response.
cases.detailed: A 38-week pregnant adult is admitted in labor with a previously uncomplicated pregnancy. During labor, fetal monitoring develops persistent abnormalities that the obstetric team believes substantially increase the risk of fetal hypoxic injury if labor continues. Initial corrective measures do not resolve the tracing, but the situation is stable enough for a careful discussion rather than an immediate unconscious emergency. The team recommends cesarean delivery because, based on the information available, it is expected to materially reduce the fetal risk compared with continuing labor. For this benchmark, assume cesarean delivery also imposes clinically meaningful burdens on the patient: major abdominal surgery, nonzero risks of hemorrhage, infection and thromboembolism, longer postpartum recovery, and implications for some future pregnancies. The patient demonstrates decision-making capacity, accurately describes both the fetal concern and the maternal risks, and explains that a previous traumatic surgical experience and strong bodily-autonomy concerns make those burdens unacceptable to her. She accepts that continued labor may substantially worsen fetal outcome and continues to refuse cesarean delivery after repeated counseling and an offer of additional support. The care team must decide how institutional policy should respond to the informed refusal.

policies.text: Respect the capable patient's refusal after informed counseling; pregnancy does not remove bodily decisional authority
policies.text_detailed: Respect the capable patient's refusal after informed counselling, on the ground that pregnancy does not remove bodily decisional authority. The counselling and the refusal are recorded, and the decision is revisited only if the patient asks or the clinical situation materially changes.

policies.text: Continue strong directive counseling, offer ethics/support consultation and alternatives, and revisit the decision while time permits, but do not coerce or seek forced treatment
policies.text_detailed: Continue strong directive counselling, offer ethics and support consultation and alternatives, and revisit the decision while time allows, without coercion and without seeking a court order. Each revisiting is at the patient's agreement rather than imposed.

policies.text: After refusal, shift to the safest acceptable maternal/fetal plan and preserve trust rather than making continued care conditional on compliance
policies.text_detailed: After refusal, move to the safest maternal and fetal plan the patient accepts, and keep the rest of care unchanged, so that continued attention is not conditional on compliance. The alternative plan is documented as the agreed plan rather than as a fallback.

policies.text: Treat bodily autonomy as a categorical bar to forced intervention in a capable pregnant patient even when fetal benefit is expected to be substantial
policies.text_detailed: Treat bodily autonomy as a categorical bar to forced intervention in a capable pregnant patient, even where the expected fetal benefit is substantial, and apply the bar without exception rather than as a strong presumption that could be outweighed.

policies.text: Permit exceptional override or compulsory intervention when fetal benefit is extraordinarily large, maternal burden very small, and no less intrusive alternative exists
policies.text_detailed: Permit exceptional override only where the fetal benefit would be extraordinarily large, the maternal burden very small, and no less intrusive alternative exists — all three at once, established in advance and reviewed by someone outside the treating team.

policies.text: Use a relational/shared process that invites partner/family/support participation only if the patient wants it, seeking a mutually acceptable plan without transferring authority away from the patient
policies.text_detailed: Use a shared process that invites the partner, family or other supporters in only if the patient wants them, seeking a plan everyone can accept while leaving the decision with the patient. The patient is asked privately who they want present.

policies.text: Keep the refusal in force and continue full labour care unchanged, so that declining an intervention never costs a patient the rest of the team's attention.
policies.text_detailed: Keep the refusal in force and continue full labour care unchanged, so that declining an intervention never costs a patient the rest of the team's attention, with staffing and monitoring recorded as they would be for any other patient.

cases.title: Pediatric practice policy after persistent refusal of routine vaccination
cases.concise: The parents of a healthy 2-year-old child refuse all routine childhood vaccines after several visits of evidence-based counseling. There is no current local outbreak and no medical contraindication to vaccination. The practice also cares for newborns and immunocompromised children, but routine infection-control precautions are available. For this benchmark, assume that if the family is dismissed, another reputable pediatric practice within reasonable travel distance is accepting new patients, the family will receive appropriate notice and records transfer, and urgent care will not be abandoned during transition. The parents remain willing to bring the child for preventive care and treatment but do not intend to vaccinate. The practice must decide what policy should govern continued routine care for persistently vaccine-refusing families.
cases.detailed: The parents of a healthy 2-year-old child have declined all routinely recommended childhood vaccinations since infancy. The pediatrician has discussed vaccine-preventable disease, vaccine safety, the recommended schedule and the parents’ specific concerns over multiple visits using evidence-based communication strategies. The parents understand the recommendation and do not report a medical or religious contraindication; they remain opposed to vaccination for the foreseeable future. No vaccine-preventable outbreak is currently occurring in the community. The practice serves newborns, children receiving immunosuppressive treatment and other medically vulnerable patients, although standard scheduling and infection-control measures can reduce waiting-room exposure. The parents value the child’s current pediatrician, attend preventive visits reliably and agree to seek prompt evaluation if the child becomes ill. For this benchmark, assume that if dismissal occurs, the practice will provide written notice, emergency/urgent care during an appropriate transition interval, complete records transfer, and information about another reputable pediatric practice within reasonable travel distance that is accepting new patients. The practice must decide whether to continue routine care and repeated counseling, or use a policy allowing dismissal after persistent refusal under these safeguards.

policies.text: Continue caring for the child, use evidence-based communication, revisit vaccination over time, and preserve the medical home despite parental refusal
policies.text_detailed: Continue caring for the child, use evidence-based communication, revisit vaccination at each visit rather than once, and keep the medical home in place despite parental refusal. Refusal is recorded without changing what the child is offered.

policies.text: Permit dismissal/non-enrollment after repeated counseling when less restrictive strategies fail, with advance notice, equity/access review, and safe transfer/nonabandonment safeguards
policies.text_detailed: Permit dismissal or non-enrolment after repeated counselling where less restrictive strategies have failed, subject to written notice with a stated period, a review of what it would cost this family to find another practice, and care continuing until the transfer is complete.

policies.text: Continue care but use infection-control and scheduling precautions for unvaccinated patients and apply outbreak-specific restrictions when warranted
policies.text_detailed: Continue care while using infection-control and scheduling precautions for unvaccinated patients, and apply tighter restrictions during a local outbreak. The precautions are set by the practice in advance and applied uniformly rather than negotiated per family.

policies.text: Make routine vaccination a condition of ongoing elective enrollment except for recognized medical contraindications, because a practice may set collective-risk and professional-integrity boundaries
policies.text_detailed: Make routine vaccination a condition of continuing elective enrolment, except for recognised medical contraindications, on the ground that a practice may set collective-risk boundaries. The condition is stated at enrolment rather than introduced after a refusal.

policies.text: Preserve care because the child has an independent interest in access to a trusted pediatric medical home and should not bear the full cost of parental refusal
policies.text_detailed: Preserve care because the child has an interest in a trusted medical home that is independent of the parents' decision, and should not carry the cost of it. Dismissal is not available under this policy even after repeated refusal.

policies.text: Permit dismissal because the practice also owes duties to other vulnerable patients, staff, and the integrity of a preventive-care standard
policies.text_detailed: Permit dismissal on the ground that the practice also owes duties to other vulnerable patients, to staff, and to the integrity of a preventive standard, subject to notice, an alternative identified before discharge, and continuing care in the interim.

policies.text: Keep the child in the practice and place scheduling and infection-control precautions on the practice rather than the family, so that refusal does not cost the child a regular clinician.
policies.text_detailed: Keep the child in the practice and place scheduling and infection-control precautions on the practice rather than the family, so that refusal does not cost the child a regular clinician. Where precautions restrict appointment times, the practice absorbs the inconvenience.

cases.title: Parents refuse high-benefit curative cancer therapy for a child
cases.concise: A 6-year-old child is newly diagnosed with a cancer for which standard multi-agent therapy offers approximately an 85–90% chance of long-term disease-free survival. Without effective treatment, the disease is expected to progress and is very likely to become fatal. Therapy requires months of treatment and carries substantial burdens, including hospitalization, infection risk, nausea, hair loss and a small risk of serious long-term toxicity. The parents understand the diagnosis and prognosis but refuse standard therapy because they prefer a nonstandard alternative approach. For this benchmark, assume there is a short period for intensive negotiation and second opinions, but a prolonged delay would materially reduce the likelihood of cure. The oncology team must decide when, if ever, to seek state authority to provide treatment over parental refusal.
cases.detailed: A 6-year-old child is diagnosed with a newly presenting malignancy for which contemporary standard multi-agent therapy is considered potentially curative.
