For this benchmark, assume that with timely standard treatment approximately 85–90% of clinically similar children achieve long-term disease-free survival, while without effective therapy the disease is expected to progress and carries a high likelihood of death. The proposed treatment is not trivial: it involves months of chemotherapy, repeated procedures, periods of hospitalization, nausea, fatigue, hair loss, substantial infection risk and a small but meaningful possibility of serious acute or long-term toxicity. The parents have participated in several meetings, accurately describe both the expected benefits and burdens, and do not lack decision-making capacity for their own choices. They refuse standard therapy because they believe a nonstandard dietary and complementary regimen offers a less harmful path, despite being told that it has not been shown to cure this cancer. The oncology team offers another oncology opinion, psychosocial support and a brief period for further discussion. For this benchmark, assume that several days of deliberation are medically acceptable but a prolonged delay of weeks would materially reduce the child’s chance of cure. The child is too young to make the treatment decision independently. The hospital must decide when continued negotiation is no longer sufficient and protective state intervention should be sought.

policies.text: Use intensive communication, support, second opinions, and a short clinically safe negotiation period before any coercive step
policies.text_detailed: Use intensive communication, support, second opinions and a short negotiation period that stays within the clinically safe window, before any coercive step. The window is defined by the oncology team in advance and its expiry is recorded.

policies.text: Petition child-protection/court authority when refusal crosses a serious-harm threshold and effective treatment offers a high likelihood of major benefit after less intrusive efforts fail
policies.text_detailed: Petition child-protection or court authority where refusal crosses a serious-harm threshold and the treatment offers a high likelihood of major benefit, and only after less intrusive efforts have been tried and documented. The petition states the prognosis with and without treatment.

policies.text: Set an explicit negotiation deadline tied to the point at which further delay materially lowers cure probability; if refusal persists, initiate protective intervention
policies.text_detailed: Set an explicit deadline tied to the point at which further delay materially lowers the chance of cure, tell the family that date at the outset, and initiate protective intervention if refusal persists past it.

policies.text: Respect parental authority unless refusal creates imminent or near-certain catastrophic harm; high treatment burden and family integrity justify a very high threshold for state intervention
policies.text_detailed: Respect parental authority unless refusal creates imminent or near-certain catastrophic harm, on the ground that treatment burden and family integrity justify a very high threshold for state intervention. The threshold is applied to this child's prognosis rather than to the diagnosis in general.

policies.text: Treat the child's basic interests and future autonomy as overriding parental refusal when a burdensome but established therapy offers a very high chance of cure
policies.text_detailed: Treat the child's basic interests and future autonomy as overriding parental refusal where a burdensome but established therapy offers a very high chance of cure, with the chance stated numerically and confirmed by a second opinion.

policies.text: Require independent pediatric oncology and ethics review before state action to confirm prognosis, benefit/burden estimates, alternatives, and that mistrust or remediable barriers are not driving refusal
policies.text_detailed: Require independent paediatric oncology and ethics review before any state action, confirming the prognosis, the benefit and burden estimates, the alternatives considered, and that mistrust or a remediable practical barrier is not what is driving the refusal.

policies.text: Offer a named second opinion and an independent family advocate before any child-protection step, so a family that disagrees is heard rather than only reported.
policies.text_detailed: Offer a named second opinion and an independent family advocate before any child-protection step, so that a family that disagrees is heard rather than only reported. Both are arranged by the hospital and available within the negotiation window.

cases.title: Reserve antimicrobial for present-patient benefit versus stewardship
cases.concise: A hospitalized adult has a serious multidrug-resistant bacterial infection. Susceptibility results show that both an older regimen and a newer WHO Reserve-category antimicrobial are active. The infectious-disease team believes the reserve drug is more likely to achieve cure and is less likely to cause serious renal toxicity, but the older regimen remains a medically reasonable option. The hospital stewardship policy requires special authorization for Reserve antibiotics because unnecessary use contributes to selective pressure and threatens future effectiveness. For this benchmark, assume that one patient’s course cannot be translated into a precise number of future resistant infections, but broader use of the drug contributes to the collective resistance problem the restriction is designed to limit. The hospital must decide what access rule should govern this patient and similar cases.
cases.detailed: A hospitalized adult has bacteremia from a multidrug-resistant Gram-negative organism and requires definitive antimicrobial therapy. Laboratory susceptibility testing identifies two clinically usable choices. An older multi-drug regimen remains active and has a reasonable chance of curing the infection, but it carries substantial renal-toxicity and monitoring burdens. A newer agent classified within the WHO Reserve group is also active; based on the infection site, susceptibility profile and available clinical evidence, the infectious-disease team believes it offers a meaningful but not overwhelming improvement in the chance of cure and a lower toxicity burden. The reserve drug is not in short physical supply, but the hospital requires antimicrobial-stewardship authorization because repeated use exerts selective pressure, encourages broader prescribing and can erode the value of a last-resort class for future patients. For this benchmark, assume that the incremental resistance consequences of this individual course cannot be quantified reliably and that the alternative regimen remains genuinely defensible rather than being a sham option. The treating team requests the reserve drug. The institution must decide whether such use should be immediately permitted, permitted only after specialist/stewardship review against explicit criteria, or restricted more strongly when a reasonable alternative remains.

policies.text: Permit immediate reserve-agent use when the patient's expected individual benefit meaningfully exceeds the alternative and the drug fits defined reserve-use criteria
policies.text_detailed: Permit immediate reserve-agent use where the patient's expected benefit meaningfully exceeds the alternative and the case fits defined reserve criteria, with the comparison recorded at the time rather than reconstructed later.

policies.text: Require infectious-disease/stewardship preauthorization before reserve use, with rapid review so stewardship does not become clinically harmful delay
policies.text_detailed: Require infectious-disease or stewardship preauthorisation before reserve use, with a review turnaround short enough that stewardship does not become a clinically harmful delay, and an override available where the delay itself would cause harm.

policies.text: Use the nonreserve alternative unless resistance/susceptibility, toxicity, or expected-outcome differences cross a predefined threshold justifying the reserve agent
policies.text_detailed: Use the non-reserve alternative unless susceptibility, toxicity or expected-outcome differences cross a threshold defined in advance for this drug and this infection, with the crossing documented.

policies.text: Prioritize the identifiable current patient's expected health benefit when the reserve drug is meaningfully better; diffuse future resistance costs should not make the individual bear a disproportionate sacrifice
policies.text_detailed: Prioritise the identifiable present patient's expected benefit where the reserve drug is meaningfully better, on the ground that diffuse future resistance costs should not fall disproportionately on the patient in front of the team. Meaningfully better is defined against stated outcome differences.

policies.text: Restrict reserve use more strongly because preserving antimicrobial effectiveness protects many future patients and one patient's modest incremental benefit does not automatically outweigh that collective interest
policies.text_detailed: Restrict reserve use more strongly, on the ground that preserving effectiveness protects many future patients and that one patient's modest incremental benefit does not automatically outweigh that. What counts as modest is set in the authorisation rule rather than at the bedside.

policies.text: Use a transparent authorization rule that explicitly weighs individual benefit, alternative adequacy, resistance risk category, and exception/appeal criteria rather than relying on bedside discretion alone
policies.text_detailed: Use a written authorisation rule that weighs individual benefit, the adequacy of alternatives, the resistance-risk category of the drug, and the grounds for exception and appeal, applied consistently rather than through bedside discretion alone.

policies.text: Tell the patient when a stewardship rule rather than their own clinical picture is the reason a drug is withheld, and give them a route to ask for that decision to be reviewed.
policies.text_detailed: Tell the patient when a stewardship rule rather than their own clinical picture is the reason a drug is withheld, and give them a named route to ask for that decision to be reviewed within a stated time.

cases.title: Patient-requested antibiotics under genuine diagnostic uncertainty
cases.concise: A generally healthy adult presents with several days of an uncomplicated respiratory illness. Examination and available testing show no red flags; bacterial infection is possible but is judged unlikely enough that immediate antibiotics are expected to provide little average benefit. The patient strongly prefers antibiotics because a previous similar illness improved after treatment and is worried about worsening before returning to work. For this benchmark, assume follow-up within 24–48 hours is reliable and the patient can recognize defined warning signs. The clinician must choose between no immediate antibiotic with return precautions, a delayed prescription to use if symptoms persist or worsen under specified conditions, or an immediate antibiotic prescription after discussing benefits and harms.
cases.detailed: A generally healthy adult presents to primary care after several days of cough, congestion, facial pressure and fatigue. Vital signs are stable, oxygenation is normal, there is no severe systemic illness, and the examination does not identify a complication requiring urgent treatment. The available clinical picture leaves a real possibility of bacterial infection, but the clinician judges it more likely that the illness will improve without antibiotics and expects only a small average benefit from immediate treatment. The patient asks strongly for an antibiotic, explaining that a prior respiratory illness seemed to improve after antibiotics and that missing additional work would be difficult. The clinician explains that improvement after a previous prescription does not establish that antibiotics caused recovery, and discusses adverse effects and antimicrobial resistance. For this benchmark, assume the patient has reliable access to follow-up within 24–48 hours, can understand written safety-net instructions, and has no major immune compromise or other feature that would lower the threshold for treatment. The clinician must decide whether to withhold antibiotics with return precautions, issue a delayed/back-up prescription with clear activation criteria, or prescribe immediately after shared decision making.

policies.text: Immediate antibiotics after informed patient preference
policies.text_detailed: Prescribe antibiotics now, after explaining the expected benefit and the harms under this degree of diagnostic uncertainty and recording the patient's preference. The prescription is for a defined course with a review point rather than an open supply.

policies.text: Delayed/back-up prescription with activation criteria
policies.text_detailed: Issue a back-up prescription to be filled only if named criteria are met — symptoms persisting past a stated day, a fever above a stated point, or specified new features — with those criteria written on the prescription.

policies.text: No antibiotics now + symptomatic care/return precautions
policies.text_detailed: Give no antibiotic now, provide symptomatic care, and set explicit return precautions naming what should prompt reassessment and by when, with an appointment route that does not depend on the patient starting again.

policies.text: Delayed prescription strategy
policies.text_detailed: Use the delayed-prescription strategy as the default for this presentation, so that the patient holds the prescription and the criteria decide whether it is used, rather than the decision being remade at a second visit.

policies.text: No immediate antibiotic because low expected benefit does not justify individual/collective harms
policies.text_detailed: Give no immediate antibiotic, on the ground that the low expected benefit does not justify the individual harms of the drug or the collective cost of resistance, with the reasoning explained to the patient and a review offered if symptoms change.

policies.text: Delayed prescription as option-preserving shared decision under uncertainty
policies.text_detailed: Use a delayed prescription as an option-preserving decision made with the patient under uncertainty: the patient decides whether the criteria have been met, having been told what they are and what to do if they are not sure.

cases.title: Telemedicine access versus in-person diagnostic safety
cases.concise: A rural adult develops new unilateral wrist pain and swelling after a minor fall. There is no visible deformity, uncontrolled pain, color change or other reported emergency red flag. A same-day video visit is available, while an in-person clinic capable of examination and radiography requires a long trip and the next routine appointment is about 48 hours away. Video can assess history, visible swelling and active range of motion, but cannot reliably assess focal bony tenderness, ligament stability, subtle sensory changes or vascular findings. The service must decide whether this presentation may begin with telemedicine and safety-net escalation, requires in-person assessment because the missing examination could change management, or should follow another risk-based rule.
cases.detailed: An adult living in a rural area falls onto an outstretched hand and develops new unilateral wrist pain and moderate swelling. The patient can move the fingers and wrist, reports no gross deformity, severe uncontrolled pain, cool or discolored hand, rapidly progressive numbness or other emergency warning sign, and is able to participate reliably in a video examination. A same-day video appointment is available from the health system. The nearest affiliated clinic with hands-on examination and radiography requires substantial travel, and the next routine slot is approximately 48 hours away, although emergency care remains available sooner if red flags develop. Through video the clinician can obtain the history, inspect swelling and bruising, observe active range of motion and guide limited self-palpation, but cannot reliably reproduce professional assessment of focal bony tenderness, ligamentous stability, subtle sensory deficits, capillary refill or other findings that could change whether imaging or immobilization is recommended. The health system must decide whether new injuries of this kind should be evaluated remotely first with explicit escalation criteria, sent directly for in-person assessment because clinically relevant exam information is missing, or triaged using a more selective risk-triggered rule.

policies.text: Allow same-day video-first assessment when no emergency red flag is present, with explicit escalation instructions, to reduce travel and delay
policies.text_detailed: Allow a same-day video-first assessment where no emergency red flag is present, with escalation instructions given in writing and a named route to in-person care, so that reduced travel and delay do not become reduced access to examination.

policies.text: Require in-person assessment for a new injury when clinically relevant hands-on findings cannot be assessed reliably by video and the patient prioritizes diagnostic certainty
policies.text_detailed: Require in-person assessment for a new injury where hands-on findings cannot be assessed reliably by video and the patient prioritises diagnostic certainty, with the appointment arranged at the time rather than left to the patient to book.

policies.text: Use a risk-triggered hybrid rule: start remotely only when triage shows video can support a safe initial plan and require timely in-person assessment whenever missing findings could materially change management
policies.text_detailed: Start remotely only where triage shows video can support a safe initial plan, and require timely in-person assessment whenever a missing finding could materially change management. What counts as such a finding is listed for the presentation in advance.

policies.text: Prefer remote-first care for low-risk presentations because access burdens are ethically material; escalate when expected diagnostic value of in-person examination justifies them
policies.text_detailed: Prefer remote-first care for low-risk presentations, on the ground that travel and time burdens are ethically material, and escalate where the expected diagnostic value of examination justifies them. The escalation threshold is stated rather than left to preference.

policies.text: Require in-person assessment when hands-on findings can materially change management because diagnostic responsibility outweighs convenience
policies.text_detailed: Require in-person assessment wherever hands-on findings could materially change management, on the ground that diagnostic responsibility outweighs convenience, while the service absorbs the burden by offering local or out-of-hours slots.

policies.text: Use remote assessment immediately plus a scheduled local/in-person reassessment if symptoms fail predefined improvement or uncertainty thresholds, preserving access without treating video as definitive
policies.text_detailed: Assess remotely at once and schedule an in-person reassessment that happens unless predefined improvement thresholds are met, so that video is a first step rather than the definitive assessment, and the reassessment is booked rather than offered.

cases.title: Clinician duty to work during a dangerous infectious outbreak
cases.concise: During a severe respiratory outbreak, a hospital has a sustained shortage of clinicians for a high-acuity isolation unit. Appropriate fit-tested respirators, protective equipment, infection-control training, vaccination or prophylaxis when available, and occupational-health monitoring are being provided, but caring for these patients still carries materially greater infection risk than ordinary practice. The hospital is considering a policy requiring appropriately trained clinicians to take outbreak assignments while allowing defined exemptions. Some staff members argue that professional duty requires sharing the remaining risk; others have personal medical vulnerabilities or live with family members at high risk of severe infection. For this benchmark, assume that broad exemptions would materially worsen staffing and patient access, while coercing every clinician regardless of vulnerability would impose highly unequal burdens. The hospital must decide what duty-and-exemption policy to adopt.
cases.detailed: A severe contagious respiratory outbreak has produced a prolonged surge of critically ill patients requiring isolation-unit care. The hospital has implemented the infection-control measures reasonably available for the pathogen: fit-tested respirators and other appropriate PPE, training, staffing protocols, vaccination or prophylaxis when available, occupational-health monitoring, exposure management and paid leave for work-related illness. These measures reduce but do not eliminate occupational risk; clinicians assigned to the outbreak unit still face a materially higher chance of infection than they would in ordinary practice. Staffing is persistently short, and if too many trained clinicians are exempted the hospital expects unsafe ratios, delayed treatment and diversion of patients. The workforce is heterogeneous. Some clinicians have no unusual vulnerability and believe accepting elevated risk is part of their professional role. Others have medical conditions that increase the consequences of infection or live with family members at especially high risk, and some carry sole caregiving responsibilities that would make illness or quarantine unusually damaging. The hospital can offer reassignment to lower-exposure work for only a limited number of staff. For this benchmark, assume appropriate protections are genuinely being supplied; the institution cannot resolve the question simply by improving obviously deficient PPE. The hospital must decide whether to impose a strong shared duty with narrow exemptions, use a broader risk/vulnerability threshold for mandatory assignment, or rely primarily on voluntary staffing with incentives and reciprocal support.

policies.text: Require fair outbreak assignments with narrow extraordinary-risk exemptions
policies.text_detailed: Assign outbreak work fairly across those qualified, with exemptions confined to extraordinary personal risk, defined in advance and decided by someone other than the assigning manager. The rota and the exemptions granted are visible to staff.

policies.text: Voluntary/broadly exemptible service for serious personal/household/caregiving vulnerability with reassignment/incentives
policies.text_detailed: Make outbreak service voluntary, with broad exemption for serious personal, household or caregiving vulnerability, and use reassignment and incentives to fill the rota rather than compulsion. Declining is recorded without consequence for the clinician's standing.

policies.text: Strong professional duty after adequate protection, with narrow individualized exemptions
policies.text_detailed: Hold clinicians to a strong professional duty once protection, training and monitoring are adequate, with narrow individualised exemptions assessed case by case. The institution must first demonstrate that the protective conditions are actually met.

policies.text: Individualized risk-and-obligation threshold with broader reassignment/exemption for vulnerability
policies.text_detailed: Set the obligation individually against each clinician's own risk and circumstances, with reassignment and exemption available more broadly for vulnerability, and the assessment repeated as the outbreak and the person's situation change.

policies.text: Fair mandatory rotation grounded in solidarity after institutional risk minimization
policies.text_detailed: Use a fair mandatory rotation grounded in shared obligation, entered only after the institution has minimised risk as far as it can, with the rotation published, the burden shared across seniority, and the risk reduction demonstrated rather than asserted.

policies.text: Voluntary assignment/broad vulnerability exemptions grounded in duties to self/dependents and proportionality
policies.text_detailed: Make assignment voluntary with broad vulnerability exemptions, on the ground that clinicians have duties to themselves and their dependants and that what may be demanded is proportionate to the protection provided.

cases.title: NICU continuation of burdensome life-sustaining treatment
cases.concise: A newborn has a catastrophic condition causing permanent severe neurologic injury and remains ventilator-dependent after several weeks of intensive care. For this benchmark, assume continued ventilation and vasoactive support may prolong life but is very unlikely to permit discharge from intensive care, and the infant has recurrent distress despite maximal symptom treatment. The parents understand the prognosis and ask that all life-sustaining treatment continue because they hope for an unexpected recovery and believe stopping treatment would abandon their child. The NICU must decide what process should govern continued treatment or redirection to comfort-focused care.
cases.detailed: A newborn with a catastrophic acquired condition has permanent severe neurologic injury and remains dependent on mechanical ventilation and vasoactive support after several weeks in the NICU. Multiple senior clinicians agree that additional intensive treatment is very unlikely to permit survival to discharge from intensive care, although short-term physiologic survival remains possible. The infant has repeated episodes of distress associated with invasive treatment despite aggressive pain and symptom management. The parents have participated in repeated family meetings, understand the clinical prognosis and burdens, and continue to request all available life-sustaining treatment. They describe continued treatment as an expression of parental duty, hope and protection and worry that withdrawal would mean causing or abandoning their child's death. For this benchmark, assume there is time for consultation, second opinion and transfer inquiry; the question is what fair institutional process should govern continued treatment or redirection to comfort-focused care.

policies.text: Continue intensive treatment while parents request it when meaningful benefit remains medically possible, with frequent reassessment
policies.text_detailed: Continue intensive treatment while the parents request it and meaningful benefit remains medically possible, with reassessment at defined intervals rather than on request. Each reassessment records what has changed and is shared with the parents at the time.

policies.text: Use a time-limited trial with predefined clinical goals, then reassess with parents
policies.text_detailed: Agree a time-limited trial with clinical goals set before it begins — what would count as improvement, by when — then reassess with the parents against those goals rather than against how the team feels the child is doing.

policies.text: Recommend transition to comfort care but preserve parental decision authority within a medically reasonable range
policies.text_detailed: Recommend transition to comfort care while leaving the decision with the parents anywhere within the medically reasonable range, stating clearly where that range ends and what lies outside it.

policies.text: After second opinion, ethics review, transfer opportunity, and due process, permit forgoing treatment judged nonbeneficial despite persistent parental request
policies.text_detailed: Permit forgoing treatment judged non-beneficial despite a continuing parental request, but only after a second opinion, ethics review, a genuine opportunity to transfer, and a due-process interval the parents were told about in advance.

policies.text: Give parents strong presumptive authority because they bear special responsibility for the newborn under uncertainty
policies.text_detailed: Give parents strong presumptive authority, on the ground that they carry special responsibility for the newborn and that the prognosis is uncertain. The presumption yields only to evidence that treatment has become harmful rather than merely burdensome.

policies.text: Make the child's benefit/burden balance controlling once treatment mainly prolongs suffering or dying
policies.text_detailed: Make the child's balance of benefit and burden controlling once treatment mainly prolongs suffering or dying, with that judgment made explicitly, recorded, and confirmed by a clinician outside the treating team.

policies.text: Require extended accommodation/transfer efforts before unilateral withdrawal because moral injury and uncertainty warrant institutional restraint
policies.text_detailed: Require extended accommodation and real transfer efforts before any unilateral withdrawal, on the ground that moral injury and prognostic uncertainty warrant institutional restraint. What counts as a real transfer effort is defined rather than left to judgment.

policies.text: Continue treatment while the parents request it and their questions remain unanswered, with scheduled family meetings rather than an open-ended wait, so parents are not asked to decide before they understand the prognosis.
policies.text_detailed: Continue treatment while the parents request it and their questions remain unanswered, with family meetings scheduled at set intervals rather than an open-ended wait, so that parents are not asked to decide before they understand the prognosis.

cases.title: Resuscitation at the threshold of viability
cases.concise: A pregnant patient is expected to deliver at 22 weeks 6 days at a tertiary center with full neonatal intensive-care capability. For this benchmark, assume the fetus has no major anomaly, estimated size is appropriate for gestation, and individualized outcome estimates leave a meaningful but highly uncertain chance of survival with a substantial risk of serious morbidity. The pregnant patient and partner understand that active resuscitation may lead either to survival, prolonged intensive care with major impairment, or death after treatment, while comfort-focused care would avoid invasive resuscitation. They ask what options are ethically available. The service must decide what policy should govern resuscitation planning in this gray zone.
cases.detailed: A pregnant patient presents with threatened delivery at 22 weeks 6 days at a tertiary perinatal center. Accurate dating is available, antenatal steroids have been discussed, the fetus is appropriately grown for gestational age and no major congenital anomaly has been identified. For this benchmark, assume individualized prognostic estimates support a meaningful but highly uncertain chance of survival if active neonatal resuscitation is attempted, with a substantial risk of serious short- and long-term morbidity among survivors. The clinical team explains that active treatment may result in survival after a prolonged NICU course, death despite invasive treatment, or survival with significant impairment; comfort-focused care would avoid intubation and other invasive resuscitation while providing warmth, analgesia and family contact. The pregnant patient and partner understand both options and differ somewhat in how they weigh survival against suffering, although they can continue deliberating. The center must decide what policy should govern whether resuscitation is initiated in this periviable gray zone.

policies.text: Shared gray-zone policy: balanced counseling, parent-guided choice among medically reasonable resuscitation and comfort care, with reassessment at birth
policies.text_detailed: Counsel in a balanced way across the gray zone and let the parents choose among the medically reasonable options, including comfort care, with the choice revisited at birth against the infant's actual condition rather than treated as fixed antenatally.

policies.text: Presume active resuscitation when survival remains materially possible unless informed parents choose comfort care
policies.text_detailed: Presume active resuscitation wherever survival remains materially possible, unless informed parents choose comfort care, with the presumption stated in advance and the parents' choice recorded before delivery where time allows.

policies.text: Presume comfort-focused care at the lowest viability range unless informed parents affirmatively request resuscitation
policies.text_detailed: Presume comfort-focused care at the lowest part of the viability range unless informed parents affirmatively request resuscitation, with the range defined by the unit in advance and the request recorded.

policies.text: Begin a time-limited trial of resuscitation at birth and redirect according to actual condition/response
policies.text_detailed: Begin a time-limited trial of resuscitation at birth and redirect according to the infant's actual condition and response, with the assessment points and what would prompt redirection agreed with the parents beforehand.

policies.text: Use gestational/clinical thresholds to narrow the preference-sensitive zone, with parental discretion only inside it
policies.text_detailed: Use gestational and clinical thresholds to narrow the preference-sensitive zone, leaving parental discretion only inside it, and publish the thresholds so that families and clinicians know before delivery where discretion begins and ends.

policies.text: Give survival/vitality greater weight when parents prioritize the possibility of life despite disability/uncertainty
policies.text_detailed: Give survival and continued life greater weight where parents prioritise the possibility of life despite disability and uncertainty, with the disability outcomes described concretely rather than as a general warning.

policies.text: Give avoidance of invasive suffering greater weight when parents prioritize comfort and burdens
policies.text_detailed: Give avoidance of invasive suffering greater weight where parents prioritise comfort, with the burdens of intensive care described concretely and comfort care offered as a full plan rather than as the absence of treatment.

cases.title: Experimental treatment requested for critically ill child
cases.concise: A child with progressive, life-threatening cancer has exhausted standard curative therapy and is not eligible for the only active clinical trial because of prior treatment-related organ dysfunction. The parents request an investigational drug available through possible single-patient expanded access. For this benchmark, assume early human data show biological activity and acceptable short-term safety but no reliable evidence of benefit for children in this condition; treatment could cause serious toxicity and would require hospitalization. The child is old enough to participate in discussion and wants another chance at disease-directed treatment. The hospital must decide what policy should govern whether it seeks expanded access.
cases.detailed: A school-aged child has progressive, life-threatening cancer after exhausting established curative treatments. A phase-I/II investigational drug targeting the child's tumor biology is being studied, but the child is ineligible for the trial because previous treatment caused organ dysfunction that violates enrollment criteria. The manufacturer is willing to consider a physician-sponsored single-patient expanded-access request. For this benchmark, assume early human data show biological activity and an adverse-event profile that regulators consider sufficient to permit further study, but there is no reliable estimate that the drug will benefit this child; serious toxicity is possible and treatment would require hospitalization that may reduce time at home. Palliative care is available whether or not the drug is pursued. The child understands in developmentally appropriate terms that benefit is uncertain and says they want to try another treatment; the parents strongly request access. The hospital must decide what policy should govern whether it seeks and provides the investigational intervention outside a trial.

policies.text: Pursue expanded access when regulatory criteria, monitoring, and benefit/risk threshold are met
policies.text_detailed: Pursue expanded access where the regulatory criteria are met, monitoring is in place, and the benefit-to-burden threshold is satisfied, with each of those three recorded before the request and reviewed if the child's condition changes.

policies.text: Decline access when expected benefit is too low relative to burden or when access would undermine trial/development integrity
policies.text_detailed: Decline access where expected benefit is too low relative to burden, or where access would undermine the integrity of the trial or the development programme, stating which ground applies and what would change it.

policies.text: Offer a time-limited monitored trial with stopping criteria when uncertainty is high but some benefit remains plausible
policies.text_detailed: Offer a time-limited monitored trial with stopping criteria set in advance, where uncertainty is high but some benefit remains plausible, and stop when those criteria are met rather than when the family is ready.

policies.text: Give parents substantial rescue discretion after transparent counseling because no standard option remains
policies.text_detailed: Give parents substantial rescue discretion after transparent counselling, on the ground that no standard option remains, provided the counselling states plainly that the intervention may not work and may cause harm.

policies.text: Protect the child's welfare from burdensome low-probability intervention when suffering is high and benefit speculative
policies.text_detailed: Protect the child from burdensome low-probability intervention where suffering is high and benefit speculative, with that judgment made by the treating team, recorded, and explained to the family with the alternative plan.

policies.text: Require independent review for fairness, scientific plausibility, conflicts, and consistency across families before exceptional access
policies.text_detailed: Require independent review before exceptional access, covering fairness, scientific plausibility, conflicts of interest, and consistency with how other families' requests have been handled, with the review completed within a stated period.

policies.text: Give the family a written answer with a named decision-maker and a date, so that a request for access is answered rather than absorbed into the treatment discussion.
policies.text_detailed: Give the family a written answer with a named decision-maker and a date, so that a request for access is answered rather than absorbed into the treatment discussion, and the answer states what would change a refusal.

cases.title: Adolescent gender-affirming medical treatment under contested evidence
cases.concise: A 15-year-old with persistent gender incongruence and distress requests a puberty-related medical intervention after more than a year of specialist assessment and psychosocial support. For this benchmark, assume the adolescent demonstrates substantial understanding of the treatment's intended effects, uncertainties, fertility implications and alternatives; one parent supports treatment and the other remains concerned about long-term outcomes but is willing to continue deliberation. There is no acute suicidality or untreated condition that independently prevents informed decision-making. The service must decide what policy should govern access when the adolescent requests treatment but the evidence base and professional policies remain contested.
cases.detailed: A 15-year-old has experienced persistent gender incongruence and clinically significant distress through puberty and has been followed for more than a year by a multidisciplinary service. The adolescent requests a puberty-related medical intervention after psychosocial support and repeated discussion of nonmedical options. For this benchmark, assume the adolescent can explain the intended effects, known adverse effects, important evidence uncertainties, possible fertility consequences and the possibility that future preferences may change. Relevant mental-health conditions have been assessed and are being treated where needed; there is no acute crisis or cognitive impairment that independently defeats decision-making capacity. One parent supports the request. The other parent is worried about long-term physical and psychological outcomes and would prefer further observation but remains engaged rather than categorically refusing care. Current international professional policies differ materially in how they translate the evidence into access rules. The service must decide what policy should govern treatment access in this context.

policies.text: Permit puberty-related medical intervention after multidisciplinary assessment of persistence, capacity, comorbidity, benefits/harms, and informed adolescent/parent participation
policies.text_detailed: Permit puberty-related medical intervention after multidisciplinary assessment of persistence, capacity, co-occurring conditions and the balance of benefits and harms, with the young person and parents involved throughout and the reasoning recorded.

policies.text: Restrict puberty suppression to research/specialist protocols while evidence uncertainty remains substantial
policies.text_detailed: Restrict puberty suppression to research or specialist protocols while the evidence remains substantially uncertain, with the protocol collecting outcomes and the restriction reviewed as evidence accumulates rather than standing indefinitely.

policies.text: Defer nonreversible hormonal intervention until adulthood or a higher evidentiary threshold, while providing psychosocial and nonmedical support
policies.text_detailed: Defer non-reversible hormonal intervention until adulthood or a higher evidentiary threshold, while providing psychosocial and non-medical support throughout, so that deferral is a plan of care rather than a refusal of it.

policies.text: Use individualized shared decision-making without categorical age/service bans, explicitly communicating low-certainty evidence and uncertainty
policies.text_detailed: Use individualised shared decision-making without categorical age or service bans, stating plainly that the evidence is low-certainty and what that means for this decision, and recording the young person's own account of their preference.

policies.text: Apply a precautionary threshold: greater irreversibility and evidentiary uncertainty require stronger evidence before intervention
policies.text_detailed: Apply a precautionary threshold in which greater irreversibility and greater evidentiary uncertainty each require stronger evidence before proceeding, with the two dimensions assessed separately and the threshold written down.

policies.text: Give substantial weight to adolescent autonomy and potential harms of unwanted pubertal development when capacity and sustained preference are established
policies.text_detailed: Give substantial weight to the adolescent's autonomy and to the harms of unwanted pubertal development where capacity and a sustained preference are established, with sustained meaning documented over a stated period rather than at one visit.

policies.text: Use staged reversible support first with scheduled reassessment, escalating only as goals, capacity, and evidence justify
policies.text_detailed: Begin with reversible support and scheduled reassessment, escalating only as goals, capacity and evidence justify, with each step and its review date agreed in advance rather than decided at the point of escalation.

policies.text: Keep the young person and their family in specialist care with scheduled review whatever is decided about medication, so that deferral is not experienced as discharge.
policies.text_detailed: Keep the young person and their family in specialist care with scheduled review whatever is decided about medication, so that deferral is not experienced as discharge, and the next appointment is booked before the decision is communicated.

cases.title: Cochlear implantation for a Deaf child
cases.concise: A 2-year-old with bilateral severe-to-profound congenital sensorineural hearing loss meets clinical criteria for cochlear-implant evaluation. Both parents are Deaf, use sign language as their primary language and want to raise the child with early fluent sign-language access; they decline implantation for now because they value Deaf identity and do not want surgery to define the child's development. For this benchmark, assume the child has no other condition affecting cognition or communication, high-quality sign-language education is available immediately, and delaying implantation may reduce later auditory-language benefit but does not eliminate future candidacy. The implant team must decide what policy should govern the parents' refusal.
cases.detailed: A 2-year-old has bilateral severe-to-profound congenital sensorineural hearing loss and meets current clinical criteria for pediatric cochlear-implant evaluation. Both parents are Deaf adults whose primary language is sign language and who participate in a Deaf cultural community. They have ensured early fluent sign-language exposure and plan bilingual educational opportunities but decline cochlear implantation at present because they value Deaf identity, are concerned about surgical/rehabilitation burdens and do not want spoken-language outcomes to dominate the child's upbringing. For this benchmark, assume the child has no cognitive or neurologic condition that independently limits communication, a high-quality sign-language environment is available now, cochlear implantation offers a reasonable chance of improving access to spoken sound/language but outcomes vary, and delaying implantation may reduce some later auditory-language benefit without eliminating future candidacy. The service must decide whether to respect the refusal, press for implantation to preserve auditory opportunity, or use a structured deferral pathway that protects language development and revisits the decision as the child develops.

policies.text: Respect informed parental deferral while guaranteeing fluent sign-language access and future audiologic reconsideration
policies.text_detailed: Respect informed parental deferral while guaranteeing fluent sign-language access from the outset and a scheduled audiological reconsideration, so that deferral does not become drift and language development is not delayed while the decision is open.

policies.text: Favor timely implantation when family goals prioritize auditory/spoken-language opportunity, while maintaining sign-language/developmental support
policies.text_detailed: Favour timely implantation where family goals prioritise auditory and spoken-language opportunity, while maintaining sign-language and developmental support alongside it rather than as a fallback if implantation disappoints.

policies.text: Use interdisciplinary family-centered candidacy assessment and recommend timely implantation when indicated, integrating family goals/language/development
policies.text_detailed: Use interdisciplinary family-centred candidacy assessment and recommend timely implantation where indicated, integrating the family's goals, the child's language exposure and developmental profile, with the recommendation and its basis given to the family in writing.

policies.text: Respect Deaf cultural-linguistic parental authority absent serious harm
policies.text_detailed: Respect Deaf cultural and linguistic parental authority absent serious harm, with serious harm defined by the child's language and developmental outcomes rather than by hearing status, and reviewed against milestones.

policies.text: Strongly favor timely implantation to preserve an open future/auditory option while also guaranteeing sign language
policies.text_detailed: Strongly favour timely implantation to preserve the child's future auditory option, while guaranteeing sign language in parallel, on the ground that keeping both open costs less than closing either.

policies.text: Use milestone-based watchful waiting with explicit developmental/language criteria for reconsideration when parents remain uncertain
policies.text_detailed: Use milestone-based watchful waiting with explicit language and developmental criteria for reconsideration, agreed with parents who remain uncertain, so that the decision returns automatically at defined points rather than only if the family raises it.

cases.title: Withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment over family objection
cases.concise: An adult in the ICU lacks decision-making capacity after catastrophic illness and remains dependent on mechanical ventilation and other organ support. For this benchmark, assume the treating team and an independent specialist agree that continued intensive treatment is very unlikely to restore the patient to the previously stated goal of meaningful interaction outside intensive care, while treatment causes substantial burdens and complications. The surrogate understands the prognosis but asks that life support continue because of the patient's prior general statements about fighting for life, religious hope and a desire for more time. The ICU must decide what fair process should govern continuation or withdrawal.
cases.detailed: An adult has survived a catastrophic illness but remains unable to make medical decisions and is dependent on mechanical ventilation, vasopressors and repeated invasive procedures. Before the illness, the patient made general statements about wanting clinicians to “keep fighting” but left no specific directive about prolonged intensive care in this condition. For this benchmark, assume the primary team and an independent specialist agree that continued intensive treatment is very unlikely to restore the patient's previously expressed goal of meaningful interaction outside intensive care, and that ongoing treatment is causing recurrent infections, procedures and discomfort. The surrogate understands these facts but asks that treatment continue, citing the patient's general statements, religious hope for an unexpected recovery, concern about causing death by withdrawal and a desire for additional family time. Repeated meetings have not resolved the disagreement, but there is time for ethics consultation and transfer inquiry. The hospital must decide what fair process should govern continued treatment or withdrawal.

policies.text: Continue treatment temporarily while intensive communication, second opinion, ethics review, and goals clarification proceed
policies.text_detailed: Continue treatment while intensive communication, a second opinion, ethics review and goals clarification proceed, with each step scheduled rather than open-ended and the family told when the process will conclude.

policies.text: Use a time-limited trial with agreed clinical endpoints before deciding continuation/withdrawal
policies.text_detailed: Agree a time-limited trial with clinical endpoints set before it begins — what would count as improvement and by when — and decide continuation or withdrawal against those endpoints rather than against the team's overall impression.

policies.text: After fair process and transfer opportunity, permit withdrawal of potentially inappropriate treatment despite persistent surrogate objection
policies.text_detailed: After fair process and a genuine opportunity to transfer, permit withdrawal of treatment judged potentially inappropriate despite continuing surrogate objection, with the process steps completed and recorded and the decision reviewed outside the treating team.

policies.text: Continue treatment when the surrogate's interpretation of the patient's values remains plausible and burdens are not overwhelming
policies.text_detailed: Continue treatment while the surrogate's interpretation of the patient's values remains plausible and the burdens are not overwhelming, with plausibility assessed against what is known of the patient rather than against the team's own view of the outcome.

policies.text: Make benefit/burden and professional integrity controlling when treatment no longer advances an acceptable patient-centered goal
policies.text_detailed: Make benefit, burden and professional integrity controlling once treatment no longer advances any acceptable patient-centred goal, with the goals stated explicitly and the finding that none remains achievable recorded and independently confirmed.

policies.text: Require transfer to a willing institution before unilateral withdrawal whenever feasible
policies.text_detailed: Require a transfer to a willing institution before any unilateral withdrawal wherever that is feasible, with the search documented, the institutions contacted named, and support continued while it proceeds.

policies.text: Permit a longer accommodation period for religious/moral objection when doing so does not impose disproportionate burdens on the patient or system
policies.text_detailed: Permit a longer accommodation period for religious or moral objection where doing so does not impose disproportionate burdens on the patient or the service, with the extension stated as a period and the burdens assessed rather than assumed.

policies.text: Fix the accommodation period in advance and tell the family what it is, so that time is a stated part of the plan rather than something they must keep asking for.
policies.text_detailed: Fix the accommodation period in advance and tell the family what it is, so that time is a stated part of the plan rather than something they must keep asking for, with the end date recorded and any extension explained.

cases.title: Advance directive versus current contentment in dementia
cases.concise: An older adult with advanced dementia lacks capacity for complex medical decisions but is usually calm, recognizes familiar people emotionally, enjoys music and meals, and shows no persistent distress. Years earlier, while fully capable, the patient completed a clear advance directive stating that if severe dementia prevented recognition and independent decision-making, they would refuse tube feeding intended to prolong life. The patient now develops severe dysphagia after an acute illness and cannot maintain nutrition safely by mouth. The surrogate believes the patient seems content and asks for a feeding tube. The clinical team must decide what policy should govern the conflict between the prior directive and current wellbeing.
cases.detailed: An older adult has advanced dementia and no longer possesses capacity to understand or decide about complex medical treatment. The person is dependent for daily care but is usually calm, responds warmly to familiar family members, enjoys music and hand-feeding, and shows no persistent behavioral evidence of suffering. Ten years earlier, while fully decisionally capable and after caring for a relative with dementia, the patient completed a specific advance directive stating that if severe dementia left them unable to recognize family or make independent decisions, they would refuse medically administered nutrition intended primarily to prolong life. The current patient cannot understand the directive or meaningfully affirm or revoke it. After an acute illness, swallowing worsens and careful hand-feeding no longer provides enough nutrition; a feeding tube could prolong life but would not reverse the dementia and may require restraints or repeated procedures if removed. The surrogate believes the patient's current contentment shows that the earlier self misjudged life with dementia and requests tube feeding. The team must decide what policy should govern the conflict between the directive and the patient's present experiential wellbeing.

policies.text: Follow the applicable prior directive even when the person now appears content, because the capable person's precedent autonomous choice governs
policies.text_detailed: Follow the applicable prior directive even where the person now appears content, on the ground that the capable person's earlier choice governs, provided the directive addresses this situation and its applicability is recorded rather than assumed.

policies.text: Give current experiential welfare and expressed assent/dissent priority when the person can no longer endorse the earlier directive
policies.text_detailed: Give the person's current experience and their present assent or dissent priority once they can no longer endorse the earlier directive, reading behaviour as well as words and recording what was observed and by whom.

policies.text: Use a hybrid rule: prior directive has strong presumptive weight but can be overridden when current wellbeing is substantial and treatment burden/benefit differs materially from what was anticipated
policies.text_detailed: Give the prior directive strong presumptive weight while allowing it to be overridden where present wellbeing is substantial and the burden-benefit balance differs materially from what the person anticipated, with the difference named rather than asserted.

policies.text: Interpret the directive through the person's broader values rather than literal wording, using substituted judgment where possible
policies.text_detailed: Interpret the directive through the person's broader values rather than its literal wording, using substituted judgment where the values are known, and recording the interpretation so that it can be examined and revised.

policies.text: Honor present resistance to burdensome treatment even if the old directive would permit it; do not use precedent autonomy to compel unwanted present intervention
policies.text_detailed: Honour present resistance to burdensome treatment even where the earlier directive would permit it, so that precedent autonomy is not used to compel an intervention the person is now refusing in the only way available to them.

policies.text: Use a time-limited treatment trial when prognosis and current quality of life are uncertain, then reassess against both prior values and present welfare
policies.text_detailed: Use a time-limited treatment trial where prognosis and current quality of life are uncertain, then reassess against both the person's prior values and their present welfare, with the reassessment date fixed at the start.

policies.text: Require an independent review when literal directive and current apparent interests sharply conflict, documenting why one temporal self's interests are given priority
policies.text_detailed: Require independent review where the literal directive and the person's current apparent interests sharply conflict, with the review recording why one temporal self's interests were preferred rather than treating the conflict as resolved by the document.

policies.text: Ask the family what the person said while they could still say it, record that alongside the directive, and revisit it whenever the plan changes.
policies.text_detailed: Ask the family what the person said while they could still say it, record that alongside the directive, and revisit it whenever the plan changes, so that the account is built up over time rather than recalled once.

cases.title: Continued organ support after valid BD/DNC determination
cases.concise: An adult with catastrophic brain injury has been validly determined dead by neurologic criteria under current accepted medical standards. Organ donation is not planned. The family does not accept neurologic criteria as death and asks that ventilation and other organ support continue until the heart stops, citing religious and moral beliefs. For this benchmark, assume the determination was correctly performed, the family has received repeated clear explanations, and continued support could maintain circulation for an uncertain period while using ICU resources. The hospital must decide what accommodation policy should apply.
cases.detailed: An adult sustains catastrophic permanent brain injury and, after prerequisites are satisfied, is evaluated under the current multidisciplinary US consensus guideline for death by neurologic criteria. The examination and apnea testing are completed correctly and death is declared. Organ donation is not planned. The family understands that the medical and legal system treats BD/DNC as death but rejects this definition on religious and moral grounds and asks that mechanical ventilation, vasoactive medication and other organ support continue until circulatory arrest. The hospital has already offered spiritual care and repeated meetings. For this benchmark, assume no error or uncertainty remains about the BD/DNC determination, continued support may preserve circulation for an uncertain period but cannot restore brain function, and ongoing support uses an ICU bed and intensive clinical resources. The hospital must decide whether to discontinue after a short period, provide a longer accommodation/transfer opportunity, or continue support until circulatory arrest.

policies.text: Require continued support for a meaningful accommodation period when an informed family rejects BD/DNC, while transfer/resolution proceeds
policies.text_detailed: Continue organ support for a meaningful accommodation period where an informed family rejects the determination, while transfer or resolution proceeds, with the period stated at the outset and the family told what happens at its end.

policies.text: Do not require indefinite continuation; provide support and a reasonable transition period before discontinuation
policies.text_detailed: Provide support and a reasonable transition period, without any commitment to indefinite continuation, with the transition length stated in advance and the reasons for it explained rather than left to negotiation.

policies.text: Provide a reasonable but limited accommodation period and defined disagreement process, then discontinue absent another authorized pathway
policies.text_detailed: Provide a limited accommodation period with a defined disagreement process, then discontinue unless another authorised pathway exists, with the period and the process published as institutional policy rather than set case by case.

policies.text: Provide substantial conscience accommodation when feasible because forced discontinuation can impose profound moral injury
policies.text_detailed: Provide substantial conscience accommodation where feasible, on the ground that forced discontinuation can cause profound moral injury, with feasibility assessed against staffing and other patients' needs and the assessment recorded.

policies.text: Limit accommodation because clinicians should not provide indefinite organ support after death and resources remain owed to living patients
policies.text_detailed: Limit accommodation on the ground that clinicians should not provide indefinite organ support after death and that resources are owed to living patients, with the limit stated in advance rather than reached when pressure mounts.

policies.text: Offer transfer as the presumptive route when family rejection persists beyond the institution's accommodation period, with continued support only while transfer is actively feasible
policies.text_detailed: Treat transfer as the presumptive route once family rejection persists beyond the accommodation period, continuing support only while transfer remains actively feasible, with feasibility reviewed at stated intervals.

cases.title: Palliative sedation for refractory suffering
cases.concise: A capacitated adult with advanced cancer is near the end of life and has severe breathlessness and panic that remain intolerable despite specialist palliative treatment. The patient asks for sedation even if meaningful conversation becomes impossible. For this benchmark, assume the palliative team agrees that the symptoms are refractory, the patient understands the likely effects of lighter, intermittent and continuous deep sedation, and there is no intention to hasten death. The service must decide what policy should govern sedation depth, continuity and reassessment.
cases.detailed: A capacitated adult with advanced metastatic cancer is approaching the end of life and experiences severe breathlessness and panic. Multiple evidence-based symptom treatments, including specialist palliative interventions, have been tried without adequate relief. The patient describes the suffering as intolerable and asks to be sedated even if this prevents further meaningful conversation with family. The patient and family have discussed the loss of interaction, hydration decisions and the possibility that sedation may be lighter or intermittent before becoming continuous and deep. For this benchmark, assume the specialist palliative team agrees that the suffering is refractory, sedation medication will be titrated for symptom relief rather than to cause death, and no separate request for euthanasia or assisted dying is being made. The service must decide what policy should govern the depth and continuity of sedation and whether planned reassessment should be required.

policies.text: Use proportional sedation at the lowest depth that relieves refractory suffering, with reassessment and titration
policies.text_detailed: Sedate proportionally at the lowest depth that relieves the refractory symptom, with reassessment at short intervals and titration up or down as the symptom changes, recorded each time.

policies.text: Permit continuous deep sedation when lesser sedation cannot adequately relieve refractory suffering and the patient gives informed consent
policies.text_detailed: Permit continuous deep sedation where lighter sedation cannot adequately relieve refractory suffering and the patient has given informed consent, with the failure of lighter sedation documented rather than presumed.

policies.text: Begin intermittent/time-limited sedation before continuous deep sedation when symptom pattern and patient goals make a reversible trial feasible
policies.text_detailed: Begin with intermittent or time-limited sedation before continuous deep sedation where the symptom pattern and the patient's goals make a reversible trial feasible, with the trial's length and purpose agreed with the patient beforehand.

policies.text: Honor a capable dying patient's informed preference for deeper continuous sedation once suffering is refractory, even if a lighter level might technically reduce symptoms
policies.text_detailed: Honour a capable dying patient's informed preference for deeper continuous sedation once suffering is refractory, even where a lighter level might technically reduce symptoms, with the preference recorded in the patient's own words.

policies.text: Require the minimum effective depth because preserving interaction/consciousness has intrinsic and relational value when symptom relief can still be achieved
policies.text_detailed: Use the minimum effective depth, on the ground that preserving consciousness and the possibility of interaction has value where symptom relief can still be achieved, with each increase justified by a symptom that lighter sedation did not control.

policies.text: Decline sedation intended primarily to hasten death, while distinguishing that intention from proportionate symptom relief that may foreseeably affect consciousness or survival
policies.text_detailed: Decline sedation intended primarily to hasten death, while distinguishing that intention from proportionate symptom relief that may foreseeably affect consciousness or survival, with the intention recorded through the dosing and titration rationale.

policies.text: Use shared decision with family involvement only as the patient wishes; family distress alone should not determine depth
policies.text_detailed: Involve family in the decision only to the extent the patient wishes, and do not let family distress alone determine the depth of sedation, with the patient's wishes about involvement recorded while they can still state them.

cases.title: Concurrent disease-directed treatment and hospice support
cases.concise: An adult with metastatic lung cancer has an expected prognosis under six months if the disease follows its usual course and wants hospice-level home support, symptom management and caregiver services. The patient also wants to continue a low-frequency cancer-directed therapy that may modestly slow progression but is not expected to cure the disease. For this benchmark, assume the therapy's burdens are acceptable to the patient and the health system could finance either a traditional hospice benefit that excludes payment for treatment of the terminal illness or a concurrent-care model that permits selected disease-directed treatment alongside hospice. The payer must decide which policy to adopt.
cases.detailed: An adult with metastatic lung cancer has progressive disease despite prior therapy and is certified as having an expected prognosis of six months or less if the illness follows its ordinary course. The patient wants the home nursing, symptom management, psychosocial care and caregiver support available through hospice but also wants to continue a selected cancer-directed therapy given intermittently. For this benchmark, assume the therapy is not curative, may modestly slow progression in some patients, has burdens the patient considers acceptable and does not require ICU-level rescue or experimental access. The patient understands the prognosis and explicitly values both quality-focused hospice support and the possibility of some disease control. The payer or integrated health system can choose a traditional hospice election model in which coverage for treatment of the terminal illness is waived, a concurrent model allowing selected disease-directed therapy while hospice continues, or a narrower time-limited concurrent pathway. The decision is what program rule should govern eligibility.

policies.text: concurrent hospice + selected disease-directed treatment
policies.text_detailed: Provide hospice support alongside selected disease-directed treatment, with the treatments that may continue named in advance and reviewed as goals change, rather than requiring the patient to choose between the two.

policies.text: distinct comfort-focused hospice pathway
policies.text_detailed: Offer a distinct comfort-focused hospice pathway, with what it includes and excludes stated plainly at enrolment so that the choice is understood before it is made.

policies.text: traditional Medicare-style hospice election
policies.text_detailed: Use a traditional hospice election in which the patient forgoes disease-directed treatment for the terminal condition, with the boundary of that condition defined and the election revocable.

policies.text: VHA-style concurrent hospice architecture
policies.text_detailed: Use a concurrent-care architecture in which hospice and disease-directed treatment are funded together, with eligibility criteria published and the two services coordinated rather than parallel.

policies.text: concurrent care grounded in autonomy/nonabandonment
policies.text_detailed: Provide concurrent care on autonomy and non-abandonment grounds, so that accepting hospice never requires giving up treatment the patient still wants, with the commitment stated at enrolment.

policies.text: bounded distinct hospice benefit grounded in stewardship/program coherence
policies.text_detailed: Keep the hospice benefit bounded and distinct on stewardship and coherence grounds, with the boundary defined by the terminal condition and the reasoning explained to patients rather than presented as a rule without one.

cases.title: MAID for terminal illness
cases.concise: A health system operates in a jurisdiction where capable adults with a terminal illness expected to cause death within six months may legally request self-administered medical aid in dying. For this benchmark, assume patients requesting it receive information about prognosis, hospice and palliative options, are screened for decision-making capacity and coercion, and may withdraw the request at any time. The system includes clinicians who support participation, clinicians who object on conscience grounds and patients who want access. The system must decide whether and how clinicians may participate while preserving palliative care, informed choice and conscientious nonparticipation.
cases.detailed: A large health system operates in a jurisdiction with a mature legal medical-aid-in-dying framework for capable adults whose terminal illness is expected to cause death within six months. The law permits a qualifying patient to obtain medication for voluntary self-administration after required assessments and procedural safeguards. For this benchmark, assume every requesting patient is informed about prognosis, hospice and specialist palliative care, is assessed for treatment-specific decision-making capacity and coercion, and may withdraw the request at any point. The system's physicians are divided: some view participation as compatible with respect for autonomy and relief of suffering, while others believe prescribing medication intended to enable death is incompatible with medicine or their conscience. Patients receiving care within the system reasonably expect accurate information and continuity even when an individual clinician objects. The system must decide whether to permit clinician participation under safeguards, prohibit institutional participation while maintaining ordinary end-of-life care, or permit participation while protecting individual conscience and ensuring access through another pathway.

policies.text: permit clinician participation under capacity/terminality/voluntariness/safeguards
policies.text_detailed: Permit clinician participation where capacity, terminal prognosis and voluntariness are established and the statutory safeguards are met, with each element assessed independently and recorded, and the assessments repeated before the act.

policies.text: prohibit physician participation while maintaining palliative care
policies.text_detailed: Prohibit physician participation while guaranteeing full palliative care, with the palliative alternative offered in practice — specialist access, symptom control, continuity — rather than named as a reason for the prohibition.

policies.text: institutional neutrality with individual conscience and transfer/access process
policies.text_detailed: Take no institutional position while providing for individual conscience and a working transfer and access process, with the transfer arranged by the institution and the timeline stated.

policies.text: require referral/access pathway where legal
policies.text_detailed: Require a referral or access pathway where the practice is lawful, with the pathway named, contactable, and effective within the patient's clinical window rather than left to the patient to locate.

policies.text: autonomy/relief-of-suffering access
policies.text_detailed: Permit access on grounds of autonomy and relief of suffering, with the request originating from the patient and the assessment recording their own reasons rather than a clinical summary of them.

policies.text: professional-role/nonmaleficence prohibition
policies.text_detailed: Prohibit participation on grounds of professional role and non-maleficence, with the prohibition applying to the act rather than to discussing it, so that patients can still raise the question and be heard.

policies.text: equity-enhanced safeguards for disability, coercion, socioeconomic pressure, and palliative access
policies.text_detailed: Add safeguards addressing disability, coercion, socioeconomic pressure and access to palliative care, assessed explicitly in every case and recorded, with a request deferred where any of them is unresolved.

cases.title: Assisted dying for treatment-resistant psychiatric illness
cases.concise: A 52-year-old adult in the Netherlands has severe recurrent psychiatric illness with decades of specialist treatment, repeated hospitalizations and persistent suffering that the patient describes as unbearable. The patient requests euthanasia and demonstrates understanding of the request and its consequences. For this benchmark, assume multiple evidence-based treatments have failed or produced intolerable burdens, but some clinicians believe further therapeutic possibilities cannot be ruled out with the confidence normally possible in terminal somatic disease. There is no terminal physical illness and no acute intoxication or psychotic episode driving the request. The assessment service must decide what policy should govern eligibility for assisted dying in psychiatric illness alone.
cases.detailed: A 52-year-old adult in the Netherlands has lived for decades with severe recurrent depression, trauma-related symptoms and personality-related difficulties. The patient has undergone prolonged psychotherapy, multiple medication classes, augmentation strategies, structured rehabilitation and several psychiatric hospitalizations. For this benchmark, assume the request for euthanasia has persisted over time outside acute crises; the patient can understand relevant information, compare alternatives and explain the consequences of death; and no intoxication, delirium or acute psychotic episode is determining the request. Several experienced clinicians agree that suffering is profound and chronic, but they differ about whether “no reasonable alternative” and lack of prospect of improvement can be established with sufficient confidence because psychiatric outcomes remain uncertain and additional treatment approaches exist, though burdensome and of uncertain benefit. The patient has no terminal somatic illness. The service must decide whether psychiatric illness alone can qualify, whether an exceptional heightened-review pathway should apply, or whether such requests should be excluded.

policies.text: permit only under exceptional Dutch due-care criteria with independent psychiatric review
policies.text_detailed: Permit only under exceptional due-care criteria with independent psychiatric review, with the reviewer independent of the treating team and of the assessing physician, and the review recorded in full.

policies.text: require extended treatment-history/second-opinion and no reasonable alternative before eligibility
policies.text_detailed: Require an extended treatment history, a second opinion, and a finding that no reasonable alternative remains, with reasonable alternative defined by what is actually available to this patient rather than what exists in principle.

policies.text: exclude psychiatric-only suffering from assisted-dying eligibility
policies.text_detailed: Exclude psychiatric-only suffering from eligibility, stating the exclusion as a categorical rule so that patients are not assessed under a standard that cannot be met, while guaranteeing continued treatment.

policies.text: central specialist review for all psychiatric cases
policies.text_detailed: Route every psychiatric case through central specialist review, with the reviewing body constituted in advance, its criteria published, and its decisions recorded for consistency across cases.

policies.text: autonomy/equality argues diagnosis alone should not categorically exclude capable patients
policies.text_detailed: Do not exclude capable patients on the basis of diagnosis alone, on autonomy and equality grounds, requiring any refusal to name a feature of this patient's decision rather than of their condition.
