policies.text: vulnerability/uncertainty argues exceptional precaution or exclusion
policies.text_detailed: Apply exceptional precaution or exclusion on grounds of vulnerability and prognostic uncertainty, with the uncertainty stated — what cannot be known about the course of this illness — rather than asserted generally.

policies.text: time-limited deferral with renewed assessment after additional evidence/treatment opportunities
policies.text_detailed: Defer for a stated period with renewed assessment after further treatment opportunities, with the treatments named, made available, and the reassessment automatic rather than requiring a fresh request.

policies.text: Guarantee continued treatment and support throughout any assessment, so that asking to be assessed never reduces the care a person is offered.
policies.text_detailed: Guarantee continued treatment and support throughout any assessment, so that asking to be assessed never reduces the care a person is offered, with the treating team's obligations unchanged and stated in writing.

cases.title: Advance request for assisted dying after loss of capacity in dementia
cases.concise: A person with advanced Alzheimer disease can no longer make or communicate complex decisions. Years earlier, while fully capable, the person completed and repeatedly reaffirmed a specific advance euthanasia directive requesting euthanasia if dementia progressed to permanent inability to recognize close family and make independent decisions. Those conditions are now met. For this benchmark, assume the person is not persistently resisting care and sometimes appears calm, but clinicians cannot obtain a current verbal request or reliably establish how the person now experiences the situation. Dutch law permits an advance directive to replace an oral request only if all other due-care criteria are met. The physician must decide what policy should govern whether the advance request can be acted upon.
cases.detailed: A person with advanced Alzheimer disease has lost capacity to understand or decide about euthanasia and can no longer communicate a coherent current treatment preference. Six years earlier, while fully decisionally capable and after detailed discussion with a physician, the person completed an advance euthanasia directive stating that euthanasia should be performed if dementia progressed to a permanent inability to recognize close family and make independent decisions. The directive was reaffirmed on several later visits while capacity remained intact. Those specified conditions are now present. The person sometimes appears calm and receptive to familiar touch and music, but also has periods of fear and agitation; clinicians cannot establish a stable current judgment about whether the person experiences life as unbearable. For this benchmark, assume there is no consistent contemporaneous verbal request and no persistent physical resistance to ordinary care. Under current Dutch law, a competent advance directive can replace an oral euthanasia request after capacity is lost, but the physician must still establish all other due-care criteria. The physician must decide whether a specific prior request may control, whether current suffering/behavior must independently support implementation, or whether euthanasia should require contemporaneous communicative confirmation.

policies.text: allow valid advance directive to substitute for current oral request when all due-care criteria are met
policies.text_detailed: Allow a valid advance directive to substitute for a current oral request where every due-care criterion is met, with the directive's applicability to the present situation established and recorded by an independent assessor.

policies.text: require current communicative confirmation/observable concurrence before assisted death
policies.text_detailed: Require some current communicative confirmation or observable concurrence before proceeding, with what would count defined in advance rather than judged in the moment, and the absence of it treated as decisive.

policies.text: permit only when directive is specific, repeatedly confirmed historically, current suffering/applicability established, and independent review agrees
policies.text_detailed: Permit only where the directive is specific, was repeatedly confirmed while the person was capable, current suffering and applicability are established, and independent review agrees, with all four recorded separately.

policies.text: do not proceed when present behavior suggests resistance or material uncertainty about applicability
policies.text_detailed: Do not proceed where present behaviour suggests resistance or where the directive's applicability is materially uncertain, with resistance interpreted broadly and any doubt resolved against proceeding.

policies.text: precedent autonomy controls
policies.text_detailed: Let precedent autonomy control, on the ground that the capable person's settled choice about their own dying is theirs to make, with the directive's specificity and its confirmations documented.

policies.text: present experiential interests/current minimal autonomy control
policies.text_detailed: Let present experiential interests and current minimal autonomy control, treating the person now as the one whose life is at stake, with their present state assessed by those who know them.

policies.text: independent multidisciplinary adjudication where directive/current state conflict
policies.text_detailed: Require independent multidisciplinary adjudication wherever the directive and the person's current state conflict, with the adjudication recording why one was preferred and what evidence decided it.

cases.title: CANH in prolonged disorder of consciousness without reliable prior instruction
cases.concise: An adult has remained in a prolonged disorder of consciousness for 14 months after severe nontraumatic brain injury and receives nutrition and hydration through a feeding tube. Serial standardized assessments by an experienced team support a diagnosis of chronic unresponsive wakefulness syndrome, with no reliable evidence of command following, but clinicians explain that diagnostic and prognostic uncertainty is not zero. The patient left no advance directive and family members disagree about whether the patient would regard continued biological survival as worthwhile. For this benchmark, assume CANH can maintain life for years and has manageable but real burdens, while withdrawal would predictably lead to death with palliative symptom management. The team must decide what policy should govern continuation or withdrawal.
cases.detailed: An adult suffered severe nontraumatic brain injury 14 months ago and remains dependent on clinically assisted nutrition and hydration through a gastrostomy tube. The patient is medically stable and no longer requires ventilatory or vasopressor support. Multiple serial standardized assessments by clinicians experienced in disorders of consciousness support chronic unresponsive wakefulness syndrome; there is no reproducible command following or functional communication. For this benchmark, assume clinicians have appropriately investigated confounders and explain that diagnostic error and later recovery are unlikely but cannot be reduced to zero. The patient left no treatment-specific advance directive. One close family member believes the patient strongly valued independence and would reject years of noninteractive life; another believes food and water should continue unless there is certainty the patient cannot recover. CANH can maintain life for years but carries ongoing tube-related care, infection/procedure risks and institutional burden; withdrawal would predictably lead to death with mouth care, symptom treatment and palliative support. The team must decide what policy should govern continued CANH or withdrawal in the absence of a reliable prior instruction.

policies.text: continue CANH during diagnostic/prognostic clarification and family deliberation
policies.text_detailed: Continue clinically assisted nutrition and hydration while diagnosis and prognosis are clarified and the family deliberates, with the clarification following a defined assessment schedule rather than continuing indefinitely.

policies.text: withdraw CANH after best-interest/shared process when burdens and prognosis justify it
policies.text_detailed: Withdraw after a best-interests process shared with the family where burdens and prognosis justify it, with the assessment recording what is known of the person's values and what remains unknown.

policies.text: use time-limited continuation with predefined reassessment milestones
policies.text_detailed: Continue for a defined period with reassessment milestones set in advance, agreed with the family, and applied at those points rather than deferred when they arrive.

policies.text: continue when family reasonably interprets patient's values as favoring life preservation under uncertainty
policies.text_detailed: Continue where the family reasonably interprets the person's values as favouring preservation of life under uncertainty, with that interpretation recorded and tested against what is known rather than accepted or dismissed.

policies.text: withdraw when family reasonably interprets patient's values as rejecting prolonged dependence and burdensome intervention
policies.text_detailed: Withdraw where the family reasonably interprets the person's values as rejecting prolonged dependence and burdensome intervention, with the interpretation recorded and independently reviewed before an irreversible step.

policies.text: require independent neurorehabilitation/ethics review before irreversible withdrawal when diagnosis/prognosis is contested
policies.text_detailed: Require independent neurorehabilitation and ethics review before irreversible withdrawal wherever diagnosis or prognosis is contested, with the contest identified explicitly and the review addressing it.

cases.title: Voluntary stopping of eating and drinking
cases.concise: A capacitated adult with progressive serious illness has substantial functional dependence and suffering despite optimized palliative care but is not expected to die within days. The patient decides to stop eating and drinking in order to hasten death and asks the hospice team for anticipatory guidance, mouth care, symptom medication and support for family caregivers. For this benchmark, assume the decision is persistent, free from coercion and not driven by untreated delirium, psychosis or major depression that impairs capacity. The hospice must decide what policy should govern clinical support during VSED.
cases.detailed: A capacitated adult with progressive serious illness is increasingly dependent on others and describes the current quality of life as intolerable despite specialist treatment of pain, mood, function and other symptoms. The person is not imminently dying and does not qualify for or does not wish to pursue clinician-prescribed assisted dying. After repeated discussion, the patient decides to stop all oral food and fluids with the stated purpose of hastening death. The patient asks a hospice/palliative team to help prepare family caregivers, provide mouth care and medications for thirst, agitation and other symptoms, and remain involved if decisional clarity diminishes from dehydration. For this benchmark, assume the request is persistent, informed and free of coercion; there is no delirium, psychosis or untreated major depression that impairs decision-making capacity; and ordinary food and drink will remain available if the patient changes their mind. Family members are emotionally divided but will not forcibly feed the patient. The service must decide whether and how it should clinically accompany VSED.

policies.text: respect VSED after capacity/coercion/symptom assessment and provide anticipatory symptom care
policies.text_detailed: Respect a decision to stop eating and drinking after assessing capacity, coercion and symptoms, and provide anticipatory symptom care — mouth care, sedation for distress, family support — arranged before it begins.

policies.text: treat reversible depression, uncontrolled symptoms, misinformation, or coercion before accepting the decision as settled
policies.text_detailed: Treat reversible depression, uncontrolled symptoms, misinformation or coercion before accepting the decision as settled, with each addressed and the decision revisited afterwards rather than accepted at first statement.

policies.text: allow clinician conscientious nonparticipation while ensuring nonabandonment/transfer and symptom relief
policies.text_detailed: Allow conscientious non-participation while guaranteeing non-abandonment, transfer and symptom relief, with an alternative clinician arranged and the patient's care unchanged in the interim.

policies.text: support hospice/family with clear expectations and caregiver resources
policies.text_detailed: Support hospice and family with clear expectations about the course and duration and with the caregiver resources that sustain it, provided in advance rather than as the need becomes acute.

policies.text: autonomy-based accompaniment
policies.text_detailed: Accompany the person on autonomy grounds, providing symptom care without pressure to resume, with the accompaniment recorded as the plan rather than as acquiescence.

policies.text: life-preservation/suicide-prevention position favoring continued efforts to restore desire to eat/drink where ethically/legally permissible
policies.text_detailed: Continue efforts to restore the desire to eat and drink where that is ethically and legally permissible, with those efforts bounded, non-coercive, and stopped when the person's decision remains settled.

cases.title: Withholding versus withdrawing the same treatment
cases.concise: Two otherwise equivalent ICU decisions concern the same invasive life-sustaining treatment and the same patient-centered goal. In one, treatment has not yet been started; in the other, it was started as a short trial and has produced no improvement. For this benchmark, assume the patient's prognosis, values and expected future burdens/benefits are now identical in the two situations, and the surrogate agrees that treatment should not continue if it cannot achieve the stated goal but feels that actively stopping an existing treatment is morally harder than not starting it. The hospital must decide whether policy should treat withholding and withdrawing as ethically equivalent or require a stronger process before withdrawal.
cases.detailed: An ICU uses time-limited trials of invasive organ support when prognosis is initially uncertain. The hospital is reviewing whether its policy should distinguish between two cases that, at the moment of decision, have the same prognosis, patient values, clinical goal and expected future treatment burden. In Case A, the relevant organ-support intervention has not yet been initiated and clinicians recommend not starting it because it will not achieve the patient's agreed goal. In Case B, the intervention was begun for a short trial while prognosis was uncertain; the trial has now failed, and clinicians have the same evidence that further treatment will not achieve the same goal. For this benchmark, assume stopping the intervention in Case B does not create a new physiological harm beyond allowing the underlying illness to cause death, and adequate symptom control is available. The surrogate agrees with the treatment goal and prognosis but says it feels morally acceptable not to start treatment and morally wrong to “actively stop” something already keeping the patient alive. The hospital must decide whether its policy should treat withholding and withdrawal as equivalent or require additional safeguards for withdrawal.

policies.text: treat withholding and withdrawing as ethically equivalent when the intervention no longer serves patient goals
policies.text_detailed: Treat withholding and withdrawing as ethically equivalent once the intervention no longer serves the patient's goals, and require the same justification for each rather than a higher one for stopping.

policies.text: require a higher procedural threshold for withdrawal because stopping an established treatment creates reliance/causal/moral concerns
policies.text_detailed: Require a higher procedural threshold for withdrawal, on the ground that stopping an established treatment engages reliance and causal concerns, with the additional steps specified rather than left to local practice.

policies.text: use explicit time-limited trials so initiation does not create a presumption of indefinite continuation
policies.text_detailed: Use explicit time-limited trials so that starting does not create a presumption of continuing, with the endpoint and the review agreed before the treatment begins and recorded where the family can see them.

policies.text: when uncertainty is high, start treatment with stopping criteria rather than withhold because reversibility preserves options
policies.text_detailed: Where uncertainty is high, start treatment with stopping criteria rather than withhold, on the ground that reversibility preserves options, with the criteria fixed at the outset and applied when met.

policies.text: avoid starting when likely later withdrawal would be psychologically/institutionally harder and expected benefit is low
policies.text_detailed: Avoid starting where later withdrawal would be psychologically or institutionally harder and expected benefit is low, with that judgment made explicitly and shared with the family rather than left as a reason not offered.

policies.text: formal-equivalence framework versus morally relevant act/omission/reliance framework
policies.text_detailed: Choose between formal equivalence and a rule that treats acts, omissions and reliance as morally distinct, and state which is being applied in this case so that the reasoning is available for challenge.

cases.title: Unilateral limitation of a newly requested nonbeneficial escalation
cases.concise: An adult in the ICU lacks decision-making capacity and is receiving mechanical ventilation and vasopressors for advanced irreversible disease. The surrogate asks clinicians to initiate ECMO if cardiopulmonary failure worsens. For this benchmark, assume two experienced critical-care specialists agree that ECMO cannot reasonably restore the patient's agreed goal of surviving to leave intensive care and would add major invasive burdens; existing ventilation, symptom treatment and other current care will continue while conflict is reviewed. The surrogate understands the prognosis but requests “everything possible.” The hospital must decide what process should govern non-offer of the requested escalation.
cases.detailed: An adult with advanced irreversible disease has developed severe multiorgan failure and lacks decision-making capacity. The patient is already receiving mechanical ventilation, vasopressors and full symptom-focused care. The surrogate asks that extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) be initiated if cardiopulmonary function deteriorates further, describing a commitment to “everything possible.” For this benchmark, assume the patient and surrogate previously identified survival sufficient to leave intensive care and interact with family as the relevant treatment goal. Two experienced critical-care specialists independently conclude that ECMO cannot reasonably achieve that goal because the underlying disease is irreversible and would expose the patient to major cannulation, bleeding and other burdens without a realistic path to ICU discharge. Existing life-sustaining treatment will not be withdrawn merely because ECMO is declined, and there is time for ethics consultation and transfer inquiry. The surrogate understands the clinical judgment but continues to request ECMO. The hospital must decide what fair process should govern whether this new escalation is offered.

policies.text: do not offer escalation that cannot reasonably achieve the agreed goal, after transparent explanation
policies.text_detailed: Do not offer an escalation that cannot reasonably achieve the agreed goal, after explaining transparently what the goal is and why the escalation cannot meet it, with the explanation given in writing.

policies.text: use second opinion/ethics review/appeal before final nonoffer when disagreement persists
policies.text_detailed: Obtain a second opinion, ethics review and an appeal opportunity before any final non-offer where disagreement persists, with the timeline stated and the surrogate told how to use each step.

policies.text: offer a time-limited trial if benefit is uncertain rather than effectively absent
policies.text_detailed: Offer a time-limited trial where benefit is uncertain rather than effectively absent, with the distinction stated and the stopping criteria agreed before the trial begins.

policies.text: temporarily maintain eligibility while transfer to a willing center is explored
policies.text_detailed: Maintain eligibility temporarily while transfer to a willing centre is explored, with the search documented and support continued while it remains realistic.

policies.text: allow surrogate request to carry presumptive weight where some plausible goal-concordant benefit remains
policies.text_detailed: Give the surrogate's request presumptive weight where some plausible goal-concordant benefit remains, with plausibility assessed against the agreed goal and the assessment recorded.

policies.text: professional-integrity/nonmaleficence permits firm nonoffer when escalation cannot meet the goal
policies.text_detailed: Permit a firm non-offer on grounds of professional integrity and non-maleficence where the escalation cannot meet the goal, with that finding made institutionally rather than by the bedside team alone.

policies.text: Tell the surrogate in writing, at the time of the request, what will and will not be offered and why, with the route to a second opinion named.
policies.text_detailed: Tell the surrogate in writing, at the time of the request, what will and will not be offered and why, naming the route to a second opinion and the person who will handle it.

cases.title: Somatic support after BD/DNC during pregnancy
cases.concise: A pregnant adult at 18 weeks' gestation has been validly declared dead by neurologic criteria after catastrophic brain injury. The fetus currently has cardiac activity but is far from viability. For this benchmark, assume somatic support could potentially continue for weeks or months but success is uncertain and would require prolonged ICU-level interventions; the patient's prior wishes did not specifically address pregnancy after death. The surrogate believes the patient strongly valued continuing a wanted pregnancy but is uncertain whether she would have wanted prolonged postmortem bodily support. The hospital must decide what policy should govern whether support continues for fetal development.
cases.detailed: A pregnant adult at 18 weeks' gestation suffers catastrophic brain injury and is validly declared dead by neurologic criteria under accepted medical standards. The pregnancy was wanted and had been progressing normally. Fetal cardiac activity is present, but delivery at the current gestational age would not result in survival. For this benchmark, assume prolonged somatic support might permit fetal growth toward viability but requires mechanical ventilation, endocrine replacement, infection management, nutrition and other ICU interventions for an uncertain period, with meaningful risks of fetal loss, preterm birth and major neonatal morbidity. The patient had previously expressed enthusiasm about the pregnancy and general preferences against prolonged dependence on machines, but left no directive specifically addressing somatic support after death for fetal benefit. The appointed surrogate is uncertain how to reconcile those values. No organ-donation plan independently requires support. The hospital must decide whether to continue support based on fetal prospects and presumed maternal values, defer primarily to the surrogate's interpretation of the patient's wishes, or limit support when prognosis and burdens are disproportionate.

policies.text: follow the deceased patient's known prior wishes concerning postmortem somatic support/pregnancy
policies.text_detailed: Follow the deceased person's known prior wishes about postmortem somatic support and pregnancy, with those wishes established from a document or a recorded conversation rather than from a general impression.

policies.text: allow surrogate/family decision where prior wishes unknown and fetal survival is plausible
policies.text_detailed: Let the surrogate or family decide where prior wishes are unknown and fetal survival is plausible, with plausibility stated as a clinical estimate and the decision revisited as that estimate changes.

policies.text: continue support to a defined fetal viability/delivery threshold when prognosis is reasonable and burdens proportionate
policies.text_detailed: Continue support to a defined gestational threshold where prognosis is reasonable and burdens proportionate, with the threshold set at the outset and the burdens on the family reviewed as it approaches.

policies.text: discontinue because the patient is dead and continued bodily use conflicts with autonomy/dignity absent prior authorization
policies.text_detailed: Discontinue on the ground that the person is dead and continued use of their body conflicts with their autonomy and dignity absent prior authorisation, with the absence of authorisation established rather than assumed.

policies.text: permit continuation only after independent maternal-fetal/ethics review of fetal prognosis, burdens, resources, and prior values
policies.text_detailed: Permit continuation only after independent maternal-fetal and ethics review of fetal prognosis, burdens, resources and the person's prior values, with the review completed before support is committed rather than after.

policies.text: allow substantial family accommodation but not indefinite support where fetal benefit becomes negligible
policies.text_detailed: Allow substantial family accommodation without indefinite support, ending it where fetal benefit becomes negligible, with the point at which that is judged defined in advance and explained to the family.

cases.title: Organ donation after independently chosen MAID
cases.concise: A competent adult with grievous illness has independently requested and been found eligible for legal medical assistance in dying. After that decision, the patient asks whether organs can be donated after death and strongly wants to donate if medically suitable. For this benchmark, assume donation requires hospital-based MAID and pre-donation testing that may modestly burden the patient's final days, the patient may withdraw either decision at any time, and organs will be recovered only after death is determined under accepted criteria. The health system must decide what policy should govern offering and coordinating donation after MAID without allowing donation interests to influence the assisted-dying decision.
cases.detailed: A competent adult with grievous and irremediable illness has undergone the legally required medical-assistance-in-dying assessments and has been found eligible. The MAID decision was made before any organ-donation discussion and is documented as voluntary and independent of transplantation needs. The patient subsequently asks whether they can donate organs and describes donation as an important final act of altruism. For this benchmark, assume the patient is medically suitable for potential donation; successful donation would require additional testing, coordination and hospital-based MAID rather than the patient's preferred home setting; and these logistical changes create modest but real burdens. The patient may withdraw consent for MAID or donation at any time. Organ recovery will occur only after death has been determined under accepted criteria, and transplant clinicians will not participate in evaluating MAID eligibility. The system must decide whether eligible MAID patients should routinely be offered the opportunity to donate, whether donation should be discussed only when the patient raises it, and what safeguards are required to keep the two decisions independent.

policies.text: offer donation to medically suitable competent patients after the MAID decision is independently established, with separation, first-person consent, withdrawal rights, and dead-donor-rule compliance
policies.text_detailed: Offer donation to medically suitable competent patients only after the assisted-dying decision is independently established, with separate teams, first-person consent, an unconditional right to withdraw, and compliance with the dead-donor rule.

policies.text: discuss donation only after patient initiation or a defined neutral timing trigger to minimize influence
policies.text_detailed: Raise donation only after the patient initiates it or at a defined neutral point, with that point fixed in policy so that the timing cannot be adjusted toward a donation outcome.

policies.text: decline donation when premortem procedures or logistics impose burdens the donor has not separately authorized
policies.text_detailed: Decline donation where premortem procedures or logistics would impose burdens the donor has not separately authorised, with each such procedure consented to specifically rather than covered by a general agreement.

policies.text: autonomy-based facilitation of donation
policies.text_detailed: Facilitate donation on autonomy grounds, treating the patient's wish to donate as theirs to act on, with the arrangements made without altering the assisted-dying process.

policies.text: public-trust/noninstrumentalization safeguards requiring strict separation of care teams and decisions
policies.text_detailed: Require strict separation of care teams and decisions on public-trust grounds, with the separation structural rather than procedural and stated publicly so that it can be relied on.

policies.text: permit clinician conscience opt-out while ensuring institutional continuity/transfer
policies.text_detailed: Permit clinician conscience opt-out while the institution guarantees continuity and transfer, with the alternative clinician identified in advance rather than sought when the objection arises.

policies.text: Let the patient raise donation whenever they wish and answer fully, without allowing the donation question to alter the timing or handling of the assisted-dying decision.
policies.text_detailed: Let the patient raise donation whenever they wish and answer fully, without allowing the donation question to alter the timing or handling of the assisted-dying decision, and record that the two were kept separate.

cases.title: Family objection to BD/DNC testing
cases.concise: A child has catastrophic irreversible brain injury, no observed brain-mediated responses and no plausible confounder, and clinicians believe formal testing for death by neurologic criteria is indicated. The parents object to the neurologic examination and apnea test because they believe testing itself may hasten death and their religious tradition recognizes death only when the heart permanently stops. For this benchmark, assume the team has explained the purpose and risks of testing, no organ-donation decision is pending, and a short delay for consultation is medically feasible. The hospital must decide what process should govern whether formal BD/DNC testing proceeds over parental objection.
cases.detailed: A child in the pediatric ICU has catastrophic irreversible brain injury after a prolonged period without cerebral perfusion. The known cause of injury has been established, temperature and blood pressure are adequate, sedating/paralyzing drugs and major metabolic confounders have been excluded, and repeated bedside examinations show no brain-mediated responses. The treating team believes the child is likely to meet criteria for death by neurologic criteria and proposes the formal neurologic examination and apnea testing required by current standards. The parents object. They fear the apnea test could itself cause cardiopulmonary deterioration and explain that their religious understanding recognizes death only after irreversible circulatory arrest. For this benchmark, assume clinicians have explained that the purpose of testing is to determine whether the child is already dead by neurologic criteria rather than to decide whether life support should be withdrawn; no organ-donation decision is pending; and a short period for ethics/spiritual consultation is feasible without immediate harm to another patient. The hospital must decide whether parental consent is required, whether testing should be delayed for accommodation or alternative testing where medically appropriate, or whether clinicians should proceed despite objection as part of their duty to determine death.

policies.text: proceed after clear communication because determining death is a professional responsibility not contingent on family authorization
policies.text_detailed: Proceed after clear communication, on the ground that determining death is a professional responsibility rather than something requiring family authorisation, with the communication documented and support offered throughout.

policies.text: allow a brief accommodation period for family understanding/religious support before testing when clinically feasible
policies.text_detailed: Allow a brief accommodation period for family understanding and religious support before testing where that is clinically feasible, with the period stated and the reason for any limit explained.

policies.text: require family permission for apnea testing because it carries procedural risk and profound moral significance
policies.text_detailed: Require family permission for apnoea testing specifically, on the ground that it carries procedural risk and profound significance, while other components of the determination proceed.

policies.text: use ancillary testing instead of apnea testing when objection/risk makes that a valid guideline pathway
policies.text_detailed: Use ancillary testing in place of apnoea testing where objection or clinical risk makes that a valid guideline pathway, with the substitution recorded and the guideline basis named.

policies.text: proceed over objection only after second opinion/ethics/legal review
policies.text_detailed: Proceed over objection only after a second opinion and ethics or legal review, with each completed and recorded before testing rather than sought afterwards.

policies.text: transfer when feasible if another institution can accommodate objection without abandoning accepted death-determination standards
policies.text_detailed: Transfer where feasible if another institution can accommodate the objection without departing from accepted death-determination standards, with the search documented and support continued while it proceeds.

policies.text: Explain what the testing involves and why before it happens, and allow a short defined period for the family to gather, rather than proceeding on the clinical timetable alone.
policies.text_detailed: Explain what the testing involves and why before it happens, and allow a short defined period for the family to gather, rather than proceeding on the clinical timetable alone, with the period stated at the time.

cases.title: Allocation of publicly funded IVF
cases.concise: A public health system funds fewer IVF cycles each year than the number of eligible patients who seek treatment. All applicants in this benchmark meet the minimum clinical criteria for IVF and face no contraindication to pregnancy. Demand exceeds capacity by about one third. The program must adopt one transparent rule for assigning funded treatment slots among eligible applicants. For this benchmark, assume the legally permitted options include a clinical-prognosis priority rule, an equal-opportunity lottery after minimum eligibility, and a published multifactor priority rule incorporating time sensitivity and selected patient characteristics. The program must decide which allocation policy to use.
cases.detailed: A public health system has committed to funding IVF but cannot immediately provide treatment to every eligible applicant. Annual demand is approximately one third greater than funded capacity. All applicants considered here meet the same baseline clinical-access requirements and have no contraindication to pregnancy. The program therefore must decide how to rank eligible applicants for the limited funded cycles. One approach gives greater priority to applicants with a higher estimated probability of treatment success or greater time sensitivity because fertility is declining. A second gives all eligible applicants an equal chance through a transparent lottery or queue rule. A third uses a published multifactor score that may include prognosis, time sensitivity, prior treatment and selected distributive criteria. For this benchmark, assume each approach is legally available and the decision is the ethical design of the allocation rule, not the legality of public IVF funding itself.

policies.text: prioritize expected live-birth effectiveness/prognosis
lottery/equal chance after minimum eligibility
multifactor priority using urgency/time-sensitivity, prior access, and distributive criteria
first-come/first-served
prioritize broader access over maximizing aggregate live births
equal-access framework rejecting family-status/social-worth exclusions
efficiency framework allocating where expected benefit per funded cycle is highest

cases.title: Prenatal screening and disability justice
cases.concise: A public prenatal program offers non-invasive prenatal testing for trisomy 21 to pregnant patients. The test is safe and more accurate than older screening methods, but it is still a screening test rather than a definitive diagnosis. Disability organizations have raised concern that routinized testing can convey that lives with Down syndrome are less valuable, while many patients value early access to information. The program must decide whether to offer NIPT routinely with balanced condition information, require a more explicit opt-in counseling step before testing, or narrow the scope of routine screening. For this benchmark, assume all options are legally available and follow-up diagnostic testing is accessible.
cases.detailed: A publicly funded prenatal program is redesigning how it offers NIPT for trisomy 21. NIPT provides earlier and more accurate screening than older methods without the procedure-related miscarriage risk of invasive diagnostic tests, but positive results still require confirmation before irreversible decisions. Most patients value the opportunity to receive information, yet disability advocates and families of people with Down syndrome have raised concerns that highly routinized screening can create subtle pressure, present disability mainly through deficits, and contribute to stigma or reduced social support. The program can make NIPT a routine universal offer accompanied by balanced condition information, require an explicit opt-in counseling encounter emphasizing that testing is optional and presenting lived-experience information, or limit routine screening more narrowly where the social harms of routinization are judged substantial. The program must choose a policy that preserves meaningful informed choice without treating disability as a life not worth living.

policies.text: routine universal NIPT offer with balanced condition/disability information
explicit opt-in after values-oriented pretest counseling
narrower testing scope for serious health conditions, resisting routinized trait expansion
disability-inclusive counseling with lived-experience/support information as a required component of informed choice
non-directive availability emphasizing autonomous reproductive choice
stronger program-level limits when routinization predictably increases stigma/service erosion
universal offer with standardized neutral information but no mandatory values session

cases.title: Multifetal pregnancy reduction
cases.concise: A patient becomes pregnant with triplets after fertility treatment. Continuing all three fetuses carries higher maternal and perinatal risk than a singleton or twin pregnancy, but reduction itself carries procedural and moral burdens and a small risk of losing the entire pregnancy. The patient is medically stable and has decision-making capacity. The service must decide whether to use a nondirective patient-choice policy, recommend reduction when a specified risk threshold is met while leaving the final decision to the patient, or restrict reduction without a strong medical indication. For this benchmark, assume each policy is legally available and timely specialist counseling is accessible.
cases.detailed: A patient who conceived through fertility treatment is found in the first trimester to have a viable triplet pregnancy. The clinical team explains that higher-order multifetal pregnancy increases maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality compared with singleton pregnancy and that reduction to twins or a singleton can reduce some of these risks. The team also explains that multifetal pregnancy reduction ends one or more fetal lives and carries a small procedure-related risk to the remaining pregnancy. The patient is medically stable, has capacity and has time for specialist counseling within the procedure window. The service must choose a standing policy: nondirective counseling with access based on the patient's informed choice; a policy in which clinicians make a recommendation for reduction when predefined maternal/perinatal risk thresholds are reached but do not override refusal; or a more restrictive policy limiting reduction to cases with a strong medical indication. For this benchmark, all three institutional policies are legally permissible.

policies.text: provide nondirective counseling and access, respecting patient choice
strongly recommend reduction above a defined maternal/fetal risk threshold while leaving final choice to patient
continue pregnancy with intensive high-risk care when patient declines reduction
restrict reduction requested solely for nonmedical preference below a specified fetal number/risk threshold
autonomy framework favoring patient control
maternal/fetal beneficence framework favoring reduction when expected morbidity reduction is large
Provide the counselling and, where chosen, the procedure at the centre already managing the pregnancy, so that acting on the decision does not require travel or repeating the history.

cases.title: Uterus transplantation
cases.concise: A specialized center can perform uterus transplantation for carefully selected patients with absolute uterine factor infertility. The procedure can enable gestation and live birth, but it requires major transplantation surgery, temporary immunosuppression and later graft removal; living donation can also expose a healthy donor to major surgery. The center has trained staff and outcome monitoring. A medically eligible patient understands that adoption and, where lawful, gestational surrogacy avoid transplantation risks but strongly values the possibility of carrying a pregnancy. The center must decide whether to offer UTx as selected clinical care, limit access to a prospective registry/research-style program, or decline routine provision because the intervention is non-life-saving and risk intensive.
cases.detailed: A tertiary transplant and reproductive-medicine center has the technical expertise to perform uterus transplantation for patients with absolute uterine factor infertility. Published programs have now produced live births, but UTx remains resource intensive and exposes the recipient to transplantation surgery, immunosuppression, pregnancy under transplant management and a later operation to remove the graft. Living-donor programs additionally expose a healthy donor to substantial surgery; deceased-donor grafts avoid that donor risk but introduce other limitations. A medically eligible patient has received detailed counseling and strongly prefers the possibility of gestating a pregnancy, while understanding that adoption and, where legally available, gestational surrogacy do not carry transplantation risks. The program must choose whether UTx should be available as carefully selected clinical treatment, only within a tightly governed prospective registry or research-like pathway, or not routinely offered because the reproductive benefit does not justify the aggregate donor, recipient, fetal and resource burdens.

policies.text: offer routine-but-highly-specialized UTx to selected informed candidates meeting program criteria
restrict UTx to prospective registry/research protocols and expert centers
decline routine provision because transplant/donor/pregnancy burdens are disproportionate for a non-life-saving reproductive benefit
prefer deceased-donor pathway where feasible to reduce living-donor harm
reproductive-autonomy framework recognizing gestational parenthood as a substantial interest
nonmaleficence framework giving high weight to recipient/donor surgical and immunosuppression risks

resource-justice rule requiring transparent comparison with other transplant/reproductive priorities rather than assuming infertility treatment is trivial or automatically equivalent to lifesaving transplantation
Publish what the programme offers, its outcomes so far and its selection criteria, so that patients can judge for themselves whether to seek it.

cases.title: Posthumous use of stored gametes/embryos
cases.concise: A fertility program stores reproductive material created or banked during a couple's treatment. One genetic contributor dies before the material is used. The surviving partner asks to proceed with reproduction. The clinic's records contain strong evidence that the deceased wanted children with the surviving partner but the consent form does not contain an explicit signed posthumous-use authorization. There is no evidence the deceased opposed posthumous reproduction. The program must decide whether reproductive use should require explicit written authorization, may proceed for a surviving spouse or partner when strong evidence of the deceased's wishes exists, or should be prohibited whenever contemporaneous consent cannot be obtained. For this benchmark, assume all three policies are legally available.
cases.detailed: A fertility program is storing cryopreserved reproductive material originally banked for family building by a couple. One genetic contributor dies unexpectedly before the material is used. The surviving partner wants to use the stored material to attempt pregnancy. The deceased repeatedly expressed a plan to have children with this partner and participated in fertility treatment, but the clinic's older consent form did not separately ask for signed authorization for posthumous reproductive use. There is no contrary statement and no dispute from another person with a stronger reproductive claim. The clinic distinguishes the decision to preserve or retrieve reproductive tissue from the later decision to use it for reproduction. It must adopt a policy for reproductive use: explicit written authorization only; allow a surviving spouse/partner when strong reliable evidence shows posthumous use accords with the deceased's wishes; or prohibit use whenever the deceased cannot give contemporaneous consent. For this benchmark, each policy is legally available, counseling is available and the surviving partner has had time to grieve before deciding.

policies.text: written-authorization-only use
permit surviving spouse/partner use without written directive only when strong evidence shows deceased's reproductive wishes and no contrary evidence
categorical nonuse absent explicit authorization
honor a specific prior prohibition even if survivor wants use
precedent reproductive autonomy framework favoring deceased's prior intent
surviving partner/reliance framework allowing use where a jointly formed reproductive plan is strongly evidenced and no objection exists

cases.title: Institutional abortion-service policy
cases.concise: A general hospital provides obstetric, gynecologic and emergency care in a region where abortion is lawful under the circumstances represented here. The hospital can staff abortion care directly but leadership is considering a narrower service policy because some clinicians and community stakeholders object. Other local providers exist, though referral can add travel and delay. The hospital must choose whether to provide abortion broadly within ordinary clinical/legal limits, provide only a narrower set of indications while guaranteeing timely referral or transfer for other lawful care, or ordinarily decline abortion provision while maintaining emergency treatment and an access pathway elsewhere. For this benchmark, assume all three institutional policies are lawful.
cases.detailed: A regional general hospital offers comprehensive obstetric and gynecologic care and has clinicians capable of providing medication and procedural abortion. Abortion is lawful for the patients and gestational ranges relevant to this benchmark. Hospital leaders are considering whether the institution should integrate abortion into ordinary reproductive care, restrict direct provision to a narrower set of gestational ages or clinical indications while guaranteeing a timely external pathway, or generally decline direct abortion services except urgent health-preserving care while directing patients elsewhere. Some staff and community members have moral objections; other patients and clinicians argue that exclusion from a comprehensive hospital creates stigma, delay and unequal access. Alternative providers are available but may require additional travel and several days of delay. The hospital must choose its standing service policy, not adjudicate the morality of an individual abortion.

policies.text: broad in-system provision within clinical/legal limits
narrower direct provision plus guaranteed timely referral/transfer for services not offered
referral-centered non-provision except urgent medically necessary care
hospital-level conscience accommodation only if equivalent timely access is institutionally guaranteed
access-justice/professional-duty framework favoring mainstream integrated provision
institutional pluralism framework permitting narrower service identity while imposing nonabandonment/access duties
Publish what the hospital does and does not provide, so that a patient knows before arriving rather than at the point of need.

cases.title: Permanent contraception requested by a young childfree adult
cases.concise: A competent 25-year-old adult with no children requests bilateral salpingectomy for permanent contraception. The patient has made the same request at more than one visit, understands that the procedure is intended to be irreversible, understands surgical risks and contraceptive alternatives, and states a stable desire never to become pregnant or parent. There is no coercion, acute psychiatric crisis, postpartum pressure, medical contraindication, or legal barrier. The service must decide whether to provide the procedure after ordinary informed shared decision making, require additional deliberative safeguards because of the patient's age and nulliparity, or use age/parity thresholds to defer or decline permanent contraception.
cases.detailed: A 25-year-old competent adult with no children has requested permanent contraception at two visits separated in time. The patient describes a longstanding desire not to become pregnant or parent and prefers bilateral salpingectomy over reversible contraceptive methods after counseling about efficacy, surgical risks, irreversibility, possible failure and ectopic pregnancy, and the availability of long-acting reversible options. The patient understands that future preferences can change and accepts that regret cannot be eliminated. There is no evidence of coercion, untreated acute mental illness, relationship crisis, postpartum decision pressure, financial inducement, or medical contraindication. The procedure is lawful and ordinarily available in the service. Clinicians nevertheless disagree about whether young age and nulliparity justify a mandatory waiting period, a second independent consultation, or refusal until an age/parity threshold is reached. The service must set a prospective policy governing such requests.

policies.text: provide after ordinary nonjudgmental informed shared decision making with no age/parity veto
use longitudinal counseling or optional return visit to support sustained deliberation without making delay a categorical barrier
require independent second clinical review for unusually young/nulliparous requests
impose a uniform cooling-off interval before elective permanent contraception
defer/decline below a defined age/parity threshold because of anticipated regret
reproductive-autonomy/reproductive-justice rule giving the competent patient's reproductive values primary authority while screening for coercion and demographic bias
future-self/nonmaleficence rule permitting proportionate deliberative safeguards for irreversible decisions while rejecting permanent demographic vetoes
Provide the procedure on the same terms as for any other adult, without an added waiting period, second review or parity threshold that would not apply to an older or parenting patient.

cases.title: Embryo disposition after separation
cases.concise: A fertility clinic stores embryos created with the gametes of two former partners. They are now separated and disagree about reproductive use: one wants to use an embryo to attempt pregnancy and the other does not want genetic parenthood after the relationship has ended. Their original consent form anticipated separation but did not clearly say whether a prior preference would remain binding over a later objection. The clinic must choose a prospective default policy for cases like this: require contemporaneous mutual consent for reproductive use, enforce a sufficiently specific prior written directive, or default against reproductive use when either genetic contributor currently objects. For this benchmark, assume each prospective policy is legally available.
cases.detailed: A fertility program is revising the consent policy used before couples create cryopreserved embryos. A recurrent problem arises when former partners separate and later disagree: one wants to use a jointly created embryo to attempt pregnancy, while the other objects to becoming a genetic parent after the relationship has ended. Existing forms may contain broad disposition preferences but fail to state clearly whether those preferences remain binding after a later change of mind. Fertility-patient research shows that embryo-disposition preferences can be complex, emotionally difficult and change over time. The clinic wants a clear prospective rule that future patients will understand before embryo creation. It can require contemporaneous mutual consent for any reproductive use; enforce a sufficiently explicit prior written directive even after one party changes position; or adopt a default that no embryo will be used reproductively when either genetic contributor currently objects, regardless of ambiguous prior language. For this benchmark, each policy is legally permissible and does not determine nonreproductive disposition such as storage or discard.

policies.text: contemporaneous mutual consent required for reproductive use
enforce sufficiently specific prior disposition agreement unless both revise it
default against reproductive use when either genetic contributor currently objects
permit use by one former partner when prior agreement clearly authorized it and embryos are that person's only realistic path to genetic parenthood
require advance choices plus periodic reconfirmation while both retain control
resolve ambiguity through no reproductive use but permit mutually authorized discard/donation alternatives
Put the disposition agreement in front of both people again at each storage renewal, so that what happens on disagreement is settled while both still agree.

cases.title: Unclaimed cryopreserved embryos
cases.concise: A fertility program has stored cryopreserved embryos for many years. Storage fees have not been paid, repeated attempts to contact the people with dispositional authority have failed, and no current valid instruction specifies what should happen if contact is lost. Continued indefinite storage imposes real cost and administrative burden. The program must decide whether to continue storage indefinitely unless explicit permission to discard is found, treat embryos as unclaimed after a defined notice period and thaw/discard them, or permit research or donation only when earlier specific authorization for that disposition exists. For this benchmark, assume the clinic has made extensive documented contact attempts and no controlling law requires indefinite storage.
cases.detailed: A fertility clinic has a group of cryopreserved embryos that have remained in storage for more than ten years. The people with dispositional authority have not paid storage fees, have not updated contact information and cannot be reached despite repeated letters, electronic messages, telephone attempts and a final notice sent using the clinic's documented policy. Their original forms do not contain a currently operative instruction for prolonged loss of contact. Continued storage is feasible but imposes ongoing cost, monitoring and liability and cannot be guaranteed indefinitely. The clinic is deciding its default policy for these situations. It may continue storage unless explicit permission for disposal is found; define a reasonable period and notice process after which embryos become unclaimed and may be thawed/discarded; or allow non-discard uses such as research or donation only where the patients previously gave specific written authorization for that use. For this benchmark, no law independently requires indefinite storage, and absent prior authorization the program cannot assume that research or reproductive donation was desired.

policies.text: continue storage for a long defined period before any default disposal
thaw/discard after a defined reasonable contact/notice period
transfer storage responsibility/fees under a predefined contract before default disposition
prohibit research/reproductive donation absent specific prior authorization
require prospective explicit default-disposition consent at storage initiation/renewal to minimize future unclaimed status

Treat storage without instruction as a duty owed to the people who created the embryos: act only after the notice they were promised has genuinely been given, and follow the disposition they last recorded.

cases.title: Donor anonymity and adult access to donor identity
cases.concise: A fertility program is designing its policy for future gamete donations. Donor-conceived adults increasingly seek information about genetic origins, while some prospective donors and recipient parents value anonymity or controlled contact. Home DNA databases also make practical anonymity increasingly difficult to guarantee. The program must choose whether donors will be identifiable to donor-conceived adults at age 18, whether only non-identifying information will be released with identifying contact requiring mutual consent, or whether the program will promise anonymity while warning that genetic matching may defeat it in practice. Medical and genetic information will be retained under all policies.
cases.detailed: A fertility program is redesigning the consent terms for future sperm, oocyte and embryo donation. Donor-conceived adults often report a strong interest in medical, genealogical and identifying information, and consumer DNA databases can reveal donor identities even where clinics promise anonymity. At the same time, some donors say they would not have donated under mandatory identity release, and some recipient parents prefer an anonymous model. The program wants a rule that is transparent before anyone donates or receives treatment. It can adopt an open-identity policy in which a donor-conceived adult may obtain identifying information at age 18 but the donor has no obligation to communicate; a non-identifying-information policy with identifying contact only when both adult offspring and donor consent; or an anonymity-preserving policy that withholds identifying information through the program while explicitly warning all parties that external DNA matching makes practical anonymity impossible to guarantee. Under every policy, the program permanently retains relevant medical/genetic history and clearly explains the chosen disclosure rules before consent.

policies.text: open identity at adulthood
nonidentifying information plus mutual-consent identity/contact
preserve promised anonymity while warning that DNA technology makes practical secrecy unreliable
permanent medical/genetic update channel regardless of identity release
donor-conceived right-to-know framework favoring mature access
donor privacy/reliance framework protecting the terms under which donation occurred
tiered prospective choice among identifiable/mutual-consent/limited-information donation with clear downstream consequences

cases.title: Heritable genome editing to prevent serious disease
cases.concise: A future regulator is evaluating heritable genome editing for couples at high risk of transmitting a severe, early-onset monogenic disease. For this benchmark, assume the editing method has undergone extensive preclinical study, can correct the disease-causing variant with a very low rate of unintended genomic changes, and meets a regulator-defined technical threshold for cautious first clinical use. The change would be heritable. Some prospective parents can avoid the disease through IVF with preimplantation genetic testing, but for a small subgroup PGT is unlikely to yield an unaffected genetically related embryo. The regulator must choose whether to permit carefully overseen reproductive editing for serious disease, permit it only when no reasonable reproductive alternative can achieve the same disease-prevention goal, or continue to prohibit reproductive use while allowing laboratory research.
cases.detailed: A national regulator is developing policy for a possible first clinical pathway for heritable human genome editing. The proposed use is limited to a severe, highly penetrant, early-onset monogenic disease that causes substantial morbidity and shortened life expectancy. For this benchmark, assume independent scientific review has concluded that the editing method has crossed a predefined technical threshold for cautious clinical investigation: the intended correction is highly reliable, known off-target and mosaicism risks are very low, and long-term multigenerational uncertainty remains but is no longer so large that safety alone resolves the policy question. The edit would be introduced into an embryo used to establish a pregnancy and could be inherited by descendants. Standard IVF with PGT can avoid the condition for many prospective parents, but a small subgroup has little or no realistic chance of producing an unaffected genetically related embryo without editing. The regulator must decide whether serious-disease reproductive editing should be permitted under specialized approval and long-term follow-up, limited only to cases lacking a reasonable alternative such as effective PGT, or kept outside reproductive medicine while laboratory embryo-editing research continues.

policies.text: permit severe monogenic disease use under stringent national/international oversight
permit only when PGT/other reasonable alternatives cannot reliably avoid disease
continue reproductive prohibition while allowing laboratory research
broader reproductive-choice permission for serious disease once safety is adequate
precautionary future-generation rule requiring multigenerational follow-up/registry
equity rule conditioning access on fair distribution/nonenhancement boundaries
categorical germline prohibition even after technical readiness because future persons and species-level change are not appropriately authorized
Involve affected families and people living with the condition in setting the criteria, and publish the outcome of that involvement alongside any decision to permit or refuse.

cases.title: Polygenic embryo screening for non-disease traits
cases.concise: A fertility clinic is approached by a commercial genetics service offering polygenic embryo scores for non-disease traits such as predicted adult height and cognition-related educational measures. The scores are probabilistic, depend partly on ancestry and environment, and can only modestly shift expected trait distributions among the limited embryos available in a typical IVF cycle. The clinic already performs validated genetic testing for serious monogenic disease. It must decide whether to prohibit embryo ranking for non-medical traits, allow informed patients to use available trait scores as an exercise of reproductive choice, or limit polygenic embryo ranking to health-related disease-risk applications that meet a defined evidence threshold.
cases.detailed: A fertility clinic is revising its policy on polygenic embryo screening. A commercial laboratory can calculate polygenic scores from IVF embryos for multifactorial disease risks and for non-disease traits such as predicted adult height or cognition-related educational measures. For this benchmark, assume the laboratory's analytic pipeline is technically reliable in the narrow sense that it reproduces its specified scores, but the trait predictions remain probabilistic, ancestry-sensitive and substantially influenced by environment; the expected difference between embryos available within one IVF cycle is modest. The clinic's question is not whether parents may receive ordinary genetic information, but whether clinicians should participate in ranking embryos specifically by non-disease trait scores. The clinic must choose among prohibiting such trait ranking, permitting it after detailed counseling about limitations and social risks, or allowing polygenic ranking only for validated health-related disease risks while excluding non-medical traits.

policies.text: prohibit nonmedical trait ranking
research-only until evidence thresholds met
allow validated serious health-risk applications but not height/cognition-type traits
permit informed reproductive choice for validated traits
restrict because eugenic/social stratification and ancestry-performance inequities create population harms
allow only under equity/validity thresholds across ancestry groups
clinic may decline trait selection as inconsistent with reproductive-medical purpose even if lawful

cases.title: Genetic enhancement beyond disease prevention
cases.concise: A future heritable genome-editing intervention can, for this benchmark, safely increase a well-characterized component of memory performance above the typical population range without known adverse health effects. The edit is not needed to treat disease or restore impaired function and would be inherited by future descendants. Prospective parents ask to use it during IVF. The regulator must decide whether to permit enhancement as part of reproductive liberty, prohibit heritable enhancement beyond disease prevention, or permit editing only to prevent disease or restore function into a typical healthy range.
cases.detailed: A future regulator has already established a tightly governed pathway for some disease-related genome-editing research. A new proposed reproductive application would alter a well-characterized genetic pathway so that a resulting child is expected to have a measurable improvement in a specific component of memory performance above the ordinary healthy range. For this benchmark, assume extensive evidence shows the intervention itself has a safety profile comparable to accepted reproductive interventions and does not create a known health trade-off; the enhancement is nevertheless probabilistic rather than a guarantee of educational or life success. The edit would be heritable. No disease is being treated and the prospective embryo would otherwise be expected to develop within the normal healthy range. Regulators must choose whether parents may use a safe heritable enhancement as an exercise of reproductive liberty, whether all reproductive enhancement should remain prohibited, or whether heritable editing may be confined to disease prevention and restoration of impaired function without allowing above-typical enhancement.

policies.text: permit competent parental reproductive choice for safe enhancement
permit only interventions restoring/preventing serious disease or maintaining normal species functioning
prohibit reproductive enhancement categorically
permit limited enhancement only where access is equitable and social externalities controlled
precautionary restriction because effects on future generations/social competition remain morally uncertain despite technical safety
anti-eugenics/equal-status rule barring selection that entrenches hierarchy or positional arms races
Decide by public deliberation with a published result rather than by clinic-level discretion, so that access does not turn on which programme a family happens to reach.

cases.title: Secondary findings in adult clinical genomic sequencing
cases.concise: An adult undergoes clinical genome sequencing to investigate an unexplained medical condition. The laboratory can also deliberately analyze a defined list of pathogenic variants associated with serious conditions for which established surveillance or preventive treatment can substantially reduce morbidity or mortality. These findings are unrelated to the original diagnostic question. The patient has decision-making capacity and can receive genetic counseling. The health system must decide whether to analyze and return the defined actionable findings by default with an informed opt-out, analyze them only when the patient explicitly opts in beforehand, or use a narrower policy restricted to findings meeting a particularly high threshold of penetrance and actionability.
cases.detailed: An adult with decision-making capacity is undergoing clinical exome/genome sequencing for a diagnostic indication. In addition to variants related to that indication, the laboratory can intentionally analyze a predefined set of gene–disease pairs associated with serious conditions for which surveillance, preventive treatment or other established intervention can meaningfully reduce morbidity or mortality. The findings would be analytically confirmed and clinically interpreted, and pre- and post-test genetic counseling is available. The service recognizes both potential medical benefit and a patient's interest in not receiving unwanted risk information. It must choose a standing policy: routinely analyze and offer return of the defined actionable secondary findings unless the patient opts out at consent; perform secondary analysis only after explicit opt-in; or use a narrower mandatory offer limited to findings that meet a higher threshold of penetrance and clinical actionability. The decision concerns secondary findings intentionally sought under policy, not accidental laboratory observations.

policies.text: analyze/return defined actionable list with informed opt-out
require opt-in before any secondary analysis
return only very-high-actionability/high-penetrance findings
allow patients to choose categories/timing of secondary information
return actionable findings by default because preventable morbidity justifies a weak paternalistic default
right-not-to-know framework favoring explicit prior authorization
staged recontact model permitting later choice rather than one-time all-or-none consent

cases.title: DTC genetics and relatives' interests
cases.concise: A direct-to-consumer genetic testing service identifies a result in an adult consumer that, after confirmatory testing, indicates a high risk of a serious inherited cancer syndrome. First-degree relatives have a substantial chance of carrying the same pathogenic variant, and established surveillance could reduce their risk of severe disease. The consumer does not want the service to contact relatives and says the result is private. The service must decide whether confidentiality leaves all family disclosure under the consumer's control while offering communication tools, whether it should actively support and follow up on consumer-mediated disclosure, or whether enrollment should include a narrow pre-consented pathway allowing de-identified warning of identifiable relatives when a serious actionable familial risk is confirmed and the consumer refuses to inform them.
cases.detailed: A commercial direct-to-consumer genetics service offers health-risk analysis and confirmatory clinical testing for selected high-impact results. An adult consumer is confirmed to carry a pathogenic variant associated with a serious inherited cancer syndrome. Close biological relatives have a substantial probability of carrying the same variant, and evidence-based surveillance or preventive intervention could substantially reduce morbidity or mortality if they learn of the risk. The consumer understands this but does not want relatives contacted, citing privacy and difficult family relationships. The service is not the relatives' treating clinician and does not already hold a fiduciary clinical relationship with them. It must choose its prospective policy: keep results under consumer control while providing counseling and family-letter tools; actively support, remind and facilitate consumer-mediated disclosure without contacting relatives itself; or require at enrollment a narrowly defined consent allowing the service to send a de-identified warning pathway to identifiable relatives when a validated serious actionable familial risk is present and the consumer refuses disclosure. The benchmark assumes any direct warning would reveal the minimum information needed to let a relative seek independent counseling/testing and would not disclose the consumer's full report.

policies.text: consumer controls disclosure, supported by communication tools
structured service-mediated support for proband disclosure to relatives
narrow pre-consented warning pathway for serious actionable familial risk
direct warning without consumer consent only under very high preventability/severity threshold
confidentiality/consumer-control framework
relational/familial responsibility framework giving relatives a claim to actionable risk information

cases.title: Extending the 14-day human embryo-research limit
cases.concise: Researchers propose a study of early human developmental processes that begin after day 14. The embryos were donated for research and will never be transferred for reproduction. For this benchmark, assume the scientific question cannot be answered adequately before day 14 or with available alternative models, valid donor consent has been obtained, no embryo will be used for reproduction, and a specialized independent scientific and ethics oversight process is available. The regulator must choose whether to keep the 14-day boundary absolute or permit carefully justified culture beyond it.
cases.detailed: A national embryo-research regulator is reviewing the longstanding rule that intact human embryos may not be cultured in vitro beyond 14 days or the appearance of the primitive streak. A research team proposes work on developmental events that begin after the current boundary and argues that neither animal models nor existing stem-cell-based embryo models can answer the same scientific question. Embryos would be donated voluntarily for research, would never be transferred for reproduction, and would be studied in a specialized licensed laboratory. For this benchmark, assume the proposed research cannot be answered adequately before day 14 or with available alternative models, valid donor consent and non-reproductive use are fixed, and a specialized independent review process can assess scientific merit, necessity, alternatives and the proposed developmental endpoint. The regulator must decide whether the 14-day boundary remains absolute or whether tightly controlled extension to a justified endpoint may be approved.

policies.text: retain fixed 14-day limit
permit extension to a new fixed maximum under specialized review
replace universal day cutoff with staged developmental-milestone/project-specific review
allow extension only for high scientific value/no adequate alternative
embryo moral-status precaution favors a firm boundary
research-benefit/proportionality favors controlled extension
require periodic public/legislative reauthorization rather than indefinite regulator discretion

cases.title: Stem-cell-based embryo models
cases.concise: A laboratory proposes research using three-dimensional human stem-cell-based embryo models that reproduce multiple features of early embryonic development but are not created by fertilization and are not intended for reproductive use. The models are more developmentally complete than earlier systems, and their future capabilities are uncertain. The oversight authority must decide whether all 3D human embryo models should undergo specialized review with defined endpoints, whether oversight should be tiered according to the developmental structures and capabilities each model can reproduce, or whether specified highly integrated experiments should be prohibited even within specialized review.
cases.detailed: A research institution can create three-dimensional structures from human pluripotent stem cells that reproduce increasingly complex aspects of early embryonic development. These stem-cell-based embryo models are research models rather than embryos created through fertilization, and the proposed work involves no uterine transfer or reproductive use. The models can nevertheless reproduce multiple interacting embryonic and extraembryonic features and may become more complete as the science advances. Researchers seek to use them to study developmental processes that are difficult to observe in intact human embryos. The institution has a specialized oversight body with developmental biology, stem-cell, ethics and public representation expertise. It must choose whether all 3D SCBEM research should receive specialized review and a predefined culture endpoint; whether review intensity should be tiered according to the developmental features/capabilities modeled; or whether specified highly integrated or late-endpoint model experiments should remain prohibited even when scientifically valuable.

policies.text: specialized review for all 3D SCBEM work
tiered oversight by developmental capability, integration, endpoint, and scientific purpose
prohibit reproductive transfer/high-integration experiments beyond defined limits
ordinary research oversight for low-capability models with escalation triggers
precaution framework tracking moral concern to increasing organismal resemblance/capability
research-freedom/proportionality framework opposing embryo-equivalent restrictions absent embryo-equivalent capacities
