Publish what is being made, how far it develops and what happens to it, so that oversight is checkable from outside the specialist community.

cases.title: In-vitro gametogenesis for reproduction
cases.concise: A future technique can create functional human eggs or sperm from a patient's somatic cells. For this benchmark, assume preclinical and early translational evidence has reached a regulator-defined threshold for cautious reproductive use, while long-term social and intergenerational evidence remains limited. IVG could help some people who cannot otherwise produce gametes and could eventually enable new forms of genetic parenthood. The regulator must choose whether to permit IVG broadly under ordinary assisted-reproduction safeguards, allow initial reproductive use only for defined infertility indications within licensed registries and long-term follow-up, or continue to prohibit reproductive use while permitting laboratory research until broader social evidence develops.
cases.detailed: A future regulator is considering the first durable clinical policy for human in-vitro gametogenesis. Researchers can generate functional gametes from a person's reprogrammed somatic cells, and for this benchmark assume the gametes have crossed a predefined technical threshold for cautious reproductive use: fertilization, chromosomal integrity and early offspring safety are sufficiently characterized that scientific immaturity alone does not decide the question. Important uncertainty remains about long-term offspring outcomes, scale of embryo creation, access, changes in family structure and possible uses for enhancement or selection. IVG could restore genetically related reproduction for people who cannot produce functional gametes; future applications might also include same-sex genetic parenthood or reproduction outside conventional age limits. The regulator must decide whether to treat safe IVG like other ART with standard safeguards, restrict initial reproductive use to defined infertility indications under licensed registries and long-term follow-up, or prohibit reproductive use until broader ethical/social evidence and governance are more mature while allowing laboratory IVG research.

policies.text: broad clinical use under ART safeguards once safe
initial restricted indications with registry/long-term follow-up
no reproductive use until stronger ethical/social and offspring evidence exists
infertility-only indication initially
permit access irrespective of family form where reproductive use is otherwise safe
restrict uses that enable nonconsensual genetic parenthood or large-scale enhancement/selection
equity rule addressing access and downstream intergenerational monitoring

cases.title: Mitochondrial donation
cases.concise: A patient has a very high risk of transmitting a severe mitochondrial DNA disorder to a genetically related child. Conventional IVF cannot reliably eliminate the risk, and donor eggs would avoid transmission but would also replace the patient's nuclear genetic contribution. A licensed specialist center can perform mitochondrial donation using healthy donor mitochondria, but long-term multigenerational evidence remains limited. The regulator must decide whether to permit mitochondrial donation for serious disease with individual case approval and long-term follow-up, restrict it to cases where alternative reproductive options are unlikely to achieve the patient's disease-prevention and genetic-parenthood goals, or keep reproductive mitochondrial donation prohibited pending longer-term outcome evidence.
cases.detailed: An adult with a pathogenic mitochondrial DNA variant seeks to have a child without transmitting a severe mitochondrial disorder that has caused major illness in multiple family members. Specialists judge the transmission risk high. Standard IVF/embryo testing cannot reliably identify embryos with a sufficiently low disease risk in this case. Egg donation would greatly reduce mitochondrial-disease transmission but the resulting child would not share the intending mother's nuclear genome. A nationally licensed center can perform maternal spindle transfer or pronuclear transfer using healthy donated mitochondria. The resulting child would inherit nuclear DNA from the intending parent(s) and mitochondrial DNA from the donor. The regulator recognizes encouraging clinical outcomes but also limited long-term and intergenerational experience. It must choose whether to authorize serious-disease mitochondrial donation through individual case review and follow-up; restrict authorization to cases where established alternatives offer little or no reasonable prospect of both disease-risk reduction and the intended genetic relationship; or prohibit reproductive use until substantially longer-term evidence is available.

policies.text: permit serious-disease use with case-by-case specialist approval and long-term follow-up
restrict to cases where alternatives provide little/no comparable benefit
prohibit reproductive use pending longer-term safety evidence
affected-family access position favoring availability under safeguards
future-child precaution requiring registry/intergenerational monitoring
reproductive autonomy/beneficence position
equity/public-trust rule restricting non-disease expansion and requiring transparent oversight

cases.title: Non-medical sex selection in IVF
cases.concise: An IVF clinic routinely obtains embryo sex information when patients undergo PGT-A for other clinical reasons. A patient with two healthy children of the same sex asks the clinic to select an otherwise comparable embryo of the other sex for transfer solely for family balancing. No sex-linked disease is involved, and the patient is already undergoing IVF rather than starting IVF only for sex selection. The clinic must decide whether to permit non-medical sex selection after counseling, decline use of embryo sex as a non-medical transfer criterion, or allow it only under a limited family-balancing policy for patients who already have one or more children of the same sex.
cases.detailed: A fertility clinic routinely performs IVF with PGT-A for patients who have an independent clinical indication for assisted reproduction. PGT-A makes embryo sex known even though sex is not the reason for testing. A patient with two healthy children of the same sex has several chromosomally suitable embryos and asks the clinic to transfer an embryo of the other sex because they value the experience of raising children of both sexes. There is no sex-linked disorder and no evidence of family coercion. The clinic recognizes reproductive-liberty arguments but is concerned about gender stereotyping, discrimination, social sex imbalance in some contexts and using clinical resources for a non-medical preference. It must choose a standing policy: permit patients to use sex information in embryo selection after informed counseling; exclude sex from transfer decisions unless medically indicated; or permit non-medical selection only for a defined family-balancing circumstance rather than unrestricted preference.

policies.text: permit informed nonmedical selection
decline all nonmedical sex selection
permit only family balancing
allow clinic-level transparent conscience/policy choice while requiring nondiscriminatory disclosure before treatment
reproductive-liberty framework favoring permission
gender-justice/anti-stereotyping framework favoring prohibition
permit only where coercion/population sex-ratio/social harm risk is low and counseling confirms autonomous preference

cases.title: Gestational-carrier compensation
cases.concise: A fertility program works with adult gestational carriers who have independent legal counsel, medical and psychological screening, their own health coverage, and sole authority over medical decisions during pregnancy. A carrier and intended parents agree that she should receive payment beyond documented expenses for the time, inconvenience and risks of embryo transfer, pregnancy and delivery. The program must decide whether to permit reasonable non-contingent compensation with safeguards, limit payments to reimbursement of expenses and lost income, or permit compensation only within a standardized cap intended to reduce undue inducement while recognizing burdens.
cases.detailed: A fertility program operates in a jurisdiction where compensated gestational-carrier arrangements are lawful. An adult carrier has previously completed a healthy pregnancy and independently volunteers to carry for intended parents. She has separate legal counsel, independent medical and psychological counseling, adequate pregnancy/complication insurance and full authority over prenatal testing, termination, multifetal reduction, delivery and other medical decisions. The parties propose compensation in addition to reimbursement for expenses and lost income. Payment would compensate time, inconvenience and risk and would not depend on conception, pregnancy continuation or birth of a healthy child. The program is deciding its standing policy: allow individually negotiated reasonable compensation under anti-coercion safeguards; limit payment to documented expenses/lost income; or allow compensation but within a transparent standardized range/cap designed to reduce large economic inducements while still recognizing pregnancy burdens.

policies.text: reasonable compensation for time/risk/inconvenience plus independent legal/medical safeguards
reimbursement-only
structured/capped compensation to reduce inducement while recognizing labor/risk
unrestricted market-rate compensation subject to informed consent/noncontingency on healthy birth
carrier-autonomy rule making carrier sole medical decision-maker regardless of compensation
exploitation/justice rule requiring insurance, escrow, independent counsel, and no outcome-contingent payment
Set compensation so the carrier is never out of pocket and is paid for time and risk, with terms fixed in advance and independent legal advice paid for by the programme.

cases.title: Intrafamilial gamete donation / gestational carrying
cases.concise: An adult patient's sister voluntarily offers to donate oocytes so the patient can have a genetically related child. Both adults report a close relationship and deny family pressure. The donor would receive independent counseling, medical screening and legal advice, and the resulting child would be told the donor's identity at a developmentally appropriate time. The fertility program must decide whether intrafamilial donation should be permitted under enhanced independent safeguards, restricted to cases in which unrelated donation is unavailable or impracticable, or generally declined because family obligations create unacceptable risks of coercion and role confusion.
cases.detailed: A fertility program receives a request for an adult sister to donate oocytes to her infertile sibling. The genetic and gestational relationships would not be consanguineous and the arrangement would not simulate sexual reproduction between relatives. The prospective donor initiated the offer and both siblings report that she is free to withdraw. The program can provide separate medical and psychological assessment, independent legal counseling, private interviews to assess pressure, and counseling about disclosure and future family roles. Longitudinal research on some sister-to-sister egg-donation families suggests that family roles can remain stable and relationships can be positive, but evidence is limited and family expectations can create subtle pressure even without overt coercion. The program must choose whether to permit adult intrafamilial donation under enhanced safeguards; restrict it to cases where unrelated donation is unavailable or would impose major barriers; or generally decline intrafamilial donation because family obligation, lineage complexity and long-term relational risks are judged too difficult to manage reliably.

policies.text: permit with enhanced independent counseling/consent
prohibit consanguineous/incest-simulating arrangements
require separate legal/psychological assessment for intergenerational or dependency-heavy arrangements
broadly avoid intrafamilial arrangements because relational pressure is difficult to rule out
relational-autonomy permission when family support is voluntary and role clarity is protected
anti-coercion/child-family-role framework favoring stricter limits
Give the donor a separate clinician and a private route to withdraw at any point, so that a family offer can be declined without the family learning why.

cases.title: Human reproductive cloning
cases.concise: A future reproductive laboratory claims it can create a human embryo by transferring the nucleus of an adult somatic cell into an enucleated oocyte and proposes transferring such an embryo to establish a pregnancy. For this benchmark, assume major technical risks have been substantially reduced so the decision is not determined solely by current animal-cloning failure rates. The regulator must decide whether reproductive cloning should remain categorically prohibited, whether any future use should require a separate democratic/international authorization beyond ordinary reproductive-medicine review, or whether technically safe reproductive cloning should be treated as a permissible form of reproductive choice.
cases.detailed: A national regulator is asked to reconsider its longstanding prohibition on human reproductive cloning. A laboratory proposes somatic cell nuclear transfer to create an embryo genetically very similar in nuclear DNA to an existing adult, followed by uterine transfer and pregnancy. For this benchmark, assume extensive future research has substantially reduced the developmental and obstetric safety concerns that make reproductive cloning unacceptable today, so the policy question cannot be resolved merely by pointing to present technical risk. The resulting child would still develop in a different environment, would not be psychologically or physically identical to the nuclear donor, and would be a distinct person. The regulator can maintain a categorical prohibition grounded in dignity, identity, social and intergenerational concerns; allow reconsideration only after a special democratic/international authorization process because reproductive cloning changes a fundamental boundary of human reproduction; or permit technically safe cloning under ordinary assisted-reproduction consent and child-welfare safeguards.

policies.text: categorical prohibition
future reconsideration only after safety + broad democratic authorization
permission if safety/identity concerns eventually become comparable to accepted ART
prohibition grounded in dignity/noninstrumentalization
limited research-only nuclear-transfer work without reproductive implantation
Consult broadly and publish the reasoning before any change of position, so that a prohibition is maintained or lifted by public decision rather than by the first laboratory to proceed.

cases.title: Artificial-womb technology for extreme prematurity
cases.concise: A future neonatal center can transfer an extremely premature fetus/newborn to an artificial-womb system that continues fluid-based extrauterine support rather than conventional ventilation. For this benchmark, assume early clinical evidence suggests a meaningful chance of improving survival without severe morbidity compared with standard intensive care at a narrow gestational threshold, but long-term outcome evidence remains limited. Parents can receive counseling and conventional neonatal care remains available. The program must decide whether to offer artificial-womb support as a parental option for eligible patients, restrict initial use to a tightly monitored trial/registry at defined gestational thresholds, or require it when the expected benefit over conventional care is substantial and parental refusal would expose the child to markedly worse outcomes.
cases.detailed: A future tertiary neonatal center has an artificial-womb platform intended for fetuses/newborns delivered at the edge of viability. The system provides fluid-based extrauterine support intended to continue organ maturation while avoiding some harms of immediate air ventilation. For this benchmark, assume controlled early clinical evidence indicates that, within a defined gestational and physiologic window, the technology has a meaningful prospect of improving survival without severe morbidity compared with conventional neonatal intensive care, but long-term neurodevelopmental evidence is still limited. Conventional intensive care remains a medically reasonable alternative. Parents have time for urgent but meaningful counseling. The center must choose a standing policy: offer artificial-womb support as one parental option alongside conventional care; restrict use to a prospective trial/registry with narrow eligibility until longer-term evidence matures; or treat artificial-womb support as the recommended/required rescue pathway when its expected benefit over conventional treatment crosses a high threshold, subject to ordinary limits on parental refusal of clearly superior life-saving care.

policies.text: offer as rescue option after parental consent when expected outcome exceeds conventional NICU
restrict initially to trials/specified gestational thresholds
require use when it clearly offers materially better survival/neurodevelopment than standard care
allow parent choice between conventional NICU and AWT when equipoise exists
precautionary restriction due unknown long-term developmental effects
justice/access rule preventing AWT from becoming a resource available only to privileged centers/patients
Keep the conventional neonatal option available in full, with the same staffing and follow-up, so that choosing it is not the lesser path.

cases.title: PGT/HLA matching to conceive a donor sibling
cases.concise: A couple has a child with a serious hematologic disorder that could likely be cured or substantially improve with an HLA-matched stem-cell transplant. No suitable related or unrelated donor has been found. The parents also want another child and ask to use IVF with PGT-HLA to select an embryo that is unaffected by the familial disorder and HLA-matched to the sick child. The planned initial donation is umbilical-cord blood collected at birth, which poses no direct procedural burden to the newborn donor. The fertility program must decide whether to permit PGT-HLA after other donor options are exhausted, permit it more broadly when the future child's independent welfare and family intention are adequately protected, or decline embryo selection undertaken partly for another person's medical benefit.
cases.detailed: A couple has a school-age child with a severe inherited hematologic condition for which allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation offers a high probability of cure or substantial life extension. Standard donor searches have not identified a sufficiently matched donor. The parents independently desire another child and ask the fertility program to perform IVF with PGT-M and HLA typing so that an embryo unaffected by the familial condition and HLA-matched to the sick child can be selected for transfer. The immediate planned donation is umbilical-cord blood obtained at birth; any later bone-marrow or peripheral stem-cell donation would require a separate best-interest review rather than being assumed now. The parents state that the new child would be wanted and valued irrespective of transplant outcome. The program must decide whether PGT-HLA should be permitted only after other clinical donor options are exhausted and when transplant is likely to cure or substantially prolong the existing child's life; permitted whenever the future child's independent welfare is protected and the parents have a genuine family-building intention; or declined because deliberately selecting a child partly as a tissue source creates unacceptable instrumentalization and future pressure.

policies.text: allow after alternatives exhausted and expected sibling benefit substantial
allow more broadly if new child is independently wanted and donation limited to cord blood/low-burden tissue
prohibit HLA selection for instrumental donation
permit low-burden donation but require later donor-child assent for any invasive donation
child-welfare/open-future rule limiting cumulative donation burden
parental reproductive autonomy/rescue rule favoring access
independent ethics review to confirm no reasonable donor alternative and protect future child
Give the future donor child their own clinician and record now what they will be told, so that a child conceived to donate learns their history from the family rather than by accident.

cases.title: Prenatal genome-wide sequencing / secondary findings
cases.concise: A pregnant patient undergoes trio exome/genome sequencing because fetal structural anomalies remain unexplained after standard testing. The laboratory can also identify medically actionable variants unrelated to the fetal anomalies, including findings in the fetus and in one of the parents. Some would affect childhood management; others primarily predict adult-onset disease. The family can receive detailed genetic counseling. The service must decide whether to offer actionable fetal and parental secondary findings with an informed opt-out, restrict routine return to findings relevant to pregnancy, neonatal or childhood management while deferring adult-onset fetal risk, or allow parents to choose among broader secondary-finding categories before sequencing.
cases.detailed: A prenatal genetics service performs trio exome/genome sequencing after ultrasound identifies multiple fetal structural anomalies and chromosomal microarray is nondiagnostic. The sequencing analysis may identify pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants that explain the fetal phenotype, but it can also reveal unrelated medically actionable variants in the fetus or one of the parents. Some secondary findings could change pregnancy, neonatal or childhood surveillance; others predict serious adult-onset conditions for which prevention is available only later. The service provides pre- and post-test counseling and can technically include or exclude categories before analysis. It must choose a standing policy: routinely offer a defined set of actionable fetal and parental secondary findings with informed opt-out; limit routine return to findings relevant to pregnancy, neonatal care or childhood health and defer adult-onset fetal findings to protect the future child's later choice; or let parents opt into broader secondary-finding categories after counseling, including adult-onset and parental findings.

policies.text: offer actionable fetal/parental secondary findings with opt-out
report only findings relevant to fetal/childhood management
allow opt-in to broader categories after counseling
defer adult-onset fetal findings to protect future autonomy
return serious parental actionable findings separately with consent
category-based preference menu
minimal-reporting rule limited to diagnostic indication unless immediate preventable harm would otherwise be missed

cases.title: Fertility preservation for minors facing gonadotoxic therapy
cases.concise: A 12-year-old child needs gonadotoxic cancer therapy within several days. Standard counseling indicates a high risk of future infertility. The child understands that fertility may matter later but is anxious about additional procedures. A fertility-preservation procedure can be performed without materially delaying cancer treatment; it requires anesthesia and tissue retrieval and offers a plausible but uncertain future reproductive benefit. The parents want preservation performed. The team must decide whether to offer and proceed with parent-authorized preservation while seeking the child's assent, require the child's affirmative assent before an invasive procedure when there is no immediate clinical benefit, or defer an experimental/invasive option when the child objects or when expected reproductive benefit is too uncertain relative to burden.
cases.detailed: A 12-year-old with newly diagnosed cancer must begin highly gonadotoxic therapy within several days. The oncology team estimates a substantial risk of permanent infertility from treatment. Fertility specialists can perform gonadal-tissue cryopreservation under anesthesia without materially delaying cancer therapy. For this benchmark, assume the procedure's physical risk is low but nonzero and future reproductive benefit is plausible rather than guaranteed. The procedure would not create embryos and the stored tissue would remain under disposition rules revisited when the child becomes an adult. The child can understand the basic purpose and burdens and expresses anxiety and ambivalence rather than a settled desire for future biological parenthood. The parents strongly favor preservation. The team must decide whether parent permission based on preserving the child's future options is sufficient while seeking developmentally appropriate assent; whether an invasive nontherapeutic procedure should require the child's affirmative assent when the child is capable of meaningful participation; or whether experimental/invasive preservation should be deferred when the child objects or expected benefit is too uncertain relative to burden.

policies.text: routinely offer established preservation with assent
allow parents to authorize low-burden tissue preservation when child cannot assent
respect postpubertal minor objection
defer invasive experimental preservation when delay/burden threatens cancer treatment
future-autonomy framework favoring preservation of reproductive options
present-welfare/nonmaleficence framework limiting experimental burden
Offer the counselling and the procedure without delaying cancer therapy, and record the child's own view whatever their age.

cases.title: Transfer of embryo known to carry monogenic condition
cases.concise: A patient undergoing IVF with PGT-M has one remaining embryo. The embryo is highly likely to result in a child with a serious inherited condition that requires lifelong medical management but is treatable, compatible with meaningful functioning and not expected to cause severe early debility. No unaffected embryo is available. The patient understands the prognosis and says this embryo represents the only remaining opportunity for a genetically related child. The clinic must decide whether to honor the transfer request after specialist counseling, decline transfer because clinicians should not knowingly facilitate avoidable health burdens in a future child, or use a threshold policy that permits transfer for manageable conditions but declines when expected harm crosses a defined severe-early-debility boundary.
cases.detailed: A fertility clinic has completed PGT-M for a patient at risk of transmitting a monogenic disorder. The only remaining embryo carries a pathogenic variant with high penetrance. For this benchmark, assume the expected phenotype is serious and requires lifelong treatment and monitoring, but established therapies allow many affected people to attain meaningful function and substantial life expectancy; the condition is not expected to produce severe early debility with no reasonable function. The patient has received genetic counseling and consultation with a specialist familiar with the condition, understands the likely burdens and uncertainty, and has no unaffected embryos remaining. The patient says another IVF cycle is not realistically feasible and transfer of this embryo is the only remaining opportunity for a genetically related child. The clinic must choose whether to honor the transfer request; adopt a policy declining transfer of embryos expected to produce serious avoidable disease even when manageable; or use a severity-threshold policy that permits transfer for treatable/manageable conditions but refuses requests only when a future child is highly likely to face life-threatening severe early debility with no reasonable function.

policies.text: honor transfer for manageable condition after counseling
decline transfer on child-welfare/nonmaleficence grounds
allow only when no unaffected embryo remains and severity is below defined harm threshold
reproductive-liberty framework favoring patient choice
future-child welfare framework limiting transfer above severe-harm threshold
disability-justice rule rejecting assumptions that affected life is categorically not worth living
clinic-policy transparency/advance disclosure of transfer limits
Tell patients the clinic's transfer policy before treatment begins, so that no one discovers a restriction after their embryos exist.

cases.title: Disclosure of ART laboratory errors
cases.concise: A fertility clinic discovers that a laboratory error damaged one of a patient's cryopreserved embryos and may reduce the patient's future reproductive options. The clinic knows the error occurred and can explain the known facts, but its full root cause is still being investigated. The patient has not yet been told. The clinic must decide whether to disclose the known error promptly and provide later causal updates, wait until the investigation is complete before giving a single full account, or disclose only errors judged likely to alter clinical outcome while handling clearly harmless near misses internally.
cases.detailed: A fertility clinic discovers through routine quality review that a laboratory handling error damaged one cryopreserved embryo belonging to a patient with a limited remaining embryo cohort. The event could materially reduce the patient's future reproductive opportunity. The clinic has confirmed what occurred and which embryo was affected, but the exact system cause and whether additional procedural failures contributed are still under investigation. There is no uncertainty that an adverse event occurred. The clinic is deciding its disclosure policy: tell the patient promptly what is known, acknowledge uncertainty and provide later root-cause/corrective-action updates; wait until the full investigation is complete before disclosure to avoid giving incomplete information; or use a materiality rule under which consequential errors are disclosed but clearly harmless near misses may be managed through internal quality improvement without patient notification.

policies.text: immediate disclosure of error/misdirection with ongoing updates
disclose known event promptly but stage uncertain causal details until verified
disclose even no-harm errors because genetic/reproductive information itself can matter
do not disclose clearly harmless near misses unless system-learning/patient-interest threshold met
transparency/accountability framework
risk-managed delayed-consolidated account
Tell the affected patient every laboratory error touching their material as soon as it is known, including errors the clinic judges harmless, and say what remains uncertain.

cases.title: Allocation of scarce gene-therapy capacity
cases.concise: A specialized program can provide an approved one-time gene therapy for sickle cell disease, but manufacturing and transplant-unit capacity allow only a few treatments this year. All patients being compared meet clinical eligibility and understand the therapy's substantial burdens and risks. Some have rapidly progressive organ disease and may soon become ineligible; others are currently healthier and may have better procedural safety or expected long-term benefit. The program must decide whether to prioritize patients at greatest risk of losing future eligibility, prioritize expected clinical benefit/safety, or use transparent clinical tiers followed by lottery among patients who remain comparably prioritized.
cases.detailed: A regional sickle-cell gene-therapy program has a licensed potentially curative therapy but faces severe manufacturing, apheresis, conditioning and transplant-unit capacity constraints. For the next allocation period, there are fewer treatment slots than clinically eligible patients. All patients under consideration have decision-making capacity, have completed counseling and meet the program's minimum safety/eligibility criteria. Some have progressive organ dysfunction that makes treatment more urgent because delay may render them permanently ineligible. Others have less advanced disease and therefore potentially lower procedural risk and longer expected time to benefit. Some have alternative allogeneic donor options while others do not. The program must adopt a transparent rule for sequencing access: prioritize those at greatest risk of losing future eligibility because of disease progression; prioritize those with the greatest expected net clinical benefit/safety; or establish transparent priority tiers using urgency, alternatives and disease factors and then use a lottery when patients within the highest tier cannot be ethically distinguished.

policies.text: prioritize urgency/impending loss of eligibility
maximize expected benefit/safety
lottery among clinically comparable tiers
hybrid A4R rule combining disease prevalence, urgency, donor alternative and lottery
priority to historically underserved/high-burden communities to address structural inequity
first-ready/operational sequencing subject to clinical minimums
patient-preference/severity-sensitive rule giving more weight to those willing to accept higher treatment risk under severe disease

cases.title: Placebo control when effective treatment exists
cases.concise: Investigators propose a short randomized trial of a new treatment for a chronic symptomatic condition. An established therapy improves symptoms but stopping it for several weeks is not expected to cause death, irreversible injury or major disease progression. Investigators argue that symptom variability and a large placebo response make an active-control trial unable to establish efficacy reliably. Participants assigned to placebo would receive close monitoring, rescue treatment for predefined worsening and prompt withdrawal if safety thresholds are crossed. The ethics committee must decide whether to require an active control, permit placebo under the narrow methodological/risk exception, or permit placebo only with stricter mitigation such as shorter exposure and mandatory rescue thresholds.
cases.detailed: A research ethics committee is reviewing a randomized trial for a chronic condition with fluctuating subjective symptoms. An established treatment provides meaningful symptomatic benefit but is not curative. Investigators contend that an active-comparator noninferiority trial would be scientifically difficult to interpret because assay sensitivity is uncertain and placebo response is substantial. The proposed placebo period is six weeks. For this benchmark, assume withholding established treatment during that interval creates temporary symptom burden but no expected serious or irreversible harm, and participants can restart rescue therapy promptly if prespecified deterioration occurs. All participants know that placebo is possible. The committee must choose whether the existence of effective treatment requires an active-control design; whether the study qualifies for the narrow placebo exception because the scientific rationale is compelling and risk remains below the serious/irreversible-harm threshold; or whether placebo may be allowed only after further mitigation such as a shorter exposure window, more frequent monitoring and lower rescue thresholds.

policies.text: active-control only
placebo under narrow Helsinki/CIOMS exception
placebo with short duration/rescue/monitoring safeguards
equipoise/social-value framework favoring methodologically necessary placebo
nonmaleficence framework favoring active control
participant-choice comparator permitting placebo only after unusually explicit consent where professional risk threshold is still satisfied
Guarantee that anyone assigned placebo returns to effective treatment immediately on worsening, and say plainly at consent how long they may be without it.

cases.title: Controlled human infection study
cases.concise: Investigators propose a controlled human infection study in healthy adults to answer an important vaccine and pathogenesis question that conventional field studies would answer much more slowly. The challenge strain and dose are standardized, transmission to third parties can be tightly controlled, participants would be intensively monitored and compensated for research-related harm, and informed consent includes a demanding comprehension assessment. The pathogen can cause substantial illness, but severe outcomes are expected to be rare in the selected population. An effective rescue treatment reduces risk but does not eliminate it. The ethics committee must decide whether to approve under stringent WHO-style criteria, require an even lower residual-risk threshold or highly effective rescue before approval, or reject deliberate infection because the remaining nontherapeutic risk to healthy volunteers is too high.
cases.detailed: A research ethics committee is reviewing a controlled human infection study designed to accelerate evaluation of an important vaccine and improve understanding of infection dynamics. Healthy adults would be intentionally exposed to a carefully characterized challenge strain in a specialized isolation unit. Participant selection excludes known high-risk conditions; transmission outside the unit is tightly controlled; continuous clinical monitoring, rapid diagnostics, an effective rescue treatment and intensive supportive care are available; participants receive long-term follow-up and compensation for research-related injury. Investigators argue that field trials would take much longer and may be scientifically less informative. The challenge infection nevertheless carries nonzero risk of severe disease and uncertain long-term effects. The committee must decide whether the study meets stringent international criteria for ethical CHIS; whether approval should require a still lower quantified residual risk or near-certain rescue efficacy; or whether intentional infection of healthy volunteers is impermissible above a conservative risk threshold even with consent and social value.

policies.text: approve under full WHO criteria
require effective rescue treatment as additional condition
reject above defined residual-risk/uncertainty threshold
permit without curative treatment only where severity is low, rescue/support excellent, and social value compelling
participant-autonomy/high social-value permission
nonmaleficence precautionary restriction
enhanced compensation/injury-care/community-engagement governance rule
Fix compensation, treatment for any harm and long-term follow-up before recruitment opens, and publish those terms with the participant information.

cases.title: Emergency research without prospective consent
cases.concise: Investigators propose a randomized trial for a life-threatening emergency in which patients are temporarily incapable of consent and the study intervention must be given within minutes. Existing treatments are unproven or unsatisfactory, the research offers a prospect of direct benefit, and there is no reliable way to identify likely participants prospectively. The protocol includes prior ethics/regulatory approval, community consultation and public disclosure, attempts to reach a surrogate whenever feasible, prompt notification after enrollment and an opportunity to withdraw from ongoing research procedures. The ethics committee must decide whether to approve the full exception-from-consent pathway, require surrogate authorization for enrollment even if that makes many patients ineligible, or permit only a narrower deferred-consent pathway in which enrollment occurs without prospective authorization but continued participation requires consent as soon as possible.
cases.detailed: A multicenter emergency-care trial compares two plausible interventions for a life-threatening condition such as severe traumatic hemorrhage. Eligible patients are typically unconscious or cognitively incapacitated, and the study intervention must begin within a therapeutic window of approximately ten minutes. Existing treatment is unproven or unsatisfactory, and valid evidence cannot realistically be obtained in patients capable of prospective consent. Investigators have built a protocol matching the principal safeguards of 21 CFR 50.24: prospect of direct benefit, prior IRB/regulatory review, community consultation and public disclosure, attempts to contact a legally authorized representative when feasible within the window, independent monitoring, prompt notification of the participant or surrogate after enrollment, and consent for ongoing procedures when capacity or representation becomes available. The committee must decide whether this EFIC architecture is ethically acceptable; whether prospective surrogate authorization should remain mandatory even if it excludes most otherwise eligible patients and impairs the research; or whether a narrower deferred-consent architecture should allow emergency randomization but require explicit authorization for any continued study procedures/data use once the emergency has passed.

policies.text: EFIC under full regulatory/community safeguards
surrogate consent only/no enrollment if unavailable
deferred consent with immediate enrollment and later patient/surrogate authorization where legal
consent waiver only when prospect of direct benefit and intervention window makes consent infeasible
autonomy framework favoring narrower exception
emergency social-value/justice framework permitting EFIC to generate evidence for otherwise unresearchable lethal emergencies
Consult the community the trial will enrol from before it begins and publish what was heard, so that people enrolled without consent were represented in the decision to allow it.

cases.title: Control standard in lower-resource setting
cases.concise: A trial in a lower-resource health system evaluates a new treatment for a serious condition. A more effective treatment is standard in wealthy settings but is not routinely available in the host public system because of cost and supply constraints. Investigators propose comparing the new treatment with the local public-sector standard, arguing that the trial is responsive to local needs and that a positive result could lead to an affordable locally usable intervention. The ethics committees must decide whether controls should receive the best proven global treatment, whether an enhanced local standard is acceptable when paired with fair benefit and access commitments, or whether the local standard may be used only when there is a compelling scientific reason and participants are not exposed to unacceptable avoidable harm.
cases.detailed: A sponsor proposes a randomized trial in a lower-resource country where a serious disease is common. The internationally best proven treatment substantially improves outcomes but is not routinely available in the host public health system because its cost and supply requirements make sustained access unrealistic. Participants outside the trial would ordinarily receive a less effective local standard. The investigational treatment is designed to be cheaper and easier to deliver and, if effective, the sponsor and health ministry have a credible plan for local access. Investigators argue that comparing the new intervention with the local standard will answer whether it improves care that patients can realistically receive. Critics argue that using deprivation as the comparator exposes participants to inferior care that wealthier trial populations would not accept. The ethics committees must choose among requiring the globally best proven treatment as control; allowing an enhanced local-standard comparator within a responsive trial that includes fair post-trial access/benefit commitments; or allowing the local standard only when scientific necessity is compelling and the incremental risk from not receiving the global standard remains ethically acceptable.

policies.text: global best-proven control
enhanced local standard plus responsiveness/fair benefits
local standard only when scientifically necessary and avoidable harm remains within ethical threshold
local standard because it reflects realistic implementation context
justice rule requiring sponsor-supported access to better standard during trial
sustainable-host-benefit rule allowing contextual comparator if trial materially strengthens future access
reject trial if comparator would exploit unjust background conditions
Commit in advance to what the host community gets if the treatment works, and publish that commitment with the protocol.

cases.title: Broad consent for biobank research
cases.concise: A hospital plans a longitudinal biobank linking donated blood/tissue with identifiable clinical data. Future studies will span several disease areas and some questions cannot yet be specified. Donors can withdraw future use, a governance board and research ethics committee review every secondary-use proposal, and uses outside the consented scope can trigger recontact. The biobank must decide whether to use bounded broad consent for a defined range of future research, require dynamic/recontact consent for materially new research categories, or obtain specific consent for each future study while using opt-out only for low-risk residual clinical materials under separate rules.
cases.detailed: An academic health system is establishing a biobank of identifiable biospecimens and longitudinal health data. The collection is prospective: patients are being asked to donate material specifically for future research rather than merely leaving residual tissue after clinical care. The institution can explain the types of research likely to occur, storage duration, access rules, commercial collaboration possibilities, data linkage, governance, withdrawal, handling of unsolicited findings and circumstances requiring recontact. A research ethics committee will review each future project and cannot authorize uses outside the agreed scope without additional permission or another lawful ethical basis. The biobank must choose whether one bounded broad-consent process should authorize a defined range of future research under governance; whether donors should be recontacted dynamically whenever a materially new research category or sensitive use arises; or whether each identifiable future study should require specific consent, reserving opt-out approaches for separately governed residual clinical specimens.

policies.text: bounded broad consent + governance
dynamic/recontact consent for materially new categories
specific consent for each use
broad consent with opt-out/withdrawal and transparency portal
residual clinical samples under notice/opt-out where permitted
autonomy/right-to-control framework
solidarity/social-value framework favoring broad governed reuse

cases.title: Payment to healthy research participants
cases.concise: A healthy-volunteer pharmacology study requires ten inpatient days, repeated blood sampling and major time disruption but has already passed independent scientific and risk review. Investigators propose payment substantially above local minimum-wage compensation because recruitment is difficult and the burden is high. Payment accrues as participation proceeds, reimbursement of expenses is separate, and participants keep earned compensation if they withdraw. The ethics committee must decide whether to allow fair time/burden-based compensation even when the total is high, impose a conservative cap to reduce possible undue influence, or approve higher payment only with strengthened consent/comprehension safeguards and independent confirmation that research risk remains acceptable without considering the payment.
cases.detailed: A phase-1 healthy-volunteer study requires participants to remain in a clinical research unit for ten days, undergo frequent blood sampling, follow dietary and activity restrictions and miss work or caregiving responsibilities. An independent IRB risk assessment has concluded that the protocol's physical risks are ethically acceptable regardless of payment. Investigators propose reimbursement of all direct expenses plus compensation for time, inconvenience and study burden at a rate that produces a high total payment relative to many participants' ordinary disposable income. Payments accrue proportionally rather than being withheld until completion; withdrawing participants keep what they have earned. Investigators argue that low payment would unfairly externalize research burdens and worsen recruitment. The committee must decide whether a high but fair time/burden-based payment should be approved; whether total payment should be capped because large offers may distort judgment; or whether high payment should be permitted only with strengthened consent/comprehension processes and explicit confirmation that risk evaluation has been conducted independently of compensation.

policies.text: fair compensation for time/burden without arbitrary low cap
conservative payment cap to reduce undue influence
high payment allowed with enhanced consent/comprehension safeguards
prorated earned payment preserving withdrawal
labor/fairness framework favoring market-like compensation
vulnerability/undue-influence framework favoring limits where payment predictably distorts judgment
Pay for time and burden at a rate the participant can see and check, prorated so that leaving early costs nothing already earned.

cases.title: Pediatric research without direct benefit
cases.concise: Investigators propose a study requiring children with a rare disease to undergo research-only blood draws and one imaging procedure that offers no direct benefit. The knowledge cannot be obtained from adults because the biological process is specific to childhood. Parents would give permission and children capable of assent would be asked to agree. The committee must decide whether no-direct-benefit pediatric research should be limited to minimal risk, whether a minor increase above minimal risk may be accepted when social value is compelling and the question cannot be answered otherwise, or whether the study should be rejected whenever procedures exceed minimal risk even with assent and parental permission.
cases.detailed: A research ethics committee reviews a natural-history study of a rare pediatric disorder. The study includes repeated blood sampling and one imaging procedure that is not clinically indicated and offers no prospect of direct benefit to participants. The information is important for designing future treatments and cannot be obtained from adults because the disease process changes with development. For this benchmark, assume most procedures are minimal risk but the imaging procedure creates a small additional burden that the committee could reasonably classify as a minor increase above minimal risk. Parents would give permission; school-age children and adolescents would receive developmentally tailored information and be asked for assent; refusal would ordinarily be respected. The committee must decide whether to approve only if all nonbeneficial procedures remain minimal risk, permit a minor increase above minimal risk because the social value is compelling and the research cannot be done otherwise, or reject the study unless the potentially burdensome imaging component is removed.

policies.text: minimal-risk only
minor increase over minimal risk for compelling social value/necessity with permission/assent
prohibit no-benefit procedures that exceed minor increase regardless of assent
broader permission when mature adolescent assent is strong
child-protection framework
pediatric-justice framework allowing carefully bounded burdens so children are not excluded from evidence generation

cases.title: Inclusion of pregnant people in trials
cases.concise: A medication is already used off-label during pregnancy for a serious maternal condition, but pregnant patients were excluded from pivotal trials and dosing/safety evidence is poor. Nonpregnant adult data are substantial and animal reproductive studies do not show a strong fetal safety signal, but fetal uncertainty remains. The proposed trial offers a prospect of maternal benefit and includes pregnancy-specific monitoring and long-term infant follow-up. The sponsor and ethics committee must decide whether pregnant patients should be presumptively eligible under pregnancy-specific safeguards, included only after additional nonpregnant safety data or a staged sentinel cohort, or excluded until fetal uncertainty falls below a more conservative threshold.
cases.detailed: A sponsor is designing a therapeutic trial for a serious chronic condition that commonly persists during pregnancy. Clinicians already use the drug class during pregnancy because withholding treatment can harm maternal health, yet dosing, maternal efficacy and fetal safety evidence remain limited because pregnant people were historically excluded from trials. The investigational drug has substantial nonpregnant adult safety data and no major reproductive toxicity signal in available preclinical evidence. Participation could directly benefit the pregnant participant, but fetal risks remain uncertain. The protocol includes pregnancy-specific pharmacokinetic monitoring, fetal surveillance, obstetric expertise and infant follow-up. The sponsor and ethics committee must choose whether pregnant patients should be presumptively eligible when general risk-benefit criteria and pregnancy-specific safeguards are satisfied; whether enrollment should begin only after a staged sentinel cohort and additional nonpregnant evidence; or whether pregnancy should remain an exclusion criterion until fetal uncertainty is substantially lower.

policies.text: presumptive inclusion with pregnancy-specific safeguards
staged inclusion after adequate nonpregnant data
exclude when fetal uncertainty/risk exceeds threshold
justice framework opposing routine exclusion/evidence gaps
precautionary maternal-fetal framework favoring staged evidence
participant-choice rule allowing capable pregnant participant to decide within independently acceptable risk limits
Offer pregnant patients the trial rather than deciding for them, with the uncertainty stated plainly and their own clinician involved in the decision.

cases.title: Research involving prisoners
cases.concise: Investigators propose a study of an intervention for opioid use disorder in a prison population where the condition is common. The study addresses a health need specific to incarcerated people, offers careful medical monitoring and does not affect parole, privileges or sentence conditions. Payment is modest and equivalent opportunities/benefits are not so large that they obviously overwhelm judgment. A prisoner representative sits on the IRB. The committee must decide whether to allow participation under enhanced protections, restrict enrollment to studies with direct therapeutic benefit or minimal risk, or exclude incarcerated people from nontherapeutic components because the prison environment makes voluntary consent too difficult to assure.
cases.detailed: A research ethics committee is reviewing an HHS-supported study in a correctional system evaluating an intervention for opioid use disorder, a condition that disproportionately affects incarcerated people and contributes to high overdose risk after release. The study includes a treatment component with possible direct benefit plus research-only interviews and blood sampling. Participation does not influence parole, housing, disciplinary status or access to ordinary treatment. Recruitment is conducted by research staff rather than correctional officers; compensation is modest and reviewed relative to prison conditions; confidentiality is protected to the extent possible; a prisoner representative participates in IRB review; and refusal has no effect on care. The committee must decide whether prisoners should be eligible under enhanced Subpart-C-style protections because the research is responsive to their health needs; whether eligibility should be limited to direct-benefit or minimal-risk components; or whether nontherapeutic prisoner research should be excluded because constrained living conditions and unequal incentives make voluntariness too difficult to secure reliably.

policies.text: include prisoner-relevant research with enhanced protections/prisoner IRB representation
restrict nontherapeutic studies to minimal risk/defined categories
categorical exclusion from nonbeneficial research
include where exclusion itself creates evidence injustice and coercion safeguards are robust
vulnerability/autonomy framework favoring heightened scrutiny not blanket exclusion
anti-exploitation framework setting strict benefit/relevance thresholds
Let people in prison decide without their participation affecting parole, privileges or housing, and say so in writing at consent.

cases.title: Post-trial access
cases.concise: A randomized trial of a chronic-disease therapy is ending. Some participants receiving the investigational drug have had substantial clinical benefit and their treating investigators believe abrupt discontinuation would likely worsen their condition. The intervention has been shown beneficial and reasonably safe in the trial, but regulatory approval and routine insurance or public-system access may take many months. The sponsor can continue supplying the drug, but indefinite access would create cost and operational burdens. The ethics committee must decide whether the sponsor should guarantee continued access while participants medically need the intervention, provide a defined transition period until another payer or health system can take responsibility, or use a pre-agreed post-trial plan that can limit sponsor access when a research ethics committee approves a justified exception.
cases.detailed: A multicenter clinical trial for a serious chronic condition has demonstrated that the investigational intervention is beneficial and reasonably safe. Several participants assigned to the intervention have improved substantially and remain clinically dependent on continued treatment. The trial is ending, but full regulatory approval and routine reimbursement are expected to take approximately nine to twelve months. Without a post-trial arrangement, participants may lose access despite having accepted research burdens and helped generate the evidence supporting the product. The sponsor can supply the drug during a transition period, though indefinite lifetime provision would be financially and logistically difficult. Before enrollment, the consent materials disclosed that post-trial arrangements would be determined under an ethics-approved plan. The sponsor and committee must decide whether participants who still need the intervention should receive continued sponsor-funded access for as long as medically necessary; receive a defined transition supply while the sponsor, health system and payer arrange ordinary access; or receive access according to a pre-agreed fair-benefit plan that permits a research ethics committee to approve exceptions where indefinite continued supply is disproportionate or infeasible.

policies.text: guarantee continued access while medically needed
time-limited sponsor-funded transition to health-system access
pre-agreed fair-benefit plan with REC-approved exceptions
no special post-trial entitlement beyond ordinary access once study ends
reciprocity/nonabandonment framework favoring continued access
distributive/sustainability framework allowing bounded duration when indefinite sponsor responsibility would undermine research/access equity

cases.title: Publication of negative/inconclusive trials
cases.concise: A completed randomized clinical trial fails to show the sponsor's product is superior to control. The study is scientifically interpretable, contains no unexpected safety crisis and was prospectively registered. A journal article would require additional analysis and staff time, while a registry results summary can be posted promptly. The institution and sponsor must decide whether all completed trial results should be made public promptly through a registry with journal publication pursued when scientifically useful, whether every interpretable trial should also be submitted as a full manuscript within a defined period, or whether sponsors may choose manuscript detail and timing so long as complete core results are publicly disclosed.
cases.detailed: A multicenter randomized trial sponsored by a company is complete. The primary efficacy endpoint is negative and several secondary endpoints are inconclusive. The trial was appropriately designed, sufficiently enrolled and prospectively registered. There is no reason to retract the study as invalid. The sponsor worries that a full journal manuscript will consume resources and attract unfavorable commercial attention but accepts that registry reporting is required. Investigators argue that complete negative evidence is necessary to reduce publication bias and prevent future patients, researchers and decision-makers from relying on a distorted evidence base. The institution must set policy on the minimum form and timing of public disclosure and on whether journal publication itself should be mandatory.

policies.text: timely registry/public results for every completed human trial + publication when appropriate
full manuscript publication obligation for every scientifically interpretable trial
limited sponsor/investigator discretion over manuscript detail while public results remain mandatory
participant-right/social-value framework favoring full dissemination
proportional rule allowing concise public reporting when results are uninterpretable/redundant but never suppression
Publish the result whatever it shows, within a stated period, and tell participants where to find it when they enrol.

cases.title: Cluster-randomized public-health trial / community authorization
cases.concise: Twenty schools will be randomized to two evidence-based approaches for increasing routine adolescent vaccination. The intervention changes school reminder/outreach procedures; no student is required to receive vaccination, and individual clinical consent rules remain unchanged. Researchers will use de-identified aggregate uptake data and a brief optional student survey. Requiring prior consent from every family before a school can receive its assigned outreach strategy would make cluster randomization infeasible. School leaders can authorize institutional participation and parent/student representatives can be consulted. The ethics committee must decide what consent and community-authorization process is required.
cases.detailed: A public-health research team proposes a pragmatic cluster-randomized trial in twenty secondary schools comparing two lawful, evidence-based reminder and scheduling systems intended to improve access to routine adolescent vaccination. The school-level intervention changes communications and clinic logistics, not whether an individual student is vaccinated; ordinary consent for vaccination is preserved. Primary outcomes use routinely collected de-identified school-level uptake data. A separate optional survey asks identifiable students about communication acceptability and therefore can obtain individual consent/assent. Requiring advance individual permission from every student/parent merely for the school to receive its assigned reminder system would make the cluster intervention infeasible. Each school has a legitimate administrative gatekeeper, and parent/student/community consultation is feasible.

policies.text: individual consent + gatekeeper permission/community engagement
waiver/opt-out for low-risk cluster intervention where consent infeasible
individual consent wherever feasible with no gatekeeper proxy consent
community-authorization framework giving collective interests independent procedural weight
individual-autonomy framework restricting waiver
stepped/layered model using community consultation plus individual opt-out for population-level low-risk interventions
Consult the school communities before randomisation and publish what was decided, so that families whose children are covered by the change had a route to object.

cases.title: Return of individual research findings
cases.concise: An adult research participant consented to genome sequencing for a cardiovascular study and indicated willingness to be contacted about health-relevant findings. Researchers identify an unrelated pathogenic variant associated with a serious condition for which established surveillance can substantially reduce risk. The result is analytically reliable but was generated in a research laboratory and requires clinical confirmation before medical action. The program must decide whether to offer confirmed actionable findings, offer a broader menu of valid individual findings according to participant preference, or restrict return to urgent/high-actionability findings while leaving lower-value findings within the research record.
cases.detailed: An adult with capacity participates in a longitudinal genomic research study. The consent process asked about return preferences but did not promise that every individual result would be returned. Sequencing identifies a pathogenic variant unrelated to the research question that is associated with a serious condition for which established surveillance or preventive care can materially reduce morbidity. The analytical result is sufficiently reliable to justify confirmatory testing but should not be used clinically without confirmation. The participant previously expressed interest in health-relevant results and can receive genetic counseling. The program must choose whether to offer clinically confirmed actionable findings as a routine obligation; whether to offer participants a broader preference-based menu of valid findings that may have personal value even if actionability is limited; or whether to return only urgent/high-actionability results where the expected participant value clearly outweighs uncertainty, burden and cost.

policies.text: offer confirmed clinically actionable findings with informed choice
offer broader valid findings according to participant categories/preferences
restrict return to validity/actionability threshold
return urgent actionable findings even absent prior request when serious preventable harm is at stake
right-not-to-know opt-out
participant data-access/autonomy position favoring broader return
do not return uncertain/unvalidated findings but permit future recontact after reclassification

cases.title: Sponsor control over publication
cases.concise: A company will fund a multicenter clinical trial at an academic medical center. Its proposed contract gives investigators full access to study data but requires manuscripts to be sent to the sponsor before submission. The sponsor requests the right to remove confidential proprietary information, delay publication long enough to file patents, and coordinate the first multicenter publication. The institution must decide whether to allow only a short defined review/delay, allow a longer sponsor-coordinated first-publication period with a firm investigator publication backstop, or reject any agreement that gives the sponsor power to block, rewrite or indefinitely delay unfavorable results.
cases.detailed: An academic medical center is negotiating a trial agreement with a company developing a new treatment. Investigators will participate in analysis and must retain meaningful access to supporting data. The sponsor has legitimate confidential manufacturing information and possible patentable discoveries and therefore asks to review manuscripts before submission. It also wants to coordinate publication across multiple sites. The institution will not accept a sponsor veto over whether results can be published or contractual language allowing the sponsor to rewrite scientific interpretation. The remaining policy question is how much finite review/delay is acceptable: a short review period limited to identifying confidential information and patent needs; a longer defined sponsor first-publication/coordination window with an automatic investigator right to publish afterward; or essentially no sponsor delay beyond removal of genuine confidential material.

policies.text: investigator publication freedom with short sponsor review for confidential/IP material
fixed limited patent/coordination delay
immediate publication absent narrowly defined confidential information
sponsor first-publication coordination within a hard deadline but no veto
scientific-independence framework versus legitimate IP/reliance framework
Publish the contract terms governing publication alongside the trial registration, so that participants can see what the sponsor may withhold before enrolling.

cases.title: First-in-human high-risk gene/cell therapy
cases.concise: Adults with a severe progressive disease have no curative standard therapy. A gene-modified cell intervention has a plausible mechanism, replicated preclinical efficacy and an acceptable manufacturing program, but it has never been given to humans and may persist for years. The first cohort would receive a low staged dose with intensive monitoring and long-term follow-up. The committee must decide whether the evidence and unmet need justify cautious first-in-human testing, whether stronger preclinical replication should be required before any exposure, or whether enrollment should be limited to patients with the most severe disease and no reasonable alternatives.
cases.detailed: A translational program proposes first-in-human administration of a gene-modified cell product for a severe progressive disorder. Existing therapy slows disease but does not cure it. The product has a biologically plausible mechanism, replicated efficacy in disease-relevant models and manufacturing controls designed for clinical use. Important uncertainty remains about immune effects, off-target biological consequences, cell persistence and late toxicity. The protocol uses a small sentinel cohort, staged dosing, stopping rules, independent data monitoring, enhanced consent aimed at therapeutic misconception and long-term follow-up. The committee must decide whether the current evidence and unmet need justify initiation; whether more preclinical evidence is required because the harms may be irreversible; or whether first exposure should be confined to the most severely affected patients who lack reasonable alternatives.

policies.text: proceed in severe/no-alternative adults with enhanced oversight + staged dosing
require stronger preclinical threshold before first exposure
restrict initial enrollment to highest-need/lowest-alternative group
sentinel dosing/escalation with stopping rules
rescue/innovation framework allowing carefully managed uncertainty for otherwise untreatable disease
precautionary nonmaleficence framework delaying human exposure
justice rule preventing desperation from becoming a proxy for consent quality and ensuring long-term follow-up coverage
Say plainly at consent that this is a first-in-human study and cannot be expected to treat the participant's own disease, and give the same care afterwards to those it does not help.

cases.title: Scarce trial slots versus expanded access
cases.concise: A promising investigational therapy for a rapidly fatal rare disease has enough manufactured doses for a randomized trial but little surplus. Trial enrollment is essential to establish whether the therapy works and could support future approval. Patients who are ineligible for the trial because of age or disease stage request expanded access and have no satisfactory alternatives. Supplying many expanded-access patients would delay or shrink the trial. The manufacturer must decide whether trial enrollment receives priority, whether a defined portion of supply should be reserved for expanded access to otherwise ineligible patients, or whether all nontrial supply should be allocated through transparent independent criteria or lottery without compromising the minimum supply needed for the trial.
cases.detailed: A biotechnology company has an investigational product for a rare, rapidly progressive and ultimately fatal disorder. Early evidence is promising but efficacy remains uncertain, making a controlled trial scientifically important for regulatory approval and future population access. Manufacturing is the binding constraint: enough doses exist to run the planned randomized trial, but broad expanded access would materially reduce enrollment speed and may leave the study unable to answer its primary question. Several patients who cannot enroll because of prespecified age, comorbidity or disease-stage criteria have no satisfactory approved therapy and request the drug through expanded access. FDA criteria could permit some such use if risk-benefit is favorable, but expanded access must not interfere with the controlled investigation. The company must decide whether all scarce supply above manufacturing reserve should first protect the trial; whether a transparent percentage should be reserved for otherwise ineligible expanded-access patients while preserving trial viability; or whether the trial receives a defined minimum supply and remaining doses are allocated independently by urgency/lottery rather than case-by-case advocacy.

policies.text: prioritize trial supply to generate reliable evidence
reserve transparent fraction for EA to otherwise trial-ineligible worst-off patients
trial-first with EA only from surplus/noninterfering supply
lottery within EA eligibility
urgency/worst-off prioritization within EA
evidence-generation social-value priority
rescue/compassion priority for patients excluded from trial through no fault of their own
Publish the allocation rule and the numbers available, so that patients who receive nothing can see how the decision was made rather than suspecting it.

cases.title: Sham surgery control
cases.concise: A new minimally invasive procedure is already spreading into practice despite uncertain efficacy and a large expected placebo/context effect. Investigators propose a randomized blinded trial. The sham arm would receive anesthesia and a small superficial incision but no device insertion into the target organ; the incremental sham risk is low but real. Usual-care comparison alone would not reliably separate the specific procedural effect from expectations. The committee must decide whether the sham is justified by scientific necessity and low incremental risk, require a noninvasive/usual-care control instead, or permit a sham only after further reducing procedural risk and strengthening consent.
cases.detailed: A research ethics committee reviews a blinded randomized trial of an invasive procedure that has entered clinical use before convincing efficacy evidence. Outcomes are substantially subjective and susceptible to expectation effects. Investigators argue that usual-care or open-label controls would not determine whether the procedure's specific invasive component adds benefit. The sham would include anesthesia, sterile preparation and a small superficial incision sufficient to preserve blinding, but would omit penetration of the target organ and the therapeutic maneuver. For this benchmark, assume the sham's incremental risk is low but not zero, no proven life-saving treatment is withheld, participants can receive ordinary care afterward and consent materials explicitly explain that the sham offers no direct therapeutic benefit. The committee must decide whether scientific necessity and low incremental risk justify the sham; whether no therapeutic benefit can justify any avoidable invasive exposure when a nonsham control exists; or whether a modified lower-fidelity sham should be required even at some cost to blinding.

policies.text: allow sham only when scientifically necessary and incremental risk low
require active/usual-care control when sham risk exceeds threshold
allow sham with enhanced consent/rescue/risk mitigation under equipoise
participant-autonomy position permitting low-risk sham after transparent consent
nonmaleficence position rejecting nontherapeutic invasive procedures when less risky design can answer question
methodological-validity rule permitting sham where placebo effects/procedural components make blinded causal inference otherwise unreliable
Tell participants exactly what the sham involves and its risks, and guarantee the real procedure afterwards if the trial shows it works.

cases.title: Adaptive platform trial in emergency
cases.concise: During a serious outbreak, several treatments need rapid evaluation. A national platform protocol can add new arms, stop ineffective treatments and adjust allocation using prespecified statistical rules under independent monitoring. A conventional approach would run separate fixed trials with simpler consent and governance but could duplicate controls and learn more slowly. The program must decide whether to use the adaptive platform, use separate fixed trials, or permit adaptation only when prespecified oversight, consent communication and equity safeguards are strong enough to manage changing probabilities and arm availability.
cases.detailed: A public-health emergency creates urgent demand for reliable comparative treatment evidence. Investigators propose one multicenter platform trial with a shared control group and prespecified rules for dropping futile arms, graduating successful arms and adding new interventions. Some adaptations may change allocation probabilities over time. The design can reduce duplication and accelerate learning, but it complicates participant explanation, ethics review across jurisdictions, governance of algorithmic adaptation and equitable access to newly added arms. Separate conventional trials would be easier to explain and review but could compete for patients, duplicate control groups and produce answers more slowly. The program has independent data monitoring and can publish the adaptation rules prospectively. It must decide whether a platform design should be preferred in the emergency, whether fixed trials remain the safer ethical default, or whether adaptive design should be used only with predefined independent oversight, transparent consent language, community engagement and equity protections.

policies.text: adaptive platform with prespecified independent oversight
separate fixed trials
adaptive only when emergency learning advantage justifies complexity
response-adaptive allocation favoring better-performing arms subject to inferential safeguards
learning-health/social-value framework favoring platform efficiency
transparency/autonomy framework favoring simpler fixed designs when adaptation impairs comprehensibility/local accountability
Publish the adaptation rules before the trial starts and explain to each participant how their allocation may change, so that a moving design remains something they consented to.

cases.title: National health-research agenda
cases.concise: A national public funder has a fixed five-year health-research budget that cannot fund every valuable program. One portfolio would direct most funding toward diseases responsible for the greatest current population health loss and projects with high expected near-term impact.
