policies.text_detailed: Permit donation directed to a named individual, with the named recipient assessed on ordinary clinical criteria and the direction recorded.

policies.text: reject conditions directing organs to or excluding recipients by race/religion/gender/sexual orientation
policies.text_detailed: Reject any condition directing organs toward or away from recipients by race, religion, gender or sexual orientation, with the rule stated in the donation terms and applied without exception.

policies.text: accept the donation but remove the discriminatory condition before allocation
policies.text_detailed: Accept the donation and remove the discriminatory condition before allocation, telling the donor or their family that the condition will not be applied.

policies.text: refuse the donation entirely when the condition itself threatens public trust or dignitary equality
policies.text_detailed: Refuse the donation entirely where the condition itself threatens public trust or dignitary equality, with the refusal decided institutionally and the reasoning recorded.

policies.text: donor-autonomy framework favoring wide control over a gratuitous gift
policies.text_detailed: Favour wide donor control over a gratuitous gift, with the limits on that control stated in advance so that donors know before donating what conditions will not be honoured.

policies.text: equal-status/anti-discrimination framework limiting donor control once an organ enters the allocation system
policies.text_detailed: Limit donor control once an organ enters the allocation system, on equal-status grounds, with the point at which control ends defined and stated at the outset.

policies.text: Refuse conditions the recipients themselves could not be told about, and tell donors this rule before donation rather than at the point of refusal.
policies.text_detailed: Refuse conditions the recipients themselves could not be told about, and tell donors this rule before donation rather than at the point of refusal, with the rule published in the donation information.

cases.title: Paired kidney exchange and chain obligations
cases.concise: A living kidney donor joins a paired-exchange chain so the donor's intended recipient can receive a compatible kidney from another participant. After another transplant in the chain has already occurred but before the donor's surgery, the donor develops serious doubts and wants to withdraw. The program must decide whether the donor retains an unconditional right to withdraw until surgery, whether participation can create a stronger enforceable commitment after others have relied on the chain, or whether the system should preserve withdrawal while designing sequencing and backup plans to minimize harmful reliance.
cases.detailed: A paired kidney exchange links several incompatible donor–recipient pairs. A competent donor entered voluntarily after counseling and knew their donation would trigger benefits for others. Because procedures could not all be simultaneous, another recipient has already received a kidney in reliance on the chain. Before the donor's own surgery, the donor becomes distressed and asks to withdraw without giving a medical reason. Their intended recipient has already benefited. Withdrawal may break the remaining chain and harm another waiting participant. The program must choose whether the donor's right to withdraw remains absolute until anesthesia/surgery; whether participation after chain initiation creates a stronger commitment that can ethically limit withdrawal; or whether no coercive enforcement is permissible but programs should sequence exchanges, use bridge-donor safeguards and communicate reliance explicitly to reduce the chance and harm of withdrawal.

policies.text: preserve unconditional right to withdraw without penalty up to surgery
policies.text_detailed: Preserve an unconditional right to withdraw without penalty up to surgery, stated at enrolment and repeated before each step, with no financial or clinical consequence for withdrawing.

policies.text: use scheduling/sequence design to reduce reliance on non-simultaneous promises
policies.text_detailed: Design the scheduling and sequence to reduce reliance on non-simultaneous promises, with simultaneity used where feasible and the residual exposure explained to each participant.

policies.text: require explicit advance counseling about chain consequences while prohibiting pressure to continue
policies.text_detailed: Counsel every participant in advance about what withdrawal would mean for the chain, while prohibiting any pressure to continue, with the counselling documented and the prohibition applied to staff conduct.

policies.text: allow confidential withdrawal reasons so donor need not bear interpersonal blame
policies.text_detailed: Allow withdrawal without giving reasons and keep the reasons confidential, so that a donor need not carry interpersonal blame, with the programme communicating the outcome rather than the donor.

policies.text: autonomy framework treating withdrawal as nonwaivable
policies.text_detailed: Treat the right to withdraw as non-waivable, so that no advance commitment can be enforced, with that stated in every document a participant signs.

policies.text: reliance/fairness framework supporting stronger moral—though not coercive—commitment once others have acted in reliance
policies.text_detailed: Recognise a stronger moral commitment once others have acted in reliance, expressed through counselling and support rather than any coercive mechanism, and never enforced against a withdrawing donor.

policies.text: Keep withdrawal unconditional and private, and tell every participant at the outset what happens to the chain if someone withdraws.
policies.text_detailed: Keep withdrawal unconditional and private, and tell every participant at the outset what happens to the chain if someone withdraws, so that the risk is known before anyone joins.

cases.title: Multi-organ transplantation versus separate recipients
cases.concise: A deceased donor has two organs that could be transplanted together into one critically ill candidate or separately into two single-organ candidates. For this benchmark, assume all three are medically compatible and the expected outcomes for each option are explicitly estimated. The authority must decide whether a multi-organ candidate should receive both organs whenever a clinical eligibility threshold is met, whether separate transplantation should be preferred when it benefits more patients overall, or whether a multiprinciple rule should reserve multi-organ allocation for cases where urgency and expected combined benefit cross a high threshold.
cases.detailed: A national transplant system must allocate two organs recovered from one deceased donor. Candidate A has failure of both organs and could receive a simultaneous combined transplant. Candidates B and C each need one of the organs. For this benchmark, assume compatibility and expected short-term surgical outcomes are acceptable for all three, and the allocation authority has reliable estimates of survival benefit and urgency. Giving both organs to A may offer substantial integrated benefit and avoid future organ failure, but it also means two single-organ candidates lose an opportunity. The authority must choose whether satisfying a defined medical eligibility criterion for multi-organ transplantation is sufficient for priority, whether two single-organ transplants should be preferred when aggregate expected benefit is higher, or whether multi-organ allocation should require a combined urgency/benefit threshold with safety-net protection for candidates initially receiving only one organ.

policies.text: prioritize multi-organ candidate when combined transplant provides substantially greater survival benefit and organs are jointly necessary
policies.text_detailed: Prioritise the multi-organ candidate where the combined transplant offers substantially greater survival benefit and the organs are jointly necessary, with both established clinically and recorded.

policies.text: protect single-organ access with explicit multi-organ eligibility/safety-net rules
policies.text_detailed: Protect single-organ access through explicit multi-organ eligibility and safety-net rules, with the rules published and the effect on single-organ waiting lists monitored.

policies.text: allocate organs separately when expected aggregate benefit materially exceeds the combined transplant
policies.text_detailed: Allocate the organs separately where expected aggregate benefit materially exceeds that of the combined transplant, with the comparison made on stated measures and documented.

policies.text: use a threshold rule requiring minimum incremental benefit for multi-organ allocation
policies.text_detailed: Require a minimum incremental benefit before multi-organ allocation, with the threshold stated numerically in the allocation rule rather than assessed case by case.

policies.text: urgency/rescue framework favoring multi-organ candidate
policies.text_detailed: Favour the multi-organ candidate on urgency and rescue grounds, with the urgency defined clinically and the cost to single-organ candidates stated.

policies.text: aggregate-benefit framework favoring separate recipients
policies.text_detailed: Favour separate recipients on aggregate-benefit grounds, applying the rule consistently and reporting what the multi-organ candidate's prospects were.

policies.text: procedural justice rule requiring transparent nationally consistent criteria and audit of effects on single-organ waiting lists
policies.text_detailed: Require transparent nationally consistent criteria with audit of the effect on single-organ waiting lists, with the audit published and the criteria revised where the effect is inequitable.

policies.text: Tell every candidate on the list how combined-organ decisions are made, so that a patient passed over knows the rule rather than suspecting one.
policies.text_detailed: Tell every candidate on the list how combined-organ decisions are made, so that a patient passed over knows the rule rather than suspecting one, with the rule given at listing and on request.

cases.title: Global allocation of scarce vaccine or therapeutic
cases.concise: An effective pandemic vaccine is available, but global supply is enough for only a fraction of people during the first six months. Countries differ in population size, current mortality, health-system strain and manufacturing contribution. The international mechanism must decide whether to begin with equal population-proportional shares, allocate primarily according to current epidemiologic need and expected health benefit, or reserve a limited reciprocity tranche for countries that contributed manufacturing or frontline global-response capacity while distributing the remainder by need and equity.
cases.detailed: An international financing and procurement mechanism controls a large but insufficient supply of a highly effective vaccine during a severe pandemic. All participating countries have accepted common reporting and delivery requirements. Some countries have much larger populations; some face rapidly rising mortality and fragile health systems; several invested heavily in manufacturing or supplied globally scarce inputs and health workers. Supply cannot cover all high-risk groups immediately. The mechanism must choose a transparent first-phase allocation rule: equal per-capita or population-proportional access so every country can protect a comparable initial share; dynamic need/benefit allocation weighted toward current outbreak burden, vulnerable populations and health-system collapse risk; or a multiprinciple rule that reserves a bounded reciprocity contribution for countries providing critical global-response resources while directing most doses according to need and equity.

policies.text: equal initial allocation then need/risk-based redistribution
policies.text_detailed: Allocate equally across countries at the start, then redistribute by need and risk once epidemiological data allow, with the switch point and the redistribution rule fixed before the first dose ships.

policies.text: prioritize countries with greatest epidemiologic burden and marginal health benefit
policies.text_detailed: Prioritise countries where the epidemiological burden and the marginal health benefit are greatest, using stated indicators and published data, and revisiting the ranking as the epidemic moves rather than fixing it at the outset.

policies.text: prioritize health-system/frontline protection to preserve response capacity
policies.text_detailed: Prioritise protection of health systems and frontline workers so that response capacity survives, with the covered categories defined narrowly and the same definition applied in every country.

policies.text: give reciprocity weight to countries contributing manufacturing/research resources
policies.text_detailed: Give weight to countries that contributed manufacturing or research capacity, with the weight stated in advance as a proportion rather than negotiated per shipment, and capped so that reciprocity cannot displace need entirely.

policies.text: allocate proportionally by population after minimum need threshold
policies.text_detailed: Allocate proportionally by population once a minimum need threshold is met everywhere, with the threshold defined first and proportional allocation applying only to supply above it.

policies.text: reserve a share for low-resource/worst-off countries independent of purchasing power
policies.text_detailed: Reserve a stated share for low-resource and worst-off countries, ring-fenced from purchasing power and from bilateral negotiation, and released on the same schedule as the rest of the supply.

policies.text: multiprinciple transparent allocation combining need, benefit, equity, reciprocity, and procedural fairness
policies.text_detailed: Combine need, benefit, equity, reciprocity and procedural fairness under a published rule that says how each is weighed, applied by a body whose decisions and departures from the rule are on the record.

policies.text: Distribute through a shared mechanism countries agree to in advance, and publish each allocation, so that supply does not follow bilateral deals made out of sight.
policies.text_detailed: Distribute through a shared mechanism countries agree to before supply exists, and publish each allocation as it is made, so that supply does not follow bilateral deals struck out of sight.

cases.title: International recruitment of health workers from shortage countries
cases.concise: A high-income health system has major staffing vacancies and is considering a targeted recruitment campaign in a country on WHO's 2026 health-workforce support and safeguards list. Individual clinicians from that country remain free to apply for jobs abroad. The employer must decide whether to refrain from active recruitment, recruit only through a bilateral agreement that provides proportional workforce/health-system investment to the source country, or recruit openly while relying on individual workers' right to migrate.
cases.detailed: A hospital network in a high-income country faces persistent shortages of nurses and physicians. A recruitment agency proposes a large targeted campaign in a lower-income country whose health-worker density and service coverage place it on WHO's 2026 Support and Safeguards List. The source government has not requested exemption from the safeguards. Individual health workers retain the right to seek jobs abroad and some actively want migration opportunities. WHO's amended Global Code distinguishes that individual freedom from systematic active recruitment and encourages government-to-government arrangements and proportional co-investment when recruitment occurs. The employer must decide whether to avoid active recruitment from the listed country; recruit only through a bilateral agreement that supports source-country workforce priorities; or conduct ordinary active recruitment on the view that limiting employer outreach unfairly constrains workers' opportunities.

policies.text: refrain from active recruitment from safeguard-list countries while preserving individual freedom to migrate
policies.text_detailed: Refrain from active recruitment in countries on the safeguard list, while leaving individuals free to apply on their own initiative, with the distinction defined by what the employer does rather than by how the worker arrives.

policies.text: allow recruitment only through government-to-government agreements with proportional support/co-investment for source systems
policies.text_detailed: Recruit only under government-to-government agreements that include proportional support or co-investment for the source system, with the support specified, funded, and reported rather than promised in principle.

policies.text: unrestricted recruitment where workers independently apply and contracts are fair
policies.text_detailed: Permit recruitment where workers apply independently and the contract is fair, with fairness defined by stated terms — no recruitment fees, no tied visas, portable qualifications — and audited rather than asserted.

policies.text: destination system compensates source-country training loss through financing/training partnerships
policies.text_detailed: Compensate the source country for training loss through financing or training partnerships, at a rate tied to the number recruited, paid to the health system rather than to a general fund.

policies.text: worker-autonomy framework rejecting restrictions on individual mobility
policies.text_detailed: Reject restrictions on individual mobility, on the ground that a worker's right to move is theirs rather than their government's, while leaving room to regulate what employers may do to attract them.

policies.text: global-health-equity framework limiting institutional recruitment that worsens severe shortages
policies.text_detailed: Limit institutional recruitment that worsens severe shortages, assessed against the source country's own workforce data, with the limit applying to the employer and reviewed as that data changes.

policies.text: ethical-recruitment certification with transparency, no recruitment fees, portability, and retention support
policies.text_detailed: Require ethical-recruitment certification covering transparency, no recruitment fees, qualification portability and retention support, with certification audited and withdrawable rather than granted once.

policies.text: Guarantee recruited workers full information, portable qualifications and the right to return, and refuse arrangements that bind a worker to one employer.
policies.text_detailed: Guarantee recruited workers full information before departure, portable qualifications and the right to return, and refuse any arrangement that binds a worker to a single employer or makes leaving costly.

cases.title: Pharmaceutical IP versus access during major health need
cases.concise: A patented health technology substantially reduces death from a major disease, but supply and price leave most patients in lower-income countries without timely access. Manufacturing capacity could expand if additional producers receive legal rights and technical know-how, although the patent holder argues that exclusivity supports innovation and coordinated quality control. Authorities must decide whether to preserve exclusivity while subsidizing procurement, use public-health licensing and technology-sharing tools to expand production, or negotiate tiered licensing and manufacturing transfer with the originator before using compulsory measures.
cases.detailed: A highly effective patented vaccine or therapeutic is central to controlling a major health threat. Demand greatly exceeds affordable supply in many lower-resource settings. Existing factories can expand output only gradually, while qualified manufacturers in additional regions could potentially produce the product if they receive legal authorization, detailed know-how and regulatory support. The originator argues that patent exclusivity and licensing control are needed to fund innovation, maintain quality and coordinate scale-up; access advocates argue that public investment and preventable deaths justify stronger sharing obligations. The authority must choose whether to preserve exclusivity and close the access gap through subsidized procurement; invoke or credibly threaten public-health licensing mechanisms together with technology transfer; or pursue negotiated tiered licensing/manufacturing transfer with defined access milestones and use compulsory measures only if the agreement fails.

policies.text: preserve exclusivity with subsidized procurement/donation
policies.text_detailed: Preserve exclusivity while funding subsidised procurement or donation for those who cannot pay, with the volumes and the duration committed in advance rather than adjusted as demand becomes apparent.

policies.text: negotiated tiered voluntary licensing and technology transfer
policies.text_detailed: Negotiate tiered voluntary licensing and technology transfer, with the territories, the price tiers and the transfer obligations written into the licence and published.

policies.text: compulsory licensing/TRIPS public-health flexibility when voluntary access fails
policies.text_detailed: Use compulsory licensing or other public-health flexibilities where voluntary access fails, with failure defined by stated price and supply targets and a date by which they must be met.

policies.text: public/private patent pool or shared manufacturing platform
policies.text_detailed: Place the technology in a patent pool or shared manufacturing platform, with participation terms published and the pool governed by the countries relying on it rather than by the licensor alone.

policies.text: innovation-incentive framework favoring time-limited exclusivity with access obligations
policies.text_detailed: Grant time-limited exclusivity carrying access obligations, on the ground that the incentive is what produced the technology, with the obligations enforceable and the limit fixed rather than extendable.

policies.text: right-to-health/global-justice framework favoring broad licensing/technology sharing during severe need
policies.text_detailed: Favour broad licensing and technology sharing during severe need, on the ground that a right to health is at stake, with the trigger for such need defined in advance rather than declared case by case.

policies.text: staged trigger: voluntary agreement first, compulsory mechanisms if price/supply targets unmet
policies.text_detailed: Try voluntary agreement first and move to compulsory mechanisms if price or supply targets are unmet by a stated date, with both the targets and the date public from the beginning.

policies.text: Publish what public money contributed to the technology and what the price is in each country, so that patients can see what they are being charged for.
policies.text_detailed: Publish what public money contributed to the technology and what the price is in each country, so that patients can see what they are being charged for and what was already paid on their behalf.

cases.title: Essential health care for refugees/migrants regardless status
cases.concise: A national health system must set access rules for long-term residents, refugees and migrants who lack regular immigration status. Emergency care is guaranteed. The disputed question is access to primary care, essential medicines, vaccination, pregnancy care, chronic-disease treatment and necessary specialist services. The system must decide whether essential/necessary care should be available on the same basis as for other residents, whether publicly funded entitlement should be limited largely to emergency and communicable-disease services, or whether a tiered system should guarantee a defined essential package plus continuity and public-health exceptions while restricting some elective services.
cases.detailed: A country with universal or publicly subsidized health services is revising eligibility for refugees, asylum seekers and migrants with irregular status. Emergency stabilization is not at issue. The policy dispute concerns routine primary care, maternal care, vaccinations, mental-health services, essential medicines, chronic-disease management and medically necessary specialist treatment. Exclusion can delay care and create public-health/continuity harms; broad entitlement has real fiscal and administrative costs and may differ from rules for short-term visitors. The health system must choose equal access to essential and medically necessary care irrespective of migration status; a narrow emergency/public-health entitlement; or a defined essential package with strong continuity/public-health protections while reserving some nonessential/elective services for other financing pathways.

policies.text: equal access to essential services irrespective status
policies.text_detailed: Give equal access to essential services irrespective of immigration status, with entitlement determined by presence rather than documents, and no charge that would deter someone from seeking care.

policies.text: universal emergency/communicable/maternal-child core plus staged access to broader services
policies.text_detailed: Guarantee emergency, communicable-disease and maternal and child care universally, and stage access to broader services against stated criteria, with the staging published so that people know what they can obtain now.

policies.text: residence-based enrollment in ordinary primary/chronic care with firewall from immigration enforcement
policies.text_detailed: Enrol people in ordinary primary and chronic care on the basis of residence, with a firewall between health records and immigration enforcement that is stated in law rather than in policy.

policies.text: restrict publicly funded nonurgent services to a defined essential package where resources are constrained
policies.text_detailed: Where resources are constrained, restrict publicly funded non-urgent services to a defined essential package, with the package set by clinical criteria and applied to everyone rather than by status.

policies.text: equal moral status/public-health framework favoring broad inclusion
policies.text_detailed: Include broadly on equal-status and public-health grounds, treating exclusion as both a wrong to the person and a risk to everyone, with any limit justified against both.

policies.text: stewardship framework allowing transparent scope limits but rejecting status as a proxy for worth
policies.text_detailed: Permit transparent limits on the scope of publicly funded services while rejecting immigration status as a proxy for who deserves care, with the limits stated as clinical categories and applied uniformly.

policies.text: Separate care entirely from immigration enforcement and say so publicly, so that no one avoids treatment for fear of the consequences of seeking it.
policies.text_detailed: Separate care entirely from immigration enforcement and say so publicly, so that no one avoids treatment for fear of what seeking it will bring, with the separation stated at the point of registration.

cases.title: Clinical neutrality in armed conflict
cases.concise: A hospital near an armed conflict has one ICU bed and two patients with comparable expected benefit: a local civilian and a wounded enemy combatant. Security risks can be managed separately from clinical care. The hospital must decide whether allocation should depend only on clinical urgency and expected benefit, whether civilians should receive independent priority, or whether clinical neutrality should govern bedside allocation while security and detention concerns are handled outside the medical ranking.
cases.detailed: A civilian hospital is treating wounded people from both sides of an armed conflict. One remaining ICU bed is needed by a local civilian and an enemy combatant. For this benchmark, assume both can be safely treated in the hospital, security can be managed without denying care, and the patients have closely comparable clinical urgency and expected benefit. Some community members demand civilian priority because the combatant fought for the opposing side and local resources are scarce. Clinicians invoke medical neutrality. The hospital must choose whether clinical facts alone govern allocation; whether civilian/noncombatant status receives independent priority; or whether the medical allocation remains neutral while custody/security and nonmedical resource questions are handled through separate institutional processes.

policies.text: impartial clinical triage based solely on medical need/urgency
policies.text_detailed: Triage on medical need and urgency alone, with the assessment made by clinicians who are not told, and do not ask, which side a patient came from, and the ordering recorded.

policies.text: security separation outside bedside triage without discriminatory clinical priority
policies.text_detailed: Keep any security separation outside the triage decision: guards and physical arrangements may differ, clinical priority may not, and the separation is not allowed to delay assessment.

policies.text: prioritize those most likely to benefit when resources are scarce, irrespective combatant status
policies.text_detailed: Where resources are scarce, prioritise those most likely to benefit irrespective of combatant status, with likelihood of benefit assessed on stated clinical grounds and recorded for each decision.

policies.text: civilian-priority rule
policies.text_detailed: Give civilians priority as a stated rule, applied openly rather than informally, with the rule published and the consequences for combatant care acknowledged rather than concealed.

policies.text: medical-neutrality/equal-status framework
policies.text_detailed: Treat everyone as of equal status under medical neutrality, with the commitment stated publicly, applied to staff conduct as well as triage, and defended to both sides.

policies.text: Publish the triage rule and apply it identically to everyone brought in, so that neither side's community has reason to believe the hospital treats the other first.
policies.text_detailed: Publish the triage rule and apply it identically to everyone brought in, so that neither side's community has reason to believe the hospital treats the other first, with the rule displayed at the entrance in both languages.

cases.title: Technology transfer versus immediate procurement
cases.concise: A donor has a fixed five-year budget for vaccines and diagnostics in a lower-resource region. Purchasing finished products from established international manufacturers would deliver more doses in the first two years. Funding a local manufacturing and technology-transfer partnership would deliver fewer products initially but could create regional production capacity, trained staff and faster future emergency response. The donor must choose immediate lowest-cost procurement, local-capacity priority, or a staged hybrid that guarantees current supply while tying additional investment to manufacturing milestones.
cases.detailed: An international donor supports a lower-resource country's vaccine and diagnostic program. A fixed five-year budget can either purchase large volumes from established foreign manufacturers immediately or finance a technology-transfer partnership involving equipment, regulatory strengthening, workforce training and local production. For this benchmark, assume the local project is technically credible but will produce fewer usable doses during the first two years; if successful, it will provide substantial regional capacity by years three to five and improve preparedness for future outbreaks. The donor must decide whether to maximize immediate procurement, prioritize long-term local production and technical autonomy despite near-term opportunity cost, or split funding through a staged hybrid that secures current essential products while expanding local capacity against transparent performance milestones.

policies.text: lowest-cost immediate procurement to maximize near-term doses/treatments
policies.text_detailed: Procure finished products at lowest cost to maximise doses now, stating the volumes bought and accepting that supply remains dependent on external manufacturers when the next need arises.

policies.text: invest in local production/technology transfer despite higher short-run cost
policies.text_detailed: Invest in local production and technology transfer despite higher short-run cost, with the capacity targets, the timeline and the accepted reduction in near-term volume stated up front.

policies.text: staged hybrid: procure now while financing regional capacity for future supply
policies.text_detailed: Procure now while financing regional capacity in parallel, with the split between the two published at the outset and the capacity milestones tracked rather than deferred.

policies.text: require licensing/training/quality systems as condition of donor procurement contracts
policies.text_detailed: Make licensing, training and quality systems a condition of donor procurement contracts, with the obligations written into the contract, priced into it, and verified rather than encouraged.

policies.text: near-term lives-saved framework favoring procurement
policies.text_detailed: Favour immediate procurement on the ground that near-term lives saved are the measure, stating what the choice costs in future supply resilience rather than leaving it unsaid.

policies.text: resilience/self-determination framework favoring technology transfer
policies.text_detailed: Favour technology transfer on grounds of resilience and self-determination, accepting a stated reduction in doses now for capacity that the region controls afterwards.

policies.text: equity rule prioritizing capacity in regions structurally excluded from manufacturing
policies.text_detailed: Prioritise building capacity in regions structurally excluded from manufacturing, with exclusion assessed on stated indicators and the priority applied across successive funding rounds rather than once.

policies.text: Decide with the recipient region rather than for it, and publish the agreed split between immediate supply and local capacity.
policies.text_detailed: Decide with the recipient region rather than for it, and publish the agreed split between immediate supply and local capacity, together with who took part in the decision.

cases.title: Global allocation of ultra-expensive curative gene therapy
cases.concise: An international health fund has a fixed one-year marginal budget. It could finance curative gene therapy for a small number of children with a severe fatal genetic disease, or use the same funds for vaccines, maternal care and treatment programs expected to prevent substantially more deaths and disability across a larger population. The fund must decide whether to maximize total expected health benefit, give special priority to severe rare disease and identifiable patients despite high opportunity cost, or reserve a defined portion of the budget for high-cost cures while allocating the remainder by population health impact.
cases.detailed: An international financing mechanism receives a fixed additional budget that cannot be expanded during the current cycle. One option is a one-time gene therapy that is expected to cure or substantially transform a severe childhood genetic disease, but the treatment is extremely expensive and only a limited number of children could be treated. The same budget could instead expand high-impact vaccination, maternal/newborn services and treatment for common infectious or chronic diseases, producing much larger aggregate health gains. For this benchmark, assume the gene therapy has strong evidence of clinical benefit and the population-health programs also have established effectiveness. The fund must choose an ordinary cost-effectiveness/total-health rule, a severity/rescue rule that gives extra weight to the small group facing catastrophic disease, or a portfolio rule reserving a limited share for high-cost transformative therapies while allocating most resources according to expected population health gain.

policies.text: maximize total health gain across all interventions
policies.text_detailed: Maximise total health gain across all available interventions, applying one threshold consistently and reporting what a curative therapy displaced when it was refused.

policies.text: severity/rescue priority funding some cures despite lower cost-effectiveness
policies.text_detailed: Fund some curative therapies on severity and rescue grounds despite lower cost-effectiveness, with the severity criterion defined in advance and the number of such exceptions bounded.

policies.text: reserve portfolio share for rare severe curative therapies while spending remainder on high-impact population services
policies.text_detailed: Reserve a stated portfolio share for rare severe curative therapies and spend the remainder on high-impact population services, with the share fixed before applications are considered.

policies.text: threshold with severity modifier
policies.text_detailed: Apply a cost-effectiveness threshold with a severity modifier, publishing both the threshold and the modifier so that a refusal can be checked against the rule rather than only announced.

policies.text: conditional funding tied to price reduction/evidence generation
policies.text_detailed: Fund conditionally on price reduction and evidence generation, with the price, the evidence to be collected and the review date written into the agreement and the funding ending if they are not met.

policies.text: equal-life-chance/anti-abandonment framework favoring access for small severe-disease groups
policies.text_detailed: Favour access for small severe-disease groups on equal-life-chance grounds, treating abandonment of an identifiable group as a distinct cost, and stating what population spending is foregone.

policies.text: opportunity-cost/global-justice framework prioritizing scalable interventions for the worst-off populations
policies.text_detailed: Prioritise scalable interventions for the worst-off populations on opportunity-cost and global-justice grounds, stating explicitly what the refused therapy would have done for the children concerned.

policies.text: Involve the affected families in the funding decision and publish the reasoning, including what a refusal means for the children concerned.
policies.text_detailed: Involve the affected families in the funding decision and publish the reasoning, including what a refusal means for the children concerned, rather than announcing a threshold result alone.

cases.title: Benefit sharing for international genomic data
cases.concise: A multinational genomics consortium has assembled a high-value dataset using samples and health information contributed by communities in several lower-resource countries. Commercial and academic teams can use the dataset to develop diagnostics and therapies, but most resulting products may initially be unaffordable in contributor countries. Contributors gave valid research consent and the consortium can choose its access and benefit-sharing rules. It must decide whether data should be broadly shared with general scientific benefits, shared only under negotiated benefit-sharing obligations, or governed through stronger community/country control over access and downstream commercial use.
cases.detailed: A multinational consortium holds genomic and linked health data collected through long-term partnerships with communities and hospitals in lower-resource countries. The resource has become scientifically valuable and is attracting commercial users. The original consent permitted broad health research, but did not settle how downstream commercial value should be distributed. Contributor communities face under-resourced health systems and have asked for local analytic capacity, affordable access to resulting products, acknowledgement, and continuing participation in governance. The consortium must decide whether broad responsible data sharing and general scientific benefits are sufficient; whether access should require negotiated obligations such as capacity building, affordable product access, training, authorship/attribution and local infrastructure; or whether contributor communities/countries should retain stronger licensing or access-control authority over secondary and commercial uses.

policies.text: open scientific sharing under privacy/security + general public benefit obligations
policies.text_detailed: Share openly under privacy and security safeguards with a general obligation to public benefit, with the safeguards specified and the benefit obligation stated in the access terms rather than left to goodwill.

policies.text: negotiated community/national benefit-sharing agreement before access
policies.text_detailed: Negotiate a community or national benefit-sharing agreement before access is granted, with the agreement covering what is returned, to whom and when, and access conditional on it.

policies.text: community-controlled licensing/access for sensitive or sovereign datasets
policies.text_detailed: Let contributing communities control licensing and access for sensitive or sovereign datasets, with the control exercised through a body they choose and decisions recorded.

policies.text: tiered access with local capacity-building/coauthorship/training obligations
policies.text_detailed: Grant tiered access carrying local capacity-building, co-authorship and training obligations, with each obligation specific enough to be checked and reported against annually.

policies.text: reciprocity framework requiring contributors share in scientific/economic benefits
policies.text_detailed: Require that contributors share in the scientific and economic value generated, with the mechanism — royalties, equity, guaranteed supply, training — named in the agreement rather than deferred.

policies.text: open-science framework resisting restrictive control where privacy/equity safeguards suffice
policies.text_detailed: Resist restrictive control where privacy and equity safeguards are sufficient, on the ground that open data serves the same populations, with the sufficiency of those safeguards assessed independently.

policies.text: commercial-use trigger requiring stronger financial/nonfinancial benefit sharing than nonprofit research use
policies.text_detailed: Require stronger financial and non-financial benefit sharing for commercial use than for non-profit research, with the commercial trigger defined and the stronger terms set in advance.

policies.text: Return results and capacity to the contributing communities on a published timetable, and require their agreement before commercial use.
policies.text_detailed: Return results and capacity to the contributing communities on a published timetable, and require their agreement before any commercial use, with the timetable reported against rather than merely stated.

cases.title: Involuntary isolation for infectious TB
cases.concise: An adult with highly infectious pulmonary tuberculosis repeatedly declines home isolation and infection-control measures despite housing support, transportation, directly observed treatment options and repeated counseling. The person remains contagious and regularly enters crowded indoor settings. Treatment itself is not being forced. The authority must decide whether to continue voluntary support only, impose time-limited involuntary isolation with review, or use another less restrictive supervised arrangement.
cases.detailed: An adult with confirmed contagious pulmonary TB understands the diagnosis and transmission risk but repeatedly leaves arranged housing and does not follow masking/home-isolation precautions. Public-health staff have offered treatment, food, income/housing support, transport, home-based care and supervised alternatives; these measures have failed to reduce exposure of others. The patient is not refusing because of untreated psychosis or inability to understand. The authority can continue voluntary/community measures, impose a legally authorized and regularly reviewed period of involuntary isolation until infectiousness falls, or attempt a less restrictive supervised residential arrangement. Forced medication is not part of the represented options.

policies.text: voluntary supported adherence first, involuntary isolation only as last resort with due process/review
policies.text_detailed: Support voluntary adherence first, using involuntary isolation only as a last resort with due process and review, and record what support was provided before any order is sought.

policies.text: immediate temporary isolation where risk is acute while voluntary alternatives are organized
policies.text_detailed: Isolate temporarily where the risk is acute, while voluntary alternatives are organised in parallel, with the temporary order limited to the time needed to put them in place.

policies.text: community-based directly supported treatment/housing/income measures before detention
policies.text_detailed: Provide community-based directly supported treatment, housing and income measures before any detention, with each offered concretely and the offers recorded.

policies.text: involuntary treatment not automatically permitted merely because isolation is justified
policies.text_detailed: Do not treat a justified isolation as authorising involuntary treatment: the two require separate findings, and consent to treatment is sought throughout the isolation.

policies.text: liberty/least-restrictive framework
policies.text_detailed: Apply a least-restrictive standard on liberty grounds, requiring that no lesser measure would achieve the objective, with the finding reviewable and reviewed.

policies.text: harm-prevention/reciprocity framework permitting time-limited detention only with material support and humane conditions
policies.text_detailed: Permit time-limited detention only where material support and humane conditions are provided, with both specified in the order and inspected during it.

policies.text: Provide housing, income and treatment support first, and record what was offered before any compulsory measure is considered.
policies.text_detailed: Provide housing, income and treatment support first, and record what was offered before any compulsory measure is considered, so that the record shows what was tried.

cases.title: Wastewater surveillance without individual consent
cases.concise: A city wants to expand wastewater surveillance from citywide infectious-disease monitoring to neighborhood-level monitoring for pathogens and drug markers. Individual opt-out is technically impossible. The data would not identify named people, but smaller catchments increase stigma and re-identification risks. The agency must choose whether to permit broad community-level surveillance, permit only lower-resolution pathogen surveillance with strict use limits and community oversight, or require special approval before small-area or noninfectious targets are monitored.
cases.detailed: A public-health department already monitors municipal wastewater for respiratory pathogens. It proposes adding neighborhood and institutional catchments and expanding targets to antimicrobial resistance and drug-use markers. Samples aggregate many individuals, but smaller catchments can map sensitive information to a dormitory, shelter, prison or neighborhood. Individual consent/opt-out cannot practically be obtained. The agency can keep broad surveillance authority where public-health benefit is demonstrated; restrict routine surveillance to sufficiently large catchments and infectious-disease targets while prohibiting law-enforcement or commercial use; or require community notice/ethics review before small-area or sensitive-target surveillance is added.

policies.text: community-level infectious-disease/toxin surveillance without individual consent under transparency/governance
policies.text_detailed: Conduct community-level infectious-disease and toxin surveillance without individual consent, under published governance covering what is monitored, at what resolution, and who may see it.

policies.text: prohibit or require heightened authorization for lifestyle/mental-health/drug-use surveillance
policies.text_detailed: Prohibit lifestyle, mental-health and drug-use surveillance, or require heightened authorisation for it, with the authorising body independent and its decisions published.

policies.text: allow neighborhood-level surveillance only when public-health necessity justifies stigmatization/privacy risk
policies.text_detailed: Permit neighbourhood-level surveillance only where public-health necessity justifies the stigmatisation and privacy risk, with that judgment made in advance by a named body and recorded.

policies.text: aggregate city/regional surveillance with no individual/household inference
policies.text_detailed: Aggregate to city or regional level with no household or individual inference possible, with the resolution limit stated technically and audited rather than left as policy.

policies.text: community consultation/notice + independent use-review before new targets
policies.text_detailed: Consult the community and give notice before adding a new target, with independent review of the proposed use and the outcome published before sampling changes.

policies.text: public-health-benefit framework favoring low-granularity disease surveillance
policies.text_detailed: Favour low-granularity disease surveillance on public-health-benefit grounds, keeping resolution at the lowest level that answers the question rather than the highest available.

policies.text: privacy/anti-surveillance-creep framework restricting sensitive targets/small geographic resolution
policies.text_detailed: Restrict sensitive targets and small geographic resolutions to prevent surveillance creep, with the restriction written into the sampling design rather than into a use policy that can change.

cases.title: Cross-border sharing of pathogen genomic data
cases.concise: A national laboratory identifies a new pathogen variant with possible pandemic significance. Rapid international sequence sharing could speed diagnostics and vaccines, but the country has previously received little credit, manufacturing access or benefit from samples it shared. The ministry must decide whether to release validated sequence data immediately on an open platform, share rapidly through a governed system that guarantees attribution and benefit-sharing obligations, or delay release for short national review and validation before international access.
cases.detailed: A lower-resource country's national laboratory detects a pathogen variant associated with unusual spread. The sequence and metadata are good enough to be useful but some epidemiologic details remain under validation. Previous pathogen sharing by the country led to global product development without timely local access. WHO guidance encourages timely, equitable pathogen genome sharing; in 2026 Member States are still negotiating the Pandemic Agreement's Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing annex, whose stated goal is rapid sharing on equal footing with fair/equitable access to resulting diagnostics, therapeutics and vaccines. The ministry must decide whether immediate open release best protects global health, whether rapid sharing should occur only through a system with attribution/capacity/benefit protections, or whether a short validation/national-review period is justified before release.

policies.text: rapid open sharing with standard attribution/privacy safeguards
policies.text_detailed: Share the sequence openly and immediately with standard attribution and privacy safeguards, with the deposit made to a public database rather than negotiated bilaterally.

policies.text: rapid sharing conditional on predefined benefit-sharing/access mechanism
policies.text_detailed: Share rapidly on condition of a benefit-sharing and access mechanism defined in advance, so that the terms do not have to be negotiated while the sequence is held.

policies.text: controlled platform sharing with access tiers and capacity support
policies.text_detailed: Share through a controlled platform with access tiers and capacity support, with the tiers published and support provided to laboratories that lack the capacity to use the data.

policies.text: temporary withholding until fair-benefit terms are secured
policies.text_detailed: Withhold temporarily until fair-benefit terms are secured, with the maximum period stated and the withholding reported so that it is visible rather than silent.

policies.text: global-solidarity framework favoring immediate sharing
policies.text_detailed: Share immediately on grounds of global solidarity, treating the sequence as a shared resource, and pursue benefit questions afterwards through the same mechanism each time.

policies.text: reciprocity/justice framework conditioning use on equitable countermeasure access
policies.text_detailed: Condition use on equitable access to the countermeasures the data produce, with the condition written into the access terms and enforceable rather than aspirational.

policies.text: staged rule requiring immediate minimal sequence/metadata sharing plus negotiated richer samples/data access
policies.text_detailed: Share minimal sequence and metadata immediately while negotiating access to richer samples and data, with the minimal set defined in advance so that immediate sharing is unambiguous.

policies.text: Share the sequence immediately and settle benefit terms in parallel, publishing what was agreed, so that people at risk do not wait on a negotiation.
policies.text_detailed: Share the sequence immediately and settle benefit terms in parallel, publishing what was agreed, so that people at risk do not wait on a negotiation. Immediate means on deposit rather than on agreement, and the parallel negotiation runs to a stated deadline so that it cannot become a delay by another route.

cases.title: HIV confidentiality and partner notification
cases.concise: An adult with newly diagnosed HIV has an identifiable ongoing sexual partner who may have been exposed. The patient understands the situation but refuses to notify the partner because of fear of relationship consequences. The service can offer assisted anonymous partner notification and safety planning. The decision is whether confidentiality should remain under patient control, whether provider-assisted notification should proceed without identifying the patient, or whether a targeted warning can be made after a defined threshold when supported disclosure fails.
cases.detailed: An adult receives a confirmed HIV diagnosis and reports an ongoing partner who may have had a clinically meaningful exposure. The patient is not virally suppressed yet. They refuse to disclose the diagnosis because they fear abandonment and social harm; no immediate threat of violence has been identified, and the clinic can offer counseling, anonymous/provider-assisted notification and linkage to testing. The service must decide whether to preserve confidentiality unless the patient consents, actively initiate provider-assisted notification that does not name the source, or permit a targeted warning only after supported disclosure fails and legal/public-health criteria for serious preventable harm are met.

policies.text: voluntary assisted partner notification with patient choice and safety planning
policies.text_detailed: Offer voluntary assisted partner notification with the patient choosing the route and the timing, and with safety planning done first where there is any risk of violence.

policies.text: provider-assisted notification without revealing index identity where feasible
policies.text_detailed: Notify through the service without revealing the index patient's identity where that is feasible, telling the patient in advance what will be said and what could still identify them.

policies.text: narrow direct warning where serious preventable risk and law/ethics threshold are met after voluntary efforts fail
policies.text_detailed: Warn directly only where serious preventable risk and the legal and ethical threshold are both met and voluntary efforts have failed, with each element recorded before disclosure.

policies.text: maintain confidentiality where notification would create serious violence/safety risk and alternative prevention is available
policies.text_detailed: Maintain confidentiality where notification would create a serious risk of violence and alternative prevention is available, with the risk assessed with the patient and the alternative arranged.

policies.text: confidentiality/trust framework
policies.text_detailed: Protect confidentiality on trust grounds, on the ground that people who fear disclosure do not test, with any exception narrow, stated in advance and rare in practice.

policies.text: duty-to-warn/harm-prevention framework with minimum-necessary disclosure
policies.text_detailed: Permit disclosure limited to the minimum necessary to prevent serious harm, disclosing only what the recipient needs to protect themselves and recording what was said.

policies.text: Offer to notify the partner in a way that does not name the patient, and let the patient choose the route, before any provider-led notification.
policies.text_detailed: Offer to notify the partner in a way that does not name the patient, and let the patient choose the route, before any provider-led notification, with the choice recorded.

cases.title: Mandatory testing/reporting for high-consequence infection
cases.concise: During an outbreak of a serious communicable infection, public-health officials can offer confidential voluntary testing, require laboratories to report confirmed cases by name, and in narrowly defined high-risk exposure settings can seek compulsory testing orders. The authority must decide what combination of voluntary testing, mandatory reporting and exceptional compulsory testing is ethically justified.
cases.detailed: A serious communicable infection causes substantial morbidity and can spread before symptoms are obvious. Testing is accurate and treatment/isolation can reduce transmission. Voluntary testing is widely available, but some high-risk exposures remain unresolved because individuals decline testing. Named reporting of confirmed cases would support contact tracing and outbreak control but reduces informational privacy. The authority must choose a policy that distinguishes ordinary voluntary testing from mandatory reporting of confirmed cases and from exceptional compulsory testing after a defined high-risk exposure when less restrictive measures fail.

policies.text: voluntary testing with counseling unless narrow necessity threshold met
policies.text_detailed: Test voluntarily with counselling unless a narrow necessity threshold is met, with the threshold stated in advance and its application recorded case by case.

policies.text: compulsory testing after high-risk exposure where results materially guide urgent prevention and less restrictive means fail
policies.text_detailed: Test compulsorily after high-risk exposure only where the result would materially guide urgent prevention and less restrictive means have failed, with both findings recorded.

policies.text: routine named reporting of confirmed notifiable disease under public-health law with confidentiality safeguards
policies.text_detailed: Report confirmed notifiable disease by name under public-health law with confidentiality safeguards, stating who receives the report, what they may do with it, and how long it is kept.

policies.text: deidentified/limited reporting where public-health objective can be met without names
policies.text_detailed: Report in de-identified or limited form wherever the public-health objective can be met without names, with the choice of form justified for each disease rather than set once.

policies.text: harm-prevention framework favoring mandatory measures when necessary/proportionate
policies.text_detailed: Favour mandatory measures where they are necessary and proportionate, with both assessed against this outbreak and the measures ending when the assessment changes.

policies.text: autonomy/privacy framework favoring voluntary testing and minimum data disclosure
policies.text_detailed: Favour voluntary testing and minimum data disclosure on autonomy and privacy grounds, with any mandatory element requiring a separate justification stated publicly.

policies.text: reciprocity rule requiring treatment/support/protection from discrimination whenever coercive testing/reporting is imposed
policies.text_detailed: Wherever coercive testing or reporting is imposed, guarantee treatment, support and protection from discrimination, with those provisions in place before the coercive measure begins.

policies.text: State exactly what is reported and to whom before testing, and guarantee treatment and support to anyone who tests positive.
policies.text_detailed: State exactly what is reported and to whom before testing, and guarantee treatment and support to anyone who tests positive, with both given in writing at the point of testing.

cases.title: Involuntary psychiatric treatment
cases.concise: An adult experiencing severe psychosis refuses admission and medication. The person can communicate a choice, but clinicians disagree about whether the person can appreciate the consequences and whether the current risk of serious harm is high enough to justify involuntary intervention. Community support and supported decision-making are available. The service must decide whether free and informed consent should remain controlling, whether a narrowly defined imminent-serious-harm threshold permits temporary coercion, or whether temporary intervention may instead depend on decision-specific incapacity plus necessity and repeated supported reassessment.
cases.detailed: An adult with severe psychotic symptoms refuses hospitalization and antipsychotic medication. The patient can state reasons and preferences but has impaired appreciation of some consequences; there is concerning but not certain risk of serious deterioration and injury. A trusted supporter, intensive community treatment and repeated capacity assessment are available. The legal system currently allows coercion under specified conditions, while WHO/OHCHR guidance advocates moving mental-health systems toward free and informed consent and eliminating coercive practices. The service must decide which ethical threshold should govern temporary intervention rather than treating diagnosis itself as incapacity.

policies.text: eliminate coercive treatment and rely on supported decision-making/free informed consent
policies.text_detailed: Provide no treatment without the person's free and informed consent, and meet crises with supported decision-making instead: a named supporter, a crisis plan made in advance, and time. Where consent cannot be obtained, care continues on the person's own terms rather than passing to compulsion.

policies.text: permit emergency involuntary treatment for immediate serious danger/capacity failure under strict review
policies.text_detailed: Permit involuntary treatment only for immediate serious danger together with a failure of capacity, under review that begins within a stated period and is conducted by someone outside the treating team. Both conditions must hold at the moment of the decision, and each is recorded separately.

policies.text: time-limited compulsory treatment only when necessary/least restrictive and likely to restore agency or prevent catastrophic harm
policies.text_detailed: Permit compulsory treatment only where it is necessary, the least restrictive option available, and likely either to restore the person's agency or to prevent catastrophic harm, for a fixed period stated at the outset and renewable only on fresh findings.

policies.text: advance directives/crisis plans should control where available
policies.text_detailed: Let a valid advance directive or crisis plan control where one exists, applying it as written rather than as a factor to weigh, and treat the absence of a plan as a reason to make one after the crisis rather than as licence to decide without it.

policies.text: autonomy/equal-legal-capacity framework opposing coercion
policies.text_detailed: Oppose coercive treatment on the ground that legal capacity is not lost with illness, and provide support to exercise it instead. Any measure that overrides the person's stated will requires a justification that would hold for a patient without a psychiatric diagnosis.

policies.text: harm-prevention/parens-patriae framework permitting narrow intervention
policies.text_detailed: Permit narrow intervention to prevent serious harm the person cannot presently avoid, bounded by what the harm requires, ended as soon as it is averted, and never extended for treatment goals the person has refused.

policies.text: independent advocacy/judicial or tribunal review for any continued coercion
policies.text_detailed: Require independent advocacy and judicial or tribunal review for any coercion that continues beyond the initial period, with the person present or represented, the reasons given to them, and the review at fixed intervals rather than on application.

policies.text: Give the person an independent advocate from the first assessment, and record their own account of what they want alongside the clinical judgement.
policies.text_detailed: Give the person an independent advocate from the first assessment rather than after admission, and record their own account of what they want alongside the clinical judgement, so that both are before whoever reviews the decision.

cases.title: Compulsory feeding in severe anorexia nervosa
cases.concise: An adult with severe anorexia nervosa has life-threatening malnutrition and refuses nasogastric feeding. The patient understands that death is possible but clinicians are uncertain whether illness-related values and impaired appreciation undermine decision-making capacity about nutrition. Prior treatment has included voluntary care, and the patient has expressed both a wish to live and a refusal of weight restoration. The service must decide whether to respect the refusal, use time-limited compulsory feeding to preserve life and recovery opportunity, or use a short rescue period with repeated capacity/values review before deciding whether coercion should continue.
cases.detailed: An adult with longstanding anorexia nervosa is admitted with severe malnutrition, cardiac risk and worsening biochemical abnormalities. The patient can repeat medical information and recognizes that refusing nutrition may be fatal, but interprets weight gain through intense illness-driven fears and has previously expressed ambivalence between wanting to survive and refusing restoration. Less intrusive oral and supported nutritional approaches have failed. The service can continue voluntary treatment and accept a capacitated refusal, institute compulsory enteral nutrition under applicable law to prevent imminent death, or use a narrowly time-limited rescue intervention while repeatedly reassessing decision-specific capacity, values, trauma burden and less restrictive alternatives.

policies.text: voluntary/relational treatment with intensive capacity-support first
policies.text_detailed: Treat voluntarily and relationally, with intensive support for the person's own decision-making first: their choice of setting, pace and supporters, and medical stabilisation offered rather than imposed. Compulsion is not available under this policy until that has genuinely been tried and recorded.

policies.text: compulsory feeding when immediate life-threatening risk + incapacity/necessity threshold met
policies.text_detailed: Feed compulsorily only where there is immediate life-threatening risk and the necessity and incapacity thresholds are both met, for the shortest period that resolves the danger, with the thresholds defined in advance and the assessment repeated daily.

policies.text: compulsory treatment even with apparent decision capacity in exceptional severe self-starvation under a protection threshold
policies.text_detailed: Permit compulsory treatment in exceptional severe self-starvation even where the person appears to have decisional capacity, under a protection threshold stated in advance, applied by a clinician outside the treating team and reviewed independently within days.

policies.text: time-limited rescue feeding with rapid reassessment and transition to collaborative care
policies.text_detailed: Use time-limited rescue feeding with reassessment at short fixed intervals and an explicit transition back to collaborative care as soon as the acute danger passes, with the transition planned before the feeding starts.

policies.text: respect capable refusal after robust assessment even when death risk is substantial
policies.text_detailed: Respect the capable person's refusal after robust, decision-specific assessment, even where the risk of death is substantial, provided the assessment is repeated, independently confirmed, and recorded with the person's own reasoning.

policies.text: rescue/nonmaleficence framework favoring intervention where illness impairs appreciation/choice
policies.text_detailed: Intervene where the illness itself impairs the person's appreciation of their situation, treating that impairment as the ground rather than the refusal, and stating what would count as appreciation returning.

policies.text: trauma-informed minimization rule limiting force, duration, and coercive setting
policies.text_detailed: Limit force, duration and setting to the minimum: the least restrictive method, the shortest period, the least institutional environment, with each departure recorded and reviewed, and the person's prior stated preferences about method followed where they exist.

policies.text: Involve the patient in setting the terms of any feeding while they can still speak to it, and record what they said for the next episode.
policies.text_detailed: Involve the patient in setting the terms of any feeding while they can still speak to it — method, setting, who is present, what would end it — and record what they said so it governs the next episode rather than being reconstructed under pressure.

cases.title: Disability weights and QALYs
cases.concise: A public payer evaluates an expensive treatment for a progressive condition affecting people who already live with substantial disability. Conventional QALY analysis values both survival and health-related quality of life, but disability advocates argue that some preference weights make years lived with disability count less and can therefore undervalue life extension. The agency must decide whether to retain standard QALYs, use QALYs with equity/severity modifiers and complementary measures, or replace disability-sensitive quality weighting with a measure that gives equal value to life extension while considering functional benefit separately.
cases.detailed: A national HTA agency is evaluating a treatment that extends life and improves some function for people with a severe chronic disability but does not restore them to population-average health. Standard cost-effectiveness modeling uses QALYs derived from health-state utilities. Disability advocates argue that this can encode public preferences about living with disability and make identical survival gains appear less valuable for people starting from lower measured quality of life. The agency also recognizes that QALYs capture treatment benefits beyond survival and permit comparisons across interventions. Current HTA practice offers alternatives rather than a simple binary: NICE uses QALYs but permits severity and other decision modifiers; ICER reports equal-value life years alongside QALYs. The agency must decide what measurement rule should govern reimbursement decisions.

policies.text: conventional QALY cost-effectiveness with severity modifiers
policies.text_detailed: Use conventional cost-effectiveness with QALYs and a severity modifier, stating the modifier and the threshold in advance so that the same rule applies across conditions rather than being adjusted case by case.

policies.text: QALY + equal-value life-year supplemental analysis
policies.text_detailed: Report the QALY analysis alongside an equal-value life-year analysis and present both to the decision-maker, with any divergence between them explained rather than resolved silently in favour of one.

policies.text: prohibit quality adjustment of life-extension benefit when it systematically disadvantages disabled people
policies.text_detailed: Do not quality-adjust the life-extension component of a benefit where doing so systematically disadvantages disabled people; count added years equally and apply quality adjustment only to changes in health state.

policies.text: use patient/condition-specific quality weights rather than general-population preferences
policies.text_detailed: Use quality weights elicited from people with the condition rather than from the general public, stating whose weights were used and how they were obtained, and reporting where they differ from population weights.

policies.text: retain general-population weights for societal allocation consistency
policies.text_detailed: Retain general-population weights for societal allocation, on the ground that consistency across conditions requires one source of weights, while reporting condition-specific weights alongside them so the difference is visible.

policies.text: severity/prioritarian modifier on top of QALYs
policies.text_detailed: Apply a severity or prioritarian modifier on top of the QALY calculation, with the modifier's size and the severity measure fixed in advance and published, rather than introduced when a particular result is unwelcome.

policies.text: multiperspective deliberative HTA combining QALY evidence with disability, equity, caregiver, and nonhealth considerations
policies.text_detailed: Combine the QALY evidence with disability, equity, caregiver and non-health considerations through a deliberative process that includes disabled people, and publish which considerations changed the decision.

cases.title: Seclusion and restraint in psychiatric crisis
cases.concise: An inpatient psychiatric patient becomes acutely agitated and is attempting to strike others. Verbal de-escalation, environmental modification and offered medication have failed. Staff can withdraw other patients from the area, but immediate injury risk remains. The service must decide whether coercive practices should be prohibited and managed only through noncoercive alternatives, whether brief emergency restraint may be used solely to prevent imminent injury with mandatory review, or whether a broader least-restrictive physical intervention policy should remain available.
cases.detailed: A psychiatric inpatient experiences an acute crisis and repeatedly attempts to strike staff and another patient. Trauma-informed verbal de-escalation, sensory/environmental modification, space, support-person involvement and offered medication have not reduced the immediate risk. Staff can clear most of the environment but cannot fully eliminate danger to the patient and others. WHO/OHCHR guidance calls for elimination of seclusion and restraint and development of noncoercive services; many existing clinical systems nevertheless retain emergency powers. The service must decide what ethical policy should govern this narrow residual-risk situation and what review, duration and debriefing requirements apply.

policies.text: eliminate seclusion/restraint and use noncoercive alternatives
policies.text_detailed: Use no seclusion or restraint at all, and staff the service for the non-coercive alternatives that replace them: de-escalation, sensory and support options, and enough people to use them. The commitment is to the alternatives being available, not only to the prohibition.

policies.text: emergency physical intervention only for immediate serious danger when less restrictive measures fail, shortest duration + monitoring
policies.text_detailed: Use physical intervention only for immediate serious danger after less restrictive measures have failed, for the shortest duration, with continuous monitoring, a debrief with the person afterwards, and each episode reviewed at service level.

policies.text: staff-intensive de-escalation/sensory/support alternatives as mandatory first line
policies.text_detailed: Require staff-intensive de-escalation, sensory and support alternatives as a mandatory first line, with their use recorded before any restrictive intervention, and staffing planned so that they are actually available at night and at weekends.

policies.text: restraint without seclusion versus seclusion without mechanical restraint depending immediate risk
policies.text_detailed: Choose between restraint without seclusion and seclusion without mechanical restraint according to the immediate risk, recording which was chosen and why, and following the person's recorded preference where one exists.

policies.text: trauma/autonomy framework strongly minimizing coercion
policies.text_detailed: Minimise coercion strongly on trauma and autonomy grounds: every restrictive episode is treated as a harm to be accounted for, counted, reviewed, and reduced against a stated target rather than accepted as routine.

policies.text: emergency harm-prevention framework permitting narrowly bounded force
policies.text_detailed: Permit narrowly bounded force to prevent immediate serious harm, with the bounds — what may be done, for how long, by whom — set in advance rather than judged in the moment, and any excess reported as an incident.

cases.title: Psychiatric advance directives
cases.concise: A patient completed a psychiatric advance directive while well, refusing a specific medication because of prior severe adverse effects and naming a preferred alternative. During a later psychotic crisis the patient lacks decision-making capacity about treatment. Clinicians believe the refused medication would work faster than the preferred alternative. The service must decide whether the prior directive controls, whether a narrow emergency override is permitted, or whether the appointed proxy and supported interpretation of the patient's prior values should govern.
cases.detailed: An adult with recurrent severe mental illness completed a detailed advance directive during a sustained period of capacity. It refuses one medication associated with prior intolerable effects, names an alternative, and designates a trusted proxy. During a later crisis, the patient lacks decision-specific capacity and cannot engage consistently in treatment decisions. The treating team believes the refused drug would likely restore functioning more rapidly, while the preferred drug remains clinically reasonable but may act more slowly. The service must decide how much authority the prior directive, current expressed wishes and proxy interpretation should have, and whether any emergency override should be limited to a defined serious-harm threshold.

policies.text: honor directive as controlling during incapacity where applicable
