policies.text_detailed: Honour the directive as controlling during incapacity wherever it applies, following its terms as written, and record what was followed. A clinician who finds it does not apply must say why in the record at the time.

policies.text: override only for narrowly specified emergency necessity/legal threshold
policies.text_detailed: Override only where a narrowly specified emergency necessity or legal threshold is met, with the specific clause and the reason recorded, and the override ending when the emergency does rather than continuing through the admission.

policies.text: use supported interpretation of directive and current values before override
policies.text_detailed: Interpret the directive with support — the named supporter, previous crises, what the person has said — and use that interpretation before considering override, so that an ambiguity is resolved rather than treated as a gap.

policies.text: allow patient to preauthorize specified treatments they may later resist during crisis
policies.text_detailed: Allow the person to pre-authorise specified treatments they may later resist during crisis, provided the authorisation names those treatments, was made with support while well, and can be revoked while well.

policies.text: current-resistance/autonomy framework limiting Ulysses-type clauses
policies.text_detailed: Limit pre-authorisation clauses where the person resists at the time, on the ground that present refusal carries weight the earlier self cannot extinguish, and require any use of such a clause to be reviewed independently.

policies.text: crisis-beneficence framework permitting temporary override to prevent catastrophic harm
policies.text_detailed: Permit temporary override to prevent catastrophic harm, bounded to what that harm requires, with control returned as soon as it passes and the reasons given to the person afterwards.

policies.text: independent review/advocacy for any override with postcrisis debrief and restoration of control
policies.text_detailed: Require independent review and advocacy for any override, followed by a debrief with the person and an explicit restoration of their control, with the directive revisited together rather than left as it stood.

policies.text: Give the person a route to see and revise the directive while well, and require anyone overriding it to record their reasons to the person afterwards.
policies.text_detailed: Give the person a route to see and revise the directive while well, on a schedule rather than on request, and require anyone who overrides it to record their reasons and give them to the person afterwards.

cases.title: Suicide-related treatment refusal with apparent capacity
cases.concise: An adult is medically stabilized after an intentional overdose and asks to leave. The patient can explain the diagnosis, options, and possibility of death if another attempt occurs, and gives coherent reasons for refusing admission. Clinicians still believe short-term suicide risk is high. The team must decide whether a capacitated refusal should be honored, whether temporary protection is justified despite apparent capacity, or whether a brief observation/support period should precede a final capacity and refusal decision.
cases.detailed: An adult is treated successfully after an intentional overdose. Hours later the patient denies current intent, explains the medical and psychiatric risks, reasons consistently about options, and requests discharge. There is recent major psychosocial loss, continuing hopelessness and a high estimated short-term risk of another attempt, but no psychosis or intoxication. Clinicians can offer crisis planning, family/support involvement and voluntary admission. The service must decide whether decision-specific capacity alone should control discharge, whether suicide prevention can justify temporary involuntary protection even when capacity appears intact, or whether a short, predefined observation/support period is justified before a final refusal is honored.

policies.text: emergency stabilization/observation while decisional capacity is uncertain, then reassess
policies.text_detailed: Stabilise and observe while decisional capacity is uncertain, then reassess at a defined point rather than holding indefinitely, with the uncertainty and what would resolve it recorded at the outset.

policies.text: respect refusal once robust decision-specific capacity is confirmed and immediate coercive threshold no longer applies
policies.text_detailed: Respect the refusal once robust decision-specific capacity is confirmed and no immediate coercive threshold applies, with the assessment conducted when the person is medically clear rather than during acute intoxication or delirium.

policies.text: continue involuntary protection despite apparent capacity during a narrowly defined acute suicidal crisis
policies.text_detailed: Continue protective intervention despite apparent capacity during a narrowly defined acute crisis, with the definition set in advance, the period fixed, and independent review before any extension.

policies.text: use supported decision-making and short delay where risk can be safely contained
policies.text_detailed: Use supported decision-making and a short delay where risk can be safely contained, naming the length of the delay and what it is for, and letting the person leave when it ends unless something has changed.

policies.text: autonomy framework treating competent refusal as controlling
policies.text_detailed: Treat competent refusal as controlling, with capacity assessed for this decision and not inferred from the attempt itself, and the person told what has been assessed and found.

policies.text: protection-of-life framework permitting temporary intervention where preference formation is plausibly crisis-distorted
policies.text_detailed: Permit temporary intervention where the person's preference was plausibly formed under crisis conditions, bounded to a stated period, with the judgment recorded and reassessed rather than carried forward.

policies.text: independent second capacity assessment before irreversible refusal in high-lethality context
policies.text_detailed: Require a second, independent capacity assessment before accepting a refusal in a high-lethality context, conducted by someone not involved in the person's care and recorded with its reasoning.

policies.text: Keep the person's own account of the attempt and their reasons on the record, and offer follow-up they can accept rather than only detention.
policies.text_detailed: Keep the person's own account of the attempt and their reasons in the record, and offer follow-up they will actually accept — their choice of setting and clinician — rather than detention as the only thing on offer.

cases.title: Passive digital phenotyping in mental-health care
cases.concise: A mental-health program can use smartphone and wearable data such as mobility, sleep, typing and communication patterns to detect changes associated with relapse. The model is clinically useful but imperfect and requires continuous passive collection. Patients can disable monitoring, but clinicians worry that those at highest risk may disengage just before relapse. The service must choose opt-in monitoring, default monitoring with granular controls for a narrowly defined high-risk program, or no passive monitoring outside specific validated episodes of care.
cases.detailed: A specialty clinic has validated a digital-phenotyping model that combines passive phone and wearable signals to identify increased relapse risk earlier than routine visits. Data are sensitive, false positives occur, and the raw signals could reveal behavior unrelated to treatment. Patients and caregivers want clear information about clinical utility, accuracy, privacy, control and who can access the data. The service must choose whether continuous monitoring requires affirmative opt-in; whether enrollment in a defined high-risk program can include default monitoring with clear notice, pause/delete controls and human review; or whether passive sensing should remain outside routine care except for narrowly validated indications.

policies.text: explicit opt-in for passive sensing with granular controls
policies.text_detailed: Require explicit opt-in for passive sensing, with granular control over which signals are collected, and a plain statement of what each one reveals. Consent is sought outside a crisis and can be withdrawn without affecting care.

policies.text: default-off but clinician may offer monitoring for high-risk patients
policies.text_detailed: Keep sensing off by default while allowing a clinician to offer it to patients at high risk, with the offer recorded, declining carrying no consequence, and the reason for the offer explained to the patient.

policies.text: default-on in a defined high-risk program with easy opt-out and strict use limits
policies.text_detailed: Turn sensing on by default within a defined high-risk programme, with an opt-out that takes effect immediately, strict limits on what the data may be used for, and the default reviewed as the programme's evidence accumulates.

policies.text: local/on-device or data-minimized sensing rather than continuous raw-data transfer
policies.text_detailed: Process signals on the device or in minimised form rather than transferring raw data continuously, sending only what a clinical alert requires, and stating what leaves the phone.

policies.text: allow safety alerts to clinicians under predefined thresholds but prohibit unrelated secondary use
policies.text_detailed: Allow safety alerts to clinicians against thresholds fixed in advance, and prohibit any other use of the data — service improvement, research, commercial — without separate consent for that purpose.

policies.text: patient-control framework over pause/delete/share settings
policies.text_detailed: Give the patient control over pausing, deleting and sharing, available in the app rather than by request, with deletion covering derived measures and not only the raw signal.

policies.text: beneficence/suicide-prevention framework allowing more proactive monitoring when demonstrable benefit exceeds privacy burden
policies.text_detailed: Permit more proactive monitoring where a demonstrated benefit outweighs the privacy burden for this patient, with the benefit stated in terms of what the monitoring would change, and the arrangement reviewed at intervals.

cases.title: Location monitoring for dementia wandering
cases.concise: A person with moderate dementia has twice become lost for several hours while walking independently. The person values unsupervised walks and objects to wearing a GPS device, saying it feels like being watched. A surrogate and care team believe tracking could preserve independent mobility while reducing danger. They must decide whether to use continuous monitoring despite resistance, use only triggered/minimal monitoring with repeated assent, or respect the refusal and rely on environmental and human-support alternatives.
cases.detailed: A person with moderate dementia continues to take daily neighborhood walks. Twice in the past month the person became disoriented and required assistance to return home. The person can express a stable dislike of location tracking but has difficulty appreciating the full risk of future wandering. Family and clinicians can use a GPS wearable with geofencing, arrange accompanied walks, modify routines and increase community support. Continuous tracking could preserve mobility but creates surveillance and dignity concerns. The care plan must determine whether surrogate-authorized continuous tracking is proportionate, whether monitoring should activate only during identified risk periods with repeated assent and minimal data retention, or whether the person's refusal should control while less intrusive supports are intensified.

policies.text: voluntary tracking with consent/assent where capacity permits
policies.text_detailed: Use tracking voluntarily, with the person's consent or assent wherever capacity permits, explained in a way they can engage with and revisited as their capacity changes rather than treated as settled at the start.

policies.text: surrogate-authorized least-intrusive tracking when wandering risk is substantial and person cannot decide
policies.text_detailed: Where the person cannot decide, permit surrogate-authorised tracking only where the wandering risk is substantial, in the least intrusive form that meets it, with the authorisation recorded and reviewed at set intervals.

policies.text: use geofence/alert rather than continuous live tracking to minimize intrusion
policies.text_detailed: Use a geofence with alerts rather than continuous live tracking, so that location is known only when the person leaves a defined area, with the boundary set for safety rather than convenience.

policies.text: avoid tracking when the person consistently resists and risk can be managed through environmental/support alternatives
policies.text_detailed: Do not track where the person consistently resists and the risk can be managed through environmental or support alternatives, with those alternatives put in place rather than merely considered.

policies.text: permit covert tracking only under exceptional serious-risk conditions with review
policies.text_detailed: Permit covert tracking only under exceptional serious-risk conditions, authorised outside the care team, for a fixed period, and reviewed with a presumption against renewal.

policies.text: safety/independence framework favoring technology that enables less restrictive living
policies.text_detailed: Favour technology that allows less restrictive living, on the ground that a person able to walk outside with a device is freer than one kept indoors, with that comparison made explicitly for this person.

policies.text: privacy/dignity framework requiring minimization, retention limits, and no secondary use
policies.text_detailed: Minimise what is collected, retain it only as long as the safety purpose requires, and prohibit secondary use, with retention periods stated and deletion actually carried out rather than left to the provider's discretion.

cases.title: BCI neural data and mental privacy
cases.concise: A therapeutic BCI records neural signals needed to control an assistive device. The provider can also analyze stored signals to improve algorithms and may be able to infer patterns unrelated to the immediate clinical task. The patient benefits from continued system improvement but is concerned about mental privacy. The provider must choose care-only use, explicit consent for each research/secondary use, or broader deidentified model-improvement use under strict governance.
cases.detailed: A patient uses an implanted therapeutic BCI to control a communication or mobility device. Continuous neural signals are processed to generate device commands and are partly stored for calibration and safety. Engineers can use additional neural data to improve decoding models across patients, and future analytic methods may reveal information not anticipated at enrollment. The provider must decide whether neural data may be used only for the patient's direct care; whether separate explicit consent is required for research and model improvement; or whether deidentified secondary use for narrowly defined system improvement can occur under strong governance, transparency and prohibition of unrelated commercial profiling.

policies.text: explicit specific consent for secondary neural-data use
policies.text_detailed: Require explicit, specific consent for any secondary use of neural data, naming the purpose, who receives it and for how long, with a fresh consent for a new purpose rather than a general permission given once at enrolment.

policies.text: prohibit sale/behavioral advertising or unrelated commercial profiling from neural data
policies.text_detailed: Prohibit sale, behavioural advertising and unrelated commercial profiling from neural data outright, as a term of the device contract that survives changes of ownership rather than as a policy the provider may revise.

policies.text: permit bounded research reuse under strong deidentification/governance and opt-out
policies.text_detailed: Permit bounded research reuse under strong de-identification, governed access and a working opt-out, with the permitted purposes listed and the opt-out effective for future use without ending the person's clinical care.

policies.text: allow participant-controlled data portability/access
policies.text_detailed: Allow the participant to obtain and move their own data in a usable form, on request and without charge, including the derived signals rather than only the raw recording.

policies.text: mental-privacy framework treating inferred mental states as specially protected even when raw data are shared
policies.text_detailed: Treat inferred mental states as specially protected even where the raw signals are shared, so that a permission to share data is not a permission to infer and disclose what the person was thinking or feeling.

policies.text: scientific-benefit framework permitting governed reuse where reidentification/inference risks are controlled
policies.text_detailed: Permit governed reuse where re-identification and inference risks are controlled and audited, with the controls specified, tested, and reported rather than asserted in the consent form.

policies.text: delete/cease collection when user withdraws except narrowly justified safety/regulatory retention
policies.text_detailed: Delete data and stop collection when the user withdraws, retaining only what a named safety or regulatory obligation requires, with that retention stated at consent and its duration fixed.

policies.text: Let the user see what is stored, take it with them, and stop collection, with those controls available in the device rather than on request.
policies.text_detailed: Let the user see what is stored, take it with them, and stop collection, with those controls present in the device interface rather than available on request through the provider.

cases.title: DBS and personality/value change
cases.concise: A patient with Parkinson disease has major motor improvement after DBS but family members report that the patient is more impulsive and socially different. The patient has decision-making capacity, values the increased energy and independence, and wants the settings unchanged. Before surgery the patient had said preserving certain personality traits mattered greatly. The team must decide whether current competent preferences control, whether pre-treatment values should constrain adjustment, or whether an iterative shared process should reconcile current preferences, prior goals and relational effects.
cases.detailed: A patient receives DBS for advanced Parkinson disease and obtains substantial motor benefit. Months later, the patient reports feeling more energetic, socially engaged and independent, while a spouse describes increased impulsivity and a loss of familiar traits. Formal assessment finds the patient currently capable of understanding the benefits, risks and alternatives. Preoperative counseling documented that the patient feared losing several personally meaningful characteristics, but recent patient-centered studies suggest DBS often improves rather than degrades valued characteristics and severe unwanted personality-change narratives may be overstated. The team must decide whether present capable preferences are decisive, whether pre-treatment values/advance goals should constrain programming, or whether programming should proceed through repeated shared decision-making that recognizes both identity continuity and relational consequences.

policies.text: current competent patient's treatment preferences govern adjustment
policies.text_detailed: Let the current competent patient's treatment preferences govern stimulation adjustment, with capacity assessed for this decision at the time rather than inferred from the personality change itself.

policies.text: use pre-treatment goals/values as strong interpretive evidence but not automatic veto over current competent wishes
policies.text_detailed: Use pre-treatment goals and values as strong evidence of what the patient wants, without letting them veto the current competent patient's wishes, and record where the two diverge so the divergence is visible rather than resolved silently.

policies.text: trial parameter reduction/off-period to assess reversibility and patient valuation where clinically safe
policies.text_detailed: Where clinically safe, trial a parameter reduction or off-period to see whether the change reverses and how the patient values each state, agreeing the length and the questions to be answered before it starts.

policies.text: give family observations evidentiary weight without transferring decisional authority
policies.text_detailed: Give family observations evidentiary weight as information about what has changed, without transferring any decisional authority to them, and tell the patient what the family has reported.

policies.text: authenticity/continuity framework favoring pre-treatment commitments
policies.text_detailed: Favour the patient's pre-treatment commitments where the change conflicts with them, on the ground that continuity of the person's own long-standing values is what treatment was meant to serve.

policies.text: current-self autonomy framework favoring present competent values
policies.text_detailed: Favour the present competent patient's values, on the ground that the person deciding now is the patient, and treat the earlier self's preferences as evidence rather than as a standing instruction.

policies.text: relational-welfare framework using negotiated adjustment when changes materially harm relationships yet patient remains competent
policies.text_detailed: Where the change materially harms the patient's relationships but the patient remains competent, negotiate an adjustment with the patient and those affected, with the patient retaining the decision and the negotiation recorded.

policies.text: Record the patient's own account of the change alongside the family's, and treat a disagreement between them as a reason to review the settings rather than to decide between accounts.
policies.text_detailed: Record the patient's own account of the change alongside the family's, and treat a disagreement between the two accounts as a reason to review the stimulation settings rather than to decide which account is right. Both accounts stay in the record, and the review is scheduled rather than left to whoever raises it again.

cases.title: Neuroenhancement in healthy adults
cases.concise: A noninvasive neurostimulation device has, for this benchmark, a well-characterized safety profile and produces a modest improvement in sustained attention in healthy adults. The effect is temporary and does not treat disease. A regulated clinic wants to offer it to adults seeking performance enhancement. The regulator must decide whether to permit voluntary enhancement, restrict clinical neurotechnology to treatment/restoration, or permit enhancement only with safeguards addressing coercion, fairness and access.
cases.detailed: A future noninvasive neurostimulation technology has undergone extensive testing and, for this benchmark, produces a reproducible modest improvement in sustained attention in healthy adults with no known serious adverse effects. It is not required to treat illness and the benefit is temporary. Universities and employers cannot require its use under the benchmark, but competitive pressure may still emerge if access becomes common. Public-attitude research on neuroenhancement is context-sensitive rather than uniformly permissive or prohibitive. UNESCO's 2025 neurotechnology Recommendation is cautious about non-therapeutic use and emphasizes dignity, autonomy, mental integrity, explicit consent and protection against coercive or exploitative uses. The regulator must choose the permissible scope of enhancement services.

policies.text: permit competent adult enhancement under informed-consent/safety regulation
policies.text_detailed: Permit enhancement in competent adults under informed-consent and safety regulation, with the consent stating what is known about long-term effects and what is not, and post-market monitoring in place.

policies.text: restrict to therapeutic/restorative indications
policies.text_detailed: Restrict use to therapeutic and restorative indications, with the boundary defined by a stated clinical criterion rather than by the wording of a request, and reviewed as diagnostic categories change.

policies.text: permit limited enhancement but prohibit coercive employer/school/military use
policies.text_detailed: Permit limited enhancement while prohibiting employer, school and military use that a person cannot refuse without cost, with the prohibition enforced against the institution rather than the individual.

policies.text: prohibit enhancement where positional competition/inequality externalities are substantial
policies.text_detailed: Prohibit enhancement where the positional and inequality effects would be substantial, assessing those effects for the specific capacity and setting rather than for enhancement in general.

policies.text: allow with equitable access and noncoercion safeguards
policies.text_detailed: Allow enhancement subject to equitable access and safeguards against pressure, so that availability does not depend on income and declining carries no penalty at work or in education.

policies.text: precautionary moratorium for long-term neural/personality effects despite technical efficacy
policies.text_detailed: Hold a precautionary moratorium while long-term neural and personality effects are unknown, even where short-term efficacy is established, with the moratorium tied to named evidence gaps and reviewed on a stated schedule.

policies.text: cognitive-liberty framework including both right to enhance and right not to be pressured
policies.text_detailed: Protect cognitive liberty in both directions: a right to enhance and a right not to be pressured into it, with the second enforced through employment and education rules rather than left to individual refusal.

cases.title: Increasingly complex neural organoids
cases.concise: A laboratory studies increasingly complex human neural organoids that reproduce aspects of brain development and network activity. There is no evidence that current organoids are conscious or sentient, but future systems may become more complex. The institution must decide whether enhanced oversight should begin before credible evidence of sentience, whether ordinary tissue-research governance should continue until a defined scientific threshold is reached, or whether staged monitoring with prohibited endpoints should be introduced now.
cases.detailed: A research institute develops three-dimensional neural organoids used to model development and neurological disease. The models do not have sensory organs, a body, or demonstrated consciousness, but their cellular organization and electrophysiological complexity are increasing. Some experiments involve transplantation into animals. The Nuffield Council on Bioethics' 2026 report identifies governance gaps, cautions against assuming present sentience, and recommends anticipatory governance as capabilities develop. The institution must decide whether enhanced ethics review should apply broadly now, whether ordinary tissue/research-animal rules are sufficient until a credible welfare threshold emerges, or whether staged monitoring should track defined scientific indicators and prohibit specified endpoints or experiments as concern increases.

policies.text: ordinary/specialized oversight scaled to model complexity without assuming sentience
policies.text_detailed: Scale oversight to the complexity of the model without assuming sentience, using stated features to decide the level of review, and applying ordinary research governance below the threshold.

policies.text: enhanced review when features plausibly associated with morally relevant neural function emerge
policies.text_detailed: Trigger enhanced review when features plausibly associated with morally relevant neural function emerge, with those features named in advance and monitoring in place to detect them rather than relying on investigator report.

policies.text: prohibit specified integration/transplantation/endpoints above precautionary threshold
policies.text_detailed: Prohibit specified integration, transplantation and endpoints above a precautionary threshold, with the prohibited procedures listed rather than described in general terms, and the list revisited as capability changes.

policies.text: allow research under anticipatory monitoring because current organoids lack evidence of sentience
policies.text_detailed: Permit the research under anticipatory monitoring, on the ground that current organoids show no evidence of sentience, with the monitoring designed to detect the indicators that would change that judgment.

policies.text: precautionary moral-status framework favoring stronger safeguards before certainty
policies.text_detailed: Favour stronger safeguards before certainty, on the ground that the cost of over-protecting a non-sentient model is lower than the cost of under-protecting a sentient one, with the safeguards proportionate and reviewable.

policies.text: scientific-value framework resisting embryo/person analogies absent relevant capacities
policies.text_detailed: Resist embryo or person analogies where the relevant capacities are absent, and require any restriction to name the capacity it is protecting rather than the resemblance it is responding to.

policies.text: require public/stakeholder engagement and periodic capability-triggered governance revision
policies.text_detailed: Require public and stakeholder engagement and revisit the governance whenever a capability threshold is crossed, with the engagement conducted before the threshold rather than after, and its outcome published.

policies.text: Publish what is being grown and what would trigger a stop, so that the limits are set in public before they are reached.
policies.text_detailed: Publish what is being grown and what would trigger a stop, so that the limits are set in public before they are reached, and report against them at stated intervals.

cases.title: Secondary use of health records without re-consent
cases.concise: A public health system holds longitudinal clinical records from millions of patients. Researchers propose a low-risk study using coded data under data-access controls. Re-contacting every patient would make the study impracticable. The system can use governed secondary data by default with opt-out, require study-specific opt-in consent, or use a tiered rule in which low-risk coded research is governed centrally while identifiable, sensitive or commercial uses require stronger consent.
cases.detailed: A health system maintains longitudinal electronic records collected for direct care. A research team proposes analysis of coded records to study treatment outcomes; no direct patient contact is planned and the data would remain inside a secure environment. The health system also sometimes receives requests involving identifiable data, highly sensitive conditions or commercial partners. A 2024 systematic review of more than 100 studies found public willingness to share health data is generally conditional on purpose, recipient, privacy, trust and control rather than simply pro- or anti-sharing. The NHS National Data Opt-Out is a real policy model allowing confidential patient data to be used for research/planning unless individuals opt out, subject to exemptions. The governance board must choose whether broad governed opt-out use is acceptable, whether new research requires affirmative consent, or whether consent requirements should vary with identifiability, sensitivity and recipient.

policies.text: governed secondary research use with notice/opt-out
policies.text_detailed: Permit secondary research use under published governance with notice and a working opt-out, with the notice given where patients will see it and the opt-out effective for future use without affecting their care.

policies.text: specific/reconsent for materially new or sensitive uses
policies.text_detailed: Require fresh specific consent for materially new or sensitive uses, with what counts as material defined in advance so that the boundary is not set by whoever proposes the use.

policies.text: broad consent at collection for future categories
policies.text_detailed: Take broad consent at collection for named future categories, with those categories described concretely and a route for patients to see what has actually been done under them.

policies.text: deidentified research use without reconsent under independent review
policies.text_detailed: Permit de-identified research use without re-consent under independent review, with the de-identification standard specified, tested against re-identification, and the review body's decisions published.

policies.text: prohibit commercial secondary use without explicit consent or benefit-sharing
policies.text_detailed: Prohibit commercial secondary use without explicit consent or a benefit-sharing arrangement, with commercial defined by who profits rather than by the legal form of the recipient.

policies.text: solidarity/social-value framework favoring governed reuse
policies.text_detailed: Favour governed reuse on solidarity and social-value grounds, with the value that reuse produced reported back to patients rather than assumed.

policies.text: privacy/control framework favoring granular authorization for identifiable/sensitive data
policies.text_detailed: Require granular authorisation for identifiable and sensitive data, with the categories and the choices presented in a form patients can actually use and revisit.

cases.title: Digital proximity/contact tracing
cases.concise: During a serious outbreak, a privacy-preserving Bluetooth system can identify recent close contacts faster than manual tracing and is expected to reduce transmission if uptake is high. The authority must decide whether participation should remain voluntary with strong privacy protections, whether use can be required in narrowly defined high-risk settings, or whether digital tracing should not be used beyond ordinary manual public-health methods.
cases.detailed: A novel respiratory outbreak is spreading rapidly. A decentralized Bluetooth contact-tracing tool has been independently tested and is expected to shorten notification delays relative to manual tracing. It does not collect GPS location and automatically deletes proximity data after a short period. Uptake matters to effectiveness. WHO's ethical guidance for digital proximity tracking emphasizes voluntariness, data minimization, proportionality, transparency, time limitation, privacy protection and prohibition of commercial/law-enforcement uses. Public acceptance studies show privacy, trust and perceived benefit strongly affect willingness. The authority must choose the participation/governance rule rather than assume maximum uptake automatically justifies compulsion.

policies.text: voluntary privacy-preserving app with informed participation
policies.text_detailed: Use a voluntary privacy-preserving app with informed participation, with what it collects and infers explained in plain terms before installation and no service conditioned on it.

policies.text: voluntary system plus strong access/education/integration to maximize uptake
policies.text_detailed: Keep the system voluntary while investing in access, education and integration to raise uptake, with uptake reported by group so that gaps are visible rather than averaged away.

policies.text: temporary mandatory use for a narrowly defined high-risk setting
policies.text_detailed: Require use temporarily in a narrowly defined high-risk setting, with the setting, the duration and the end condition stated in the order and the requirement lifted automatically at its end.

policies.text: decentralized/minimum-data architecture
policies.text_detailed: Use a decentralised, minimum-data architecture in which matching happens on the device, with what leaves the phone specified technically and independently verified.

policies.text: centralized public-health architecture with strict purpose/time limits when epidemiologically necessary
policies.text_detailed: Use a centralised architecture where epidemiologically necessary, with strict purpose and time limits written into law, the data deleted on schedule, and deletion audited.

policies.text: public-health solidarity framework favoring participation
policies.text_detailed: Favour participation on solidarity grounds, framed as a contribution rather than an obligation, with no penalty of any kind for those who decline.

policies.text: autonomy/privacy framework rejecting coercive or function-creeping tracing
policies.text_detailed: Reject coercive tracing and function creep, with the permitted purposes fixed at launch and any extension requiring fresh authorisation rather than a policy update.

policies.text: Keep use voluntary and the data on the phone, and publish what the system does, so that a person can decline without losing access to testing or care.
policies.text_detailed: Keep use voluntary and the data on the phone, and publish what the system does, so that a person can decline without losing access to testing or care, with that guarantee stated at installation.

cases.title: Commercial partnership using health-system data
cases.concise: A nonprofit health system can partner with a technology company to develop a model expected to improve diagnosis. The company would receive coded patient data inside a controlled environment and would own some resulting intellectual property. The health system can permit the partnership under privacy/public-benefit conditions, require a nonexclusive or public-benefit licensing model, or require individual consent before any commercial secondary use.
cases.detailed: A nonprofit health system holds a large clinical dataset collected for care. A commercial company proposes using coded data in a secure environment to develop a clinically useful predictive model. The company will invest substantial engineering resources and seeks commercial rights; the hospital would receive discounted access and research collaboration but patients would not receive individual payments. Public-attitude reviews show that commercial involvement often lowers willingness to share and raises concerns about consent, privacy, control, profit and benefit sharing, while support can remain substantial when public benefit and governance are clear. The board must decide what conditions make the partnership acceptable.

policies.text: governed partnership without individual reconsent for low-risk public-benefit analytics
policies.text_detailed: Permit a governed partnership without individual re-consent for low-risk analytics of public benefit, with the permitted analyses listed, the outputs reviewed, and the arrangement published.

policies.text: explicit opt-in for identifiable/commercial uses
policies.text_detailed: Require explicit opt-in for identifiable or commercial uses, with the opt-in specific to the use and not bundled with consent to treatment.

policies.text: opt-out with strong transparency/independent oversight
policies.text_detailed: Permit use with an opt-out, strong transparency and independent oversight, with the oversight body able to stop the arrangement and its findings published.

policies.text: benefit-sharing/reinvestment requirement where commercial value is generated
policies.text_detailed: Require benefit-sharing or reinvestment wherever commercial value is generated, with the mechanism and the amounts published rather than described in principle.

policies.text: prohibit sale/exclusive commercial access without consent
policies.text_detailed: Prohibit sale or exclusive commercial access without consent, with exclusivity defined broadly enough to cover preferential access arrangements.

policies.text: public-benefit framework allowing partnership where outputs improve care and access
policies.text_detailed: Permit partnership on public-benefit grounds where the outputs improve care and access, with the improvement measured and reported rather than asserted in the agreement.

policies.text: data-trust/intermediary model separating health system from vendor and constraining downstream use
policies.text_detailed: Interpose a data trust or intermediary between the health system and the vendor, constraining downstream use, with the trust's duties owed to patients and its decisions published.

cases.title: AI care-management allocation and structural bias
cases.concise: A validated algorithm ranks patients for intensive care management and improves overall identification of people likely to benefit. Audit shows that, because it partly learned from prior health spending, it under-ranks clinically ill patients in a disadvantaged group whose historical spending was lower despite similar illness burden. The system must decide whether to withhold deployment until disparity is corrected, deploy only with fairness correction/human review, or deploy for aggregate benefit while monitoring the gap.
cases.detailed: A health system has a model that predicts which chronically ill patients should receive scarce high-intensity care-management slots. Compared with the prior manual process, the model increases overall identification of high-need patients. Subgroup audit, however, shows materially lower sensitivity for a disadvantaged racialized population because past health expenditures imperfectly proxy health need and reflect unequal access. The disparity is known and technically reducible, though correction may modestly reduce overall predictive accuracy. The system must decide whether deployment should wait until subgroup performance meets a threshold, proceed with explicit fairness correction and human review, or proceed based on net aggregate benefit with monitoring.

policies.text: recalibrate/replace biased proxy before continued use
policies.text_detailed: Recalibrate or replace the biased proxy before continued use, with the replacement validated by subgroup and the interim arrangements stated rather than left to the model as it stands.

policies.text: add equity constraints or direct need variables even at modest overall predictive cost
policies.text_detailed: Add equity constraints or direct need variables even at a modest cost in overall prediction, with the cost quantified and the resulting subgroup performance reported.

policies.text: suspend use until subgroup performance meets threshold
policies.text_detailed: Suspend use until subgroup performance meets a stated threshold, with the threshold fixed in advance and the fallback pathway named so that suspension does not leave patients unranked.

policies.text: continue temporarily with clinician review/manual equity correction while replacement is built
policies.text_detailed: Continue temporarily with clinician review and manual equity correction while a replacement is built, with the correction procedure specified, its use recorded, and a deadline for the replacement.

policies.text: equal-performance framework favoring subgroup parity
policies.text_detailed: Require subgroup parity on equal-performance grounds, with parity defined on a stated metric and deployment conditional on meeting it.

policies.text: clinical-benefit framework permitting some performance differences if outcomes improve for every group and no less discriminatory alternative exists
policies.text_detailed: Permit some performance difference where outcomes improve for every group and no less discriminatory alternative exists, with both conditions demonstrated and re-tested as the model updates.

policies.text: continuous bias monitoring/audit + appeal pathway
policies.text_detailed: Monitor and audit for bias continuously and provide an appeal pathway, with the audit results published and the appeal available to patients rather than only to clinicians.

policies.text: Tell patients that a ranking system is used, what it uses, and how to ask for review, so that someone missed by it has a route back.
policies.text_detailed: Tell patients that a ranking system is used, what it uses, and how to ask for review, so that someone missed by it has a route back, with the notice given at registration rather than on request.

cases.title: Clinician override of validated AI recommendation
cases.concise: A clinical prediction model is highly validated for a defined treatment decision and recommends treatment A. The treating clinician believes an unusual contextual factor not represented in the model makes treatment B safer. The hospital must decide whether clinicians retain unrestricted authority to override, whether following the AI should be the default unless a documented rationale is entered, or whether escalation should depend on model confidence, case novelty and risk.
cases.detailed: A hospital deploys a validated decision-support model with strong overall and subgroup performance for a common treatment decision. In a particular case the model strongly recommends treatment A, but the clinician identifies a contextual factor—documented in the chart but not represented in model inputs—that plausibly changes the risk-benefit balance. The patient has not yet been treated. AMA AI principles call for qualified human intervention points and generally preserving the ability of clinicians to intervene or override, with earlier intervention as potential harm increases. The governance committee must decide how much procedural weight the model should have while avoiding both reflexive automation and unaccountable intuition.

policies.text: clinician may override with documented rationale and accountability
policies.text_detailed: Permit the clinician to override with a documented rationale and named accountability, with the rationale recorded at the time and reviewed in aggregate rather than case by case.

policies.text: mandatory human review before high-stakes AI recommendation is acted on
policies.text_detailed: Require human review before any high-stakes recommendation is acted on, with the categories of high-stakes decision defined in advance and the review substantive rather than a confirmation click.

policies.text: require second review when override conflicts with strongly validated model in high-risk case
policies.text_detailed: Require a second review where an override conflicts with a strongly validated model in a high-risk case, with the second reviewer independent and the outcome recorded either way.

policies.text: model-default with human override for low-risk standardized tasks
policies.text_detailed: Let the model decide by default for low-risk standardised tasks with human override available, with the task list fixed and reviewed as performance data accumulate.

policies.text: professional-responsibility framework preserving clinician authority
policies.text_detailed: Preserve clinician authority on professional-responsibility grounds, with the clinician accountable for the decision whether or not it follows the model.

policies.text: consistency/decision-quality framework requiring structured justification for override to reduce arbitrary bias
policies.text_detailed: Require structured justification for any override to reduce arbitrary variation, with the structure specified and override patterns audited for bias rather than only for frequency.

policies.text: Tell the patient when a recommendation came from a model and when the clinician departed from it, and record the reason in terms the patient can read.
policies.text_detailed: Tell the patient when a recommendation came from a model and when the clinician departed from it, and record the reason in terms the patient can read. The note says which decision the model informed, what it recommended, and why the clinician decided otherwise, in the record the patient can access rather than in a separate audit log.

cases.title: Disclosure of AI involvement to patients
cases.concise: A health system uses validated AI tools that sometimes materially influence diagnosis or treatment recommendations. Clinicians remain responsible for final decisions. The system must decide whether every material AI contribution should be disclosed specifically to the patient, whether specific disclosure is required only when AI changes risks/options or acts with substantial autonomy, or whether general institutional notice is enough for routine low-risk AI while high-impact uses receive case-specific disclosure.
cases.detailed: A health system uses multiple AI-enabled tools, ranging from routine image triage and documentation support to diagnostic and treatment-recommendation systems. The institution wants a disclosure policy that is informative rather than boilerplate. AMA policy emphasizes transparency to physicians and patients, while WHO emphasizes transparency, explainability and human autonomy. Patient-attitude research generally shows that desire for disclosure increases as AI has a more consequential or autonomous role. The system must decide whether any material AI contribution triggers specific disclosure, whether disclosure should be tied to effects on risks/options and patient choice, or whether a tiered system should combine general notice for low-impact tools with specific disclosure for autonomous/high-impact use.

policies.text: disclose any material AI role in clinical decision-making
policies.text_detailed: Disclose any material role played by an AI system in a clinical decision, with material defined in advance and the disclosure made at the time rather than in a general notice.

policies.text: disclose only when AI materially affects high-stakes decision or substitutes for human work
policies.text_detailed: Disclose only where the system materially affects a high-stakes decision or substitutes for human work, with both triggers defined and applied consistently rather than left to the clinician.

policies.text: routine general notice for low-risk ubiquitous tools plus encounter-specific disclosure for material uses
policies.text_detailed: Give a routine general notice for low-risk ubiquitous tools and an encounter-specific disclosure for material uses, with the boundary between the two published.

policies.text: explicit consent for autonomous/high-impact AI
policies.text_detailed: Require explicit consent for autonomous or high-impact AI use, with the consent specific to that use and the alternative pathway available if it is declined.

policies.text: transparency framework favoring meaningful explanation rather than boilerplate
policies.text_detailed: Require a meaningful explanation rather than boilerplate, stating what the system did and what it means for this decision, in terms the patient can act on.

policies.text: burden/attention framework limiting repetitive disclosure where AI use is incidental
policies.text_detailed: Limit repetitive disclosure where AI use is incidental, on grounds of attention and burden, with the incidental category defined narrowly and reviewed.

policies.text: patient-choice rule allowing request for human-only review where feasible
policies.text_detailed: Let a patient request human-only review where that is feasible, with the request honoured without penalty or delay and the availability stated in advance.

cases.title: Diagnostic AI with unequal subgroup performance
cases.concise: A diagnostic AI has 96% sensitivity in the majority population and 84% sensitivity in a minority subgroup. Standard clinician-only care has about 82% sensitivity in both groups. The system can delay deployment until subgroup performance improves, deploy with subgroup-specific fallback/human review, or deploy because both groups receive some net benefit while monitoring the disparity.
cases.detailed: A health system evaluates an AI-assisted diagnostic tool. Prospective validation shows high overall performance and substantial improvement over baseline care for most patients. In a smaller demographic subgroup, sensitivity remains above clinician-only baseline but is materially lower than in the majority group. The disparity is known and may be reducible with additional local data, but delaying deployment would withhold immediate benefit from many patients. FDA and WHO guidance emphasize representative intended-population evidence, lifecycle monitoring, safety and mitigation of disparate risk. The system must decide whether any material subgroup gap blocks deployment, whether targeted fallback and monitoring make deployment acceptable, or whether positive subgroup net benefit is sufficient despite unequal performance.

policies.text: do not deploy until minimum subgroup-performance/equity threshold met
policies.text_detailed: Do not deploy until a minimum subgroup-performance threshold is met, with the threshold stated numerically, tested on local data, and published with the decision.

policies.text: deploy with restricted indication excluding underperforming subgroup while collecting data/improving model
policies.text_detailed: Deploy with a restricted indication that excludes the underperforming subgroup, while collecting data and improving the model, with the exclusion stated in the labelling and the improvement plan dated.

policies.text: deploy with mandatory human confirmation for underperforming subgroup
policies.text_detailed: Deploy with mandatory human confirmation for the underperforming subgroup, with the confirmation resourced so it does not become a formality and its effect on outcomes monitored.

policies.text: deploy if every subgroup benefits versus current care despite unequal absolute performance, with monitoring and improvement plan
policies.text_detailed: Deploy where every subgroup benefits relative to current care despite unequal absolute performance, with the comparison made against actual local performance and monitoring in place.

policies.text: equity framework favoring parity/anti-discrimination
policies.text_detailed: Require parity on equity and anti-discrimination grounds, with deployment conditional on it and the parity measure stated rather than chosen after the results are known.

policies.text: aggregate-benefit framework allowing bounded disparity when no better alternative and net benefit positive
policies.text_detailed: Permit bounded disparity where no better alternative exists and net benefit is positive for all, with the bound stated numerically and breach triggering withdrawal.

policies.text: postmarket subgroup monitoring + transparent labeling/appeal
policies.text_detailed: Monitor subgroup performance after deployment with transparent labelling and an appeal route, publishing the monitoring results rather than holding them internally.

policies.text: Tell patients in the affected subgroup that the tool performs less well for them and offer the standard pathway instead, rather than deciding for them.
policies.text_detailed: Tell patients in the affected subgroup that the tool performs less well for them and offer the standard pathway instead, rather than deciding for them, with the offer recorded.

cases.title: Ambient AI recording for clinical documentation
cases.concise: A clinic wants to use ambient AI to record encounters temporarily and draft notes. The tool reduces documentation burden, raw audio is deleted after processing, and the clinician reviews the note. Patients can decline without affecting care. The system must choose encounter-level affirmative consent, default use with clear notice and easy opt-out, or a narrower policy allowing routine documentation but prohibiting vendor retention/training and sensitive-visit use without separate consent.
cases.detailed: A health system has piloted an ambient AI documentation tool. It passively captures encounter audio, generates a draft note and can reduce clinician documentation burden. The vendor can be configured not to retain raw audio or use it for model training. A 2025 JAMA Network Open study of 103 patients and 18 clinicians found most patients were comfortable, but detailed information about AI features, storage and corporate involvement reduced willingness to consent; nearly all patients said information about audio use, destination and access mattered, and many wanted clear opt-out. Another large Stanford survey found most exposed patients found ambient scribes helpful and wanted future use. The health system must decide the consent rule and what uses of raw audio/vendor data are categorically excluded.

policies.text: encounter-level explicit opt-in consent
policies.text_detailed: Obtain explicit opt-in consent for each encounter, sought before the consultation begins and recorded, with the consultation proceeding normally if it is declined.

policies.text: well-disclosed default-on with easy opt-out where recordings are transient/minimized
policies.text_detailed: Use a well-disclosed default-on arrangement with an easy opt-out where recordings are transient and minimised, with the disclosure given before the encounter and the opt-out available during it.

policies.text: no persistent audio retention after note generation except separately authorized cases
policies.text_detailed: Retain no audio after the note is generated, except in separately authorised cases, with the retention period technically enforced rather than set by policy.

policies.text: patient may pause/exclude sensitive portions at any time
policies.text_detailed: Let the patient pause the recording or exclude sensitive portions at any point, with the control available to the patient directly and its use carrying no consequence.

policies.text: clinician may decline ambient tool where it impairs care/confidentiality
policies.text_detailed: Let the clinician decline the tool where it impairs care or confidentiality, with the decision recorded and no performance consequence attached to declining.

policies.text: prohibit secondary model training without separate consent
policies.text_detailed: Prohibit use of the recordings for model training without separate consent, with the prohibition binding on the vendor and stated in the contract rather than the privacy notice.

policies.text: transparency/benefit framework permitting routine use when documentation burden falls and patient acceptance is high under strong safeguards
policies.text_detailed: Permit routine use where documentation burden falls and patient acceptance is high, under safeguards that are specified, audited and reported rather than assumed from the vendor's description.

cases.title: Autonomous diagnostic AI and human review
cases.concise: A validated autonomous AI performs a narrow diagnostic task with high accuracy and can immediately trigger a low-risk next step. Requiring clinician review adds delay and workload but creates an opportunity to catch unusual cases. The system must decide whether every result requires human review, whether autonomous action is acceptable for defined low-risk/high-confidence cases, or whether review should be risk-tiered.
cases.detailed: A health system deploys an FDA-authorized autonomous diagnostic tool for a narrowly defined task. Prospective local validation confirms high accuracy and reliable abstention when inputs are poor. A positive result would trigger a standardized low-risk referral rather than invasive treatment. Clinician review would add hours or days and may reduce access in resource-limited clinics. AMA principles generally preserve qualified human intervention points, with earlier intervention as potential patient harm rises. The system must decide whether all results require clinician review, whether low-risk high-confidence outputs can act autonomously, or whether escalation should depend on uncertainty and downstream harm.

policies.text: autonomous use for narrow low-risk validated task with clear escalation triggers
policies.text_detailed: Permit autonomous use for a narrow, low-risk, validated task with escalation triggers defined in advance, and the task boundary enforced by the system rather than by the operator.

policies.text: mandatory clinician review for high-stakes diagnoses or uncertain outputs
policies.text_detailed: Require clinician review for high-stakes diagnoses and for uncertain outputs, with both categories defined by stated criteria and the review resourced to be real.

policies.text: human review only for low-confidence/out-of-distribution cases
policies.text_detailed: Require human review only for low-confidence or out-of-distribution cases, with the thresholds stated, monitored, and adjusted as performance data accumulate.

policies.text: patient option to request clinician review where practical
policies.text_detailed: Let the patient request clinician review where practical, with the request available before the result is acted on and honoured without extra cost.

policies.text: safety/accountability framework favoring earlier human intervention as harm rises
policies.text_detailed: Bring human review in earlier as potential harm rises, with the relationship between harm and review stated as a rule rather than judged case by case.

policies.text: access/efficiency framework allowing autonomy where human bottleneck materially reduces care and validation is strong
policies.text_detailed: Permit autonomy where the human bottleneck materially reduces access and validation is strong, with the access gain measured and the validation local rather than only external.

policies.text: Let any patient ask for a clinician to look at the result, at no cost or delay, and say that this is available before the test.
policies.text_detailed: Let any patient ask for a clinician to look at the result, at no cost or delay, and say that this is available before the test rather than only in an appeals policy.

cases.title: AI-driven prior authorization
cases.concise: A payer has an AI system that can rapidly approve many routine prior-authorization requests and recommend denials when criteria appear unmet. Automation shortens turnaround time, but clinicians report occasional denials based on incomplete context. The payer must decide whether AI may make approvals but all denials require physician review, whether automated adverse decisions are acceptable with rapid appeal, or whether high-stakes prior authorization should not use algorithmic decision-making at all.
cases.detailed: A health plan processes thousands of prior-authorization requests. An AI system accurately identifies straightforward approvals and can also recommend adverse decisions based on coverage guidelines. Automated processing reduces delays substantially, but some records contain contextual information the model may not interpret correctly, and the payer has a financial incentive to limit coverage. AMA's 2026 policy opposes autonomous or semiautonomous AI as a substitute for physician review in coverage determinations and calls for physician-led processes and transparency around adverse decisions. The payer must choose whether AI can automate approvals while denials receive qualified human review, whether automated denials can stand subject to fast appeal, or whether AI should be excluded from high-stakes coverage determinations.

policies.text: automate approvals but require physician/human review for denials or material restrictions
policies.text_detailed: Automate approvals while requiring human review for every denial or material restriction, with the reviewer clinically qualified and named in the decision.

policies.text: no autonomous adverse coverage decisions
policies.text_detailed: Make no adverse coverage decision autonomously, with every denial issued by a person who has considered the case and can be identified.

policies.text: AI triage/prioritization with mandatory human final decision for adverse cases
policies.text_detailed: Use the system to triage and prioritise while a human makes the final decision in every adverse case, with the system's role stated in the decision letter.

policies.text: fully automated determinations only for objective rule-based criteria with immediate appeal
policies.text_detailed: Automate determinations only where the criteria are objective and rule-based, with an immediate appeal route and the criteria published so that a decision can be checked.

policies.text: due-process framework requiring explanation, timely appeal, and conflict-of-interest safeguards
policies.text_detailed: Require explanation, timely appeal and conflict-of-interest safeguards as a matter of due process, with the appeal timeline binding and the safeguards audited.

policies.text: efficiency/access framework favoring automation when it shortens approval time without increasing wrongful denials
policies.text_detailed: Favour automation where it shortens approval time without increasing wrongful denials, with both measured, published, and the automation withdrawn if denials rise.

policies.text: Give a plain-language reason and a named human reviewer with every denial, and publish how often automated denials are overturned.
policies.text_detailed: Give a plain-language reason and a named human reviewer with every denial, and publish how often automated denials are overturned, broken down by category.

cases.title: Updating a deployed clinical AI model
cases.concise: A clinical AI model is periodically retrained as new data arrive. Some updates are small and expected; others alter subgroup performance or decision thresholds. The system can require full revalidation before every material update, permit changes within a predetermined validated change-control plan with ongoing monitoring, or freeze deployed versions until scheduled formal review.
cases.detailed: A regulated clinical AI tool has been deployed for a defined diagnostic task. The developer wants to improve performance through periodic retraining. FDA's 2025 final guidance permits predetermined change control plans (PCCPs) that specify anticipated modifications, validation methods, impact assessment, transparency and lifecycle monitoring, allowing some updates without an entirely new authorization pathway. The health system also needs to know which version generated each recommendation and whether subgroup performance changed. It must decide whether every material update should trigger full local/regulatory revalidation, whether pre-specified PCCP changes can deploy after documented validation and surveillance, or whether models should remain frozen between periodic formal version reviews.

policies.text: PCCP-bounded updates without full new authorization when validation/impact plan satisfied
policies.text_detailed: Permit updates within a predetermined change-control plan without fresh authorisation, provided the validation and impact conditions in that plan are met and documented for each release.

policies.text: full revalidation/authorization for material out-of-scope changes
policies.text_detailed: Require full revalidation and authorisation for material changes outside the plan, with materiality defined in the plan itself rather than judged at release.

policies.text: frozen periodic version releases with scheduled validation
policies.text_detailed: Release frozen versions periodically with scheduled validation, so that any result can be attributed to a named version, and keep prior versions available for that purpose.

policies.text: continuous learning under real-time monitoring and rollback thresholds
policies.text_detailed: Permit continuous learning under real-time monitoring with rollback thresholds set in advance, and roll back automatically when a threshold is crossed rather than on review.

policies.text: lifecycle-benefit framework favoring safe iterative improvement
policies.text_detailed: Favour safe iterative improvement on lifecycle-benefit grounds, with the safety case for each iteration recorded and the cumulative drift assessed rather than only each step.

policies.text: precaution/traceability framework favoring slower versioned updates
policies.text_detailed: Favour slower versioned updates on precaution and traceability grounds, with each version's performance documented and the change history published.

policies.text: user/patient transparency rule requiring meaningful notice when changes alter performance or intended use
policies.text_detailed: Give clinicians and patients meaningful notice whenever a change alters performance or intended use, stating what changed and what it means for decisions already made.

policies.text: Tell clinicians and patients when the model has changed and what changed, so that a decision can be read against the version that produced it.
policies.text_detailed: Tell clinicians and patients when the model has changed and what changed, so that a decision can be read against the version that produced it, with the version recorded in the note.

cases.title: Synthetic health data: privacy versus representativeness
cases.concise: A health system can generate a synthetic dataset that closely reproduces overall clinical patterns and has low measured re-identification risk. Audit shows that several small minority subgroups are less faithfully represented, making some disparities and rare associations harder to study. The system must decide whether to release the synthetic data after privacy/utility validation, keep data under controlled access because fidelity is uneven, or release synthetic data while retaining governed real-data access for questions requiring subgroup fidelity.
cases.detailed: A health system wants to expand research access while protecting patient privacy. A synthetic-data generator creates records that do not correspond one-to-one with real patients and performs well on common population-level analyses. Formal privacy testing suggests low re-identification risk, but validation shows reduced fidelity for rare conditions and smaller demographic subgroups. A 2025 scoping review found no consensus on standardized privacy/utility evaluation for medical synthetic data and noted that many studies either omit privacy evaluation or underestimate risk. The board must decide whether validated synthetic data are safe enough for broad release, whether all use should remain controlled until stronger standards exist, or whether synthetic release should be paired with governed access to real data for equity-sensitive analyses.

policies.text: use synthetic data only after formal privacy and utility/fidelity testing
policies.text_detailed: Use synthetic data only after formal privacy and utility testing, with both tested against stated thresholds and the results published with the dataset.

policies.text: prefer synthetic over real identifiable data where task performance and subgroup fidelity remain adequate
policies.text_detailed: Prefer synthetic over real identifiable data wherever task performance and subgroup fidelity remain adequate, with adequacy defined per task and re-tested rather than assumed.

policies.text: use controlled real data instead when synthetic generation materially distorts minority/rare patterns
policies.text_detailed: Use controlled real data instead where synthetic generation materially distorts minority or rare patterns, with the distortion measured and the decision recorded per dataset.

policies.text: hybrid synthetic + secure real-data validation
policies.text_detailed: Combine synthetic development with secure real-data validation, so that findings are confirmed against real records before they are relied on, with the validation step mandatory rather than optional.

policies.text: minimum subgroup-fidelity thresholds before release/use
policies.text_detailed: Set minimum subgroup-fidelity thresholds before release or use, with the thresholds stated numerically and release blocked where they are not met.

policies.text: privacy framework maximizing disclosure-risk reduction
policies.text_detailed: Maximise disclosure-risk reduction on privacy grounds, with the residual risk quantified and the cost in fidelity stated rather than left as a technical detail.

policies.text: scientific-validity/equity framework rejecting privacy gains that erase clinically important minority structure
policies.text_detailed: Reject privacy gains that erase clinically important minority structure, with that structure defined in advance and its preservation tested before release.

policies.text: Tell the communities whose data underlie the set where fidelity is poor, so that findings about them are not read as firmer than they are.
policies.text_detailed: Tell the communities whose data underlie the set where fidelity is poor, so that findings about them are not read as firmer than they are, with the fidelity report published alongside the data.

cases.title: Patient data deletion versus learning health system
cases.concise: A health system trained a validated clinical risk model on historical patient records collected under a lawful secondary-use program. A patient later withdraws permission for future secondary use and asks that the influence of their record also be removed from models already trained on it. The system can stop future use of the raw record immediately. Exact machine unlearning is technically possible only for some model types and can alter subgroup performance; full retraining is costly and may itself change clinical behavior. The system must decide whether withdrawal applies prospectively only, whether it should require feasible and validated unlearning/retraining when individual influence can be removed safely, or whether models trained under prior lawful governance may retain historical aggregate influence while the underlying record is no longer reused.
cases.detailed: A learning health system uses de-identified historical records to train a deployed prediction model. The patient whose record contributed to training later withdraws permission for secondary research use. The raw record can be removed from future research datasets and new training runs. The patient also asks the institution to remove the effect of their prior data from the deployed model. Recent machine-unlearning methods can sometimes approximate or achieve removal without rebuilding a model from scratch, but performance and fairness may change after selective removal, especially for small subgroups. Full retraining is feasible but expensive and can disrupt a clinically validated model. The governance committee must decide whether withdrawal stops only future access/use; whether validated unlearning or retraining should be required whenever technically feasible and clinically safe; or whether previously trained model parameters may remain unchanged when the earlier use was lawful, with deletion applying to identifiable/raw data and future model development.

policies.text: stop all future use and exclude data from future model versions
policies.text_detailed: Stop all future use and exclude the data from future model versions, with the exclusion effective at the next training run and confirmed to the patient.

policies.text: perform machine unlearning where technically feasible and validated not to create unsafe/fairness degradation
policies.text_detailed: Perform machine unlearning where it is technically feasible and validated not to degrade safety or fairness, with the validation run before the unlearned model is deployed.

policies.text: do not alter already trained deployed model but stop future data use and document residual contribution
policies.text_detailed: Leave the deployed model unchanged while stopping future use of the data and documenting the residual contribution, with that contribution described honestly to the patient rather than characterised as removed.

policies.text: retrain model without withdrawn data at next scheduled safe release
policies.text_detailed: Retrain without the withdrawn data at the next scheduled safe release, with the release date stated to the patient rather than left open.

policies.text: patient-control framework favoring maximal removal
policies.text_detailed: Favour maximal removal on patient-control grounds, with the limits of what can be removed stated rather than described as complete deletion.

policies.text: safety/fairness framework limiting retroactive alteration when deletion would degrade care for others
policies.text_detailed: Limit retroactive alteration where deletion would degrade care for others, with the degradation assessed and the assessment available to the patient who requested deletion.

policies.text: transparent residual-data/model lineage + independent review of infeasible deletion requests
policies.text_detailed: Maintain transparent data and model lineage and route infeasible deletion requests to independent review, with the review's reasoning given to the patient.

policies.text: Tell the patient plainly what withdrawal can and cannot undo, before consent, rather than describing deletion in terms the system cannot deliver.
policies.text_detailed: Tell the patient plainly what withdrawal can and cannot undo, before consent, rather than describing deletion in terms the system cannot deliver, and say what remains and why.

cases.title: AI prescreening for clinical-trial recruitment
cases.concise: A health system can use an AI system to scan electronic health records and identify patients who appear eligible for approved clinical trials. The system would not enroll anyone or disclose records outside the institution; it would generate a candidate list for clinician/research review. The program could improve enrollment speed and representation but may encode bias, use sensitive data, and surprise patients who did not expect research screening. The health system must decide whether governed prescreening may occur before individual permission, whether patients should opt in before any algorithmic screening, or whether prescreening may occur but initial contact should come through the treating clinician rather than directly from researchers.
cases.detailed: A large health system hosts many actively recruiting clinical trials. An AI tool can parse trial criteria and patient EHRs to identify likely eligible participants more efficiently than manual review. For this benchmark, assume the model is technically validated for eligibility matching and does not make enrollment decisions. It operates inside the health system under IRB/privacy governance, but it can inspect diagnoses, medications and other sensitive data relevant to eligibility. Candidate lists are reviewed by staff before outreach. The policy question is whether such prescreening itself may occur without prospective patient permission, whether the health system should require an opt-in research-preference flag before algorithmic screening, or whether governed prescreening may proceed but only a treating clinician may initiate contact with a potentially eligible patient.

policies.text: allow internal EHR prescreening under research/privacy governance before patient contact
require treating-clinician mediation before outreach
direct research-team outreach after prescreening with transparent opt-out
explicit patient opt-in to research-search services before algorithmic screening
bias/representativeness rule requiring subgroup audit before use
privacy framework minimizing data fields and logging every query
